title: YingLan: A Multimodal Ocean Foundation Model for Unified Representation Learning from Heterogeneous Observations
abstract: Multimodal ocean modeling remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in data structures, physical semantics, and spatiotemporal characteristics across satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy observations. Existing approaches largely focus on task-specific ocean modeling, while learning transferable representations from heterogeneous observations remains an open problem. To address this challenge, we propose YingLan, a multimodal ocean foundation model that integrates physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding, Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining. Specifically, the dynamic encoding mechanism generates adaptive input projections conditioned on physical semantics and observation characteristics, enabling flexible representation of heterogeneous ocean variables. STIC models multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies through cross-scale interactions of latent temporal increments. The pretraining strategy further combines masked observation reconstruction with temporal evolution objectives to facilitate the learning of coherent ocean-state representations across different prediction horizons. YingLan is implemented using MindSpore and trained on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs, demonstrating its compatibility with domestic AI computing infrastructure. In a seven-day sea surface salinity (SSS) forecasting task conducted in the Shenzhen coastal waters, YingLan achieves an average RMSE of 0.687508 PSU, corresponding to relative error reductions of 0.58%, 5.31%, and 12.42% compared with LangYa, XiHe, and GloNet2, respectively. These results provide initial evidence of the model's effectiveness in regional ocean forecasting, while broader cross-task and cross-regional evaluations remain necessary to assess its generalization capabilities.

Abstract

Multimodal ocean modeling remains challenging due to
substantial heterogeneity in data structures, physical
semantics, and spatiotemporal characteristics across
satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and
buoy observations. Existing approaches largely focus
on task-specific ocean modeling, while learning
transferable representations from heterogeneous
observations remains an open problem.
To address this challenge, we propose YingLan,
a multimodal ocean foundation model that integrates
physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding,
Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and
ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining.
Specifically, the dynamic encoding mechanism generates
adaptive input projections conditioned on physical
semantics and observation characteristics, enabling
flexible representation of heterogeneous ocean variables.
STIC models multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies
through cross-scale interactions of latent temporal
increments. The pretraining strategy further combines
masked observation reconstruction with temporal
evolution objectives to facilitate the learning of
coherent ocean-state representations across different
prediction horizons.
YingLan is implemented using MindSpore and trained
on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs, demonstrating its
compatibility with domestic AI computing infrastructure.
In a seven-day sea surface salinity (SSS) forecasting
task conducted in the Shenzhen coastal waters,
YingLan achieves an average RMSE of 0.687508 PSU,
corresponding to relative error reductions of
0.58%, 5.31%, and 12.42% compared with LangYa,
XiHe, and GloNet2, respectively.
These results provide initial evidence of the model’s
effectiveness in regional ocean forecasting, while
broader cross-task and cross-regional evaluations
remain necessary to assess its generalization
capabilities.

Keywords:
Ocean foundation model;
Multimodal representation learning;
Indigenous deployment;
Downstream task adaptation;
Self-supervised pretraining

## 1 Introduction

Accurate characterization and prediction of the marine environment are fundamental to oceanographic research and marine environmental monitoring, with important implications for marine ecosystem conservation, marine resource management, and ocean hazard early warning [1]. Advances in satellite remote sensing, ocean numerical modeling, and in situ observation technologies have expanded the spatial coverage, temporal resolution, and range of physical variables represented in multi-source ocean observation data, providing an essential basis for multiscale characterization and dynamic analysis of the marine environment [2]. Specifically, satellite imagery captures the spatial distribution of ocean surface conditions, oceanographic products provide spatiotemporal information on variables such as temperature, salinity, and ocean currents, and in situ observations from buoys and other platforms record continuous variations in local marine conditions [3]. These observation sources are complementary in terms of spatial coverage, temporal sampling, and physical information. However, substantial differences in data structure, variable semantics, and spatiotemporal scales pose challenges to joint modeling of heterogeneous observations and knowledge transfer across downstream tasks. Consequently, large-scale pretraining on heterogeneous ocean observations to learn generalizable representations with cross-modal adaptability and spatiotemporal generalization has emerged as a promising research direction in ocean intelligence [4].

In recent years, deep learning has made substantial progress in ocean environmental forecasting and the development of ocean foundation models. For spatiotemporal ocean modeling, XiHe employs local and global spatial interactions to perform high-resolution [5], multivariate global ocean forecasting, whereas WenHai integrates air-sea flux computation with ocean-dynamics-informed network design, highlighting the importance of spatial dependency modeling and the incorporation of domain knowledge in ocean prediction [6]. In the development of foundation models, AI-GOMS explores a pretraining and downstream adaptation paradigm for multiple ocean-related tasks, demonstrating the potential of shared representations to support diverse applications [7]. Meanwhile, ocean remote sensing research has increasingly investigated the joint use of complementary observations during pretraining. The Sentinel-3 ocean-colour foundation model jointly pretrains on ocean-colour reflectance and sea surface temperature through masked modeling and evaluates the resulting representations on ocean-colour-related tasks [8]. OceanMAE combines multispectral imagery with auxiliary ocean descriptors for self-supervised reconstruction and assesses the transferability of its learned representations on ocean segmentation and bathymetry regression [9]. Despite these advances in ocean forecasting, multi-source information utilization, and domain-specific pretraining, differences in the physical attributes, spatiotemporal scales, and temporal dynamics of heterogeneous observations continue to pose challenges for unified representation learning and joint modeling. Effectively encoding heterogeneous ocean observations, characterizing dependencies across spatial scales and temporal horizons, and learning ocean-state evolution through pretraining remain important open research questions for multimodal ocean foundation models.

Despite the progress of existing studies, developing multimodal foundation models that jointly leverage satellite imagery, oceanographic fields, and buoy observations remains challenging in terms of heterogeneous representation learning, multiscale spatiotemporal modeling, and the learning of ocean-state dynamics. First, these observation types differ substantially in data structure, physical semantics, and sampling characteristics [10, 11]. Satellite imagery primarily captures the spatial distribution and textural characteristics of ocean surface conditions, oceanographic fields describe the spatial structures of variables such as temperature, salinity, and current velocity, while buoy observations record localized temporal variations at specific locations. Fixed input representations may not adequately accommodate these differences in observational attributes [12, 13], potentially limiting the effective utilization of heterogeneous information within a shared representation space. Second, marine environments exhibit multiscale spatiotemporal variability, in which local spatial structures, broader environmental contexts, and temporal variations over different horizons are interrelated. Single-scale feature extraction may therefore be insufficient to characterize these complex dependencies. Furthermore, pretraining based solely on reconstructing observed data does not necessarily encourage models to learn ocean-state evolution patterns that are predictive of future conditions [14]. Consequently, further research is needed to develop transferable multimodal ocean foundation models that effectively represent heterogeneous observations, capture multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies, and learn the temporal evolution of ocean states through pretraining.

To address these challenges, we propose YingLan, a multimodal
ocean foundation model for unified representation learning from
heterogeneous ocean observations, including satellite imagery, gridded
oceanographic fields, and buoy time series. YingLan integrates
physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding, multiscale spatiotemporal
interaction, and ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining to learn
transferable representations of ocean states across heterogeneous
observation types and temporal scales. The main contributions of this
work are summarized as follows:

• 

A multimodal foundation model for heterogeneous ocean
observations.
We develop a unified modeling framework that accommodates satellite
imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy time series, providing
a shared representation space for heterogeneous ocean observations
and supporting adaptation to diverse regional ocean monitoring and
forecasting tasks.

• 

Physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding.
We introduce a dynamic encoding mechanism that jointly incorporates
physical semantics and observation conditions into input projection
parameter generation. By distinguishing variable-specific physical
attributes from observation-specific characteristics, the proposed
mechanism enables adaptive encoding of heterogeneous ocean
observations.

• 

Multiscale spatiotemporal interaction and evolution-aware
pretraining.
We propose a Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC) module that
facilitates cross-scale information exchange through latent temporal
increments, enabling interactions between localized ocean structures
and large-scale environmental contexts. We further develop an
ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining strategy that jointly
optimizes masked observation reconstruction, horizon-conditioned
latent increment prediction, and temporal compositional consistency
to learn temporally coherent representations of ocean-state dynamics.

• 

Evaluation of regional transferability and
generalization.
We investigate the transferability of YingLan in regional ocean
applications, using Shenzhen coastal waters as a case study.
Through downstream forecasting and, where supported by the
experimental design, few-shot adaptation, cross-temporal evaluation,
and cross-region transfer, we assess the model’s predictive
performance and generalization under varying data availability
and spatiotemporal conditions.

## 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Ocean Foundation Models and Pretraining Paradigms

Existing deep learning studies on ocean modeling have primarily focused on ocean state estimation and evolution forecasting, aiming to characterize ocean physical processes and their spatiotemporal variability through data-driven approaches. Eeltink et al. [15] proposed a hybrid approach that integrates recurrent neural networks with a nonlinear wave evolution model, learning data-driven correction terms to represent wave-breaking processes and illustrating the integration of physical models with neural networks for ocean dynamics modeling. Ham et al. [16] proposed a global ocean data assimilation framework based on partial convolutions and generative adversarial learning, reconstructing ocean states by incorporating observational information and improving the handling of incomplete ocean observations. Furthermore, Cui et al. [6] introduced WenHai, which employs a Swin Transformer-based architecture to model multivariate ocean state evolution and incorporates air–sea flux information and multi-step forecasting strategies. These studies advance ocean deep learning from complementary perspectives, including physical process modeling, ocean state reconstruction, and spatiotemporal forecasting. Nevertheless, their training objectives remain primarily tied to specific ocean variables and predefined estimation or forecasting tasks, motivating the exploration of pretrained representations that can be transferred across diverse ocean applications.

Recent ocean foundation models have explored diverse pretraining strategies tailored to different types of ocean data. Xiong et al. [7] proposed AI-GOMS, which learns ocean-state representations from HYCOM reanalysis fields through Fourier-based masked autoencoding and supports downstream adaptation across ocean modeling tasks. Glaser et al. [17] introduced WV-Net, using contrastive self-supervised learning on large-scale Sentinel-1 SAR imagery to obtain transferable representations for ocean remote sensing. Complementarily, Bi et al. [18] developed OceanGPT through ocean-science corpus pretraining and domain-specific instruction tuning, while Xue et al. [19] introduced OceanPile, a multimodal ocean-science corpus designed to support foundation model training across marine imagery, sonar data, and scientific text. These studies span physical-field pretraining, image-based representation learning, and language-oriented ocean knowledge modeling, illustrating the diversity of data and objectives in ocean-domain pretraining. However, their learning frameworks address different data modalities and task requirements, leaving the unified representation of heterogeneous ocean observations an important direction for further investigation.

## 2.2 Heterogeneous Ocean Representation and Multiscale Spatiotemporal Learning

Ocean observations differ in their spatial resolution, sampling characteristics, and physical information, motivating the development of methods that can effectively integrate complementary data sources. Thiria et al. combined sea surface height (SSH) and sea surface temperature (SST) observations to reconstruct mesoscale ocean currents through CNN-based downscaling [20]. Wang et al. proposed ODF-Net, which fuses in situ measurements, satellite observations, and three-dimensional model and reanalysis data to reconstruct ocean temperature fields [21]. Champenois and Sapsis developed a machine learning framework that combines historical reanalysis with real-time satellite and buoy measurements for regional four-dimensional ocean temperature reconstruction [22]. Under sparse observation conditions, Lei et al. investigated multimodal fusion-based spatiotemporal incremental learning for ocean environment perception [23]. Collectively, these studies explore ocean data fusion through spatial downscaling, multi-source field reconstruction, and multimodal spatiotemporal learning.

Existing ocean spatiotemporal modeling methods primarily employ hierarchical feature extraction, attention mechanisms, and multiscale feature fusion to characterize spatial dependencies and temporal variations in ocean variables. Zhao et al. proposed HSSSA, a hierarchical encoder-decoder network that integrates spatial and temporal self-attention for multiscale SST forecasting [24]. Bai et al. developed MUSTAN, which progressively fuses features across spatial scales and applies spatial and temporal attention to predict SST variations [25]. Pan et al. introduced an effective attention model for global SST prediction at daily and monthly temporal resolutions, explicitly modeling spatiotemporal correlations in historical observations [26]. Tao et al. investigated multiscale spatial features and temporal attention for El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) prediction, demonstrating the use of these mechanisms in modeling large-scale ocean variability [27]. These studies illustrate complementary architectural strategies for capturing ocean dynamics across spatial scales, temporal horizons, and physical processes.

## 3 Method

## 3.1 Overall Architecture

We propose YingLan, a multimodal ocean foundation model designed for unified representation learning from heterogeneous ocean observations. The overall architecture is illustrated in Fig. 1. YingLan leverages large-scale satellite remote sensing imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy time-series observations to address heterogeneity in physical semantics, data structures, and spatiotemporal resolutions across diverse observational sources. The model aims to learn generalizable ocean representations that capture both shared cross-modal information and ocean-specific spatiotemporal dynamics. Its architecture comprises three core components: Physics-Attribute-Conditioned Dynamic Encoding, Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and Ocean-State Evolution-Aware Pretraining.

Figure 1: Overall architecture of YingLan.

YingLan first employs Physics-Attribute-Conditioned Dynamic Encoding to construct adaptive feature projections conditioned on the physical semantics and observational characteristics of individual variables. Modality-specific input adapters are used to map ocean observations with different data structures into a shared feature space. The resulting representations are subsequently processed by the STIC module, which integrates multiscale spatial representations with scale-specific temporal modeling. By coupling latent temporal increments across spatial scales, STIC captures dynamic interactions between local ocean structures and large-scale environmental contexts, producing unified spatiotemporal representations.

During pretraining, YingLan jointly optimizes masked observation reconstruction, horizon-conditioned latent increment prediction, and temporal compositional consistency. These complementary objectives enable the model to capture structural dependencies among heterogeneous observations while learning ocean-state variations across multiple temporal horizons. Following pretraining, the shared encoder is adapted to regional ocean monitoring and prediction tasks through task-specific prediction heads and parameter fine-tuning, allowing the transferability of YingLan’s pretrained representations to be evaluated in regional marine environments.

## 3.2 Physics-Attribute-Conditioned Dynamic Encoding

Satellite imagery, oceanographic fields, and buoy observations characterize the marine environment from different observational perspectives. Their heterogeneity arises not only from differences in data structures and sampling schemes, but also from the complex relationships between physical-variable semantics and observation mechanisms. Observations from different sources may represent the same physical variable under different measurement conditions, whereas a single observation platform may provide measurements with distinct physical meanings. Therefore, effective multimodal representation learning requires more than mapping heterogeneous inputs into a common feature space; the encoding process must explicitly capture the relationships between physical semantics and observation conditions.

conclusion: This work investigates unified representation learning from heterogeneous ocean observations and presents YingLan as a multimodal foundation model for ocean environmental modeling. By incorporating physical semantics and observation conditions into adaptive feature encoding, YingLan provides a flexible representation mechanism for ocean variables with diverse observational characteristics. Its multiscale spatiotemporal architecture further integrates temporal variations across spatial hierarchies, while the joint pretraining objectives encourage the learning of both observational structures and ocean-state dynamics. These designs establish a unified modeling framework for integrating satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy time-series observations. To evaluate its applicability to regional ocean forecasting, we conduct a downstream seven-day sea surface salinity (SSS) forecasting task in the Shenzhen coastal waters. YingLan achieves an average RMSE of 0.687508 PSU, yielding the lowest reported error among the evaluated methods. Beyond predictive performance, YingLan is implemented using MindSpore and trained on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs, demonstrating the feasibility of developing and training multimodal ocean foundation models within a domestic AI computing environment. Overall, this study provides a methodological basis for learning transferable ocean representations while supporting the development of ocean intelligence models on domestic computing infrastructure. Future research will investigate broader downstream task adaptation, cross-regional generalization, and robust modeling under incomplete and heterogeneous ocean observations.

title: When Are We Near Nash? Certifying Solutions in General-Sum Games
abstract: Heuristic solvers for general-sum extensive-form games produce a stream of iterates, and practice reports the NashGap of the returned profile. We ask what a solver can know about its own iterates from the regret accumulators and the terminal-distribution accumulators its updates already maintain. In two-player games the NashGap of a weighted average strategy equals, at the maximizing player, the weighted external regret plus a signed value correction. Bounding the regret by the running counterfactual-regret accumulator gives an online certificate whose cost per checkpoint is linear in the number of terminal histories. The certificate stays sound under alternating updates and in games with three or more players. The mismatch between what alternation evaluates and what the averages record enters as one signed comparator term, maximized in a single backward pass per player whose comparator weight is nonzero. The bound is read off the regret state, with no best response against the average. Run a portfolio of training-free regret-matching solvers, output the iterate with the smallest certificate, and verify that iterate once. On the benchmark's biased Leduc family a pool of sixteen training-free solvers, seven original and nine recent variants, solves $89\%$ of the $64$ instances at threshold $10^{-5}$ this way, matching the trajectory-minimum union of the solvers. The same protocol solves $92\%$ of the $64$ pre-registered held-out instances and $89\%$ again on a third set of $64$ instances that no earlier stage used. The zero-best-response certificate certifies all $57$ in-sample solves and all $57$ fresh ones, and $58$ of the $59$ held-out ones. Its exact-comparator refinement certifies every solve in the three sets. The certificate states both and attributes its bound. Code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/CertNE.

headings: 4. The Oracle Gap in Trajectory-Minimum Evaluation
5. Online Certificates from an Exact Decomposition

Abstract

Heuristic solvers for general-sum extensive-form games produce a stream of
iterates, and practice reports the NashGap of the returned profile.
A recent meta-learning benchmark reports the lowest NashGap along the
training trajectory, located by exact evaluation at every checkpoint, without
stating the selection rule or the evaluation budget behind that number. We ask
what a solver can know about its own iterates from the regret accumulators and
the terminal-distribution accumulators its updates already maintain.
In two-player games the NashGap of a weighted average strategy
equals, at the maximizing player, the weighted external regret plus a
signed value correction.
Bounding the regret by
the running counterfactual-regret accumulator gives an online certificate
whose cost per checkpoint is linear in the number of terminal histories.
The certificate stays sound under alternating updates and in games with three
or more players. The mismatch between what
alternation evaluates and what the averages record enters as one signed
comparator term, maximized in a single backward pass per player whose
comparator weight is nonzero. The bound is
read off the regret state, with no best response against the average. Run a
portfolio of training-free regret-matching solvers, output the iterate with the
smallest certificate, and verify that iterate once.
On the benchmark’s biased Leduc family a pool of sixteen training-free solvers,
seven original and nine recent variants, solves $89\%$ of the $64$ instances
at threshold $10^{-5}$ this way, matching the trajectory-minimum union of the
solvers. The same protocol solves $92\%$ of the $64$ pre-registered held-out
instances and $89\%$ again on a third set of $64$ instances that no earlier
stage used. The zero-best-response certificate certifies all $57$ in-sample
solves and all $57$ fresh ones, and $58$ of the $59$ held-out ones. Its
exact-comparator refinement certifies every solve in the three sets. At the
selected iterate the refinement tracks the true gap within a median factor of
 $1.4$ over the $36$ instances whose selected gap is above $10^{-12}$ . The
meta-trained method reports $96\%$ under the trajectory-minimum protocol.
That protocol leaves its selection rule and evaluation budget unstated. The
certificate states both and attributes its bound. Code is available at
https://github.com/lbn187/CertNE.

## 1. Introduction

Computing a Nash equilibrium of a general-sum game to precision
inverse-polynomial in the game size is PPAD-complete (Polynomial Parity
Arguments on Directed graphs), for two players
(Chen et al., 2009) and for three or more players
(Daskalakis et al., 2009). The no-regret dynamics
that solve two-player zero-sum games at scale
(Zinkevich et al., 2007; Tammelin, 2014; Li and Huang, 2026d; Li and Huang, 2026f)
guarantee only
coarse correlated equilibria in general (Anagnostides et al., 2022). Practice
therefore runs heuristic solvers and judges them afterwards by their
NashGap, the largest gain any player could obtain by deviating alone
(Lisỳ and Bowling, 2017; Davis et al., 2014).

Computing that gap exactly costs one best-response pass per player over the
game tree, the same order as one iteration for a tabular solver
(Table 4). The certificate below builds a bound from the
solver’s own regret state, without a best response. Under aligned two-player
play, where every accumulator refers to the same start-of-round profile, an
exact evaluator that also records the running realized value recovers the
same regret and value terms from its best-response values. Under alternation,
or with three or more players, the certificate adds a comparator term, the
signed functional of Section 5, which an exact evaluator
does not compute. With that term the raw regret state is a bound again.

A recent benchmark shows why the scoring protocol matters. Neural predictive
counterfactual regret minimization+ (NPCFR+)
(Sychrovský et al., 2026) meta-learns a predictive bias. On
biased two-player Leduc games it reports solving $96\%$ of instances to
NashGap $10^{-5}$ ; its untrained counterpart PCFR+ reports $16\%$ . The
metric is the lowest NashGap along the training trajectory, located
by exact evaluation at roughly $19$ checkpoints over $2^{18}$ iterations. The
reported number is therefore the output of a selection rule, the argmin of
the exact gap, and an evaluation budget of one gap per checkpoint. Neither
is part of the method or stated with the result
(Section 4). The quantity the same paper proposes for
bounding the gap without a best response combines a regret term with a
Pinsker-type correlation term. It is the natural candidate for such a rule,
and we find it sits three orders of magnitude above the true gap and grows.

We give an online NashGap certificate computed from the regret accumulators
and the terminal accumulators, together with an
account of which quantities the gap actually depends on. In two-player
games the correlation term is avoidable. The comparator term is
exact by bilinearity, and the value term becomes exact once the
distribution exchange is replaced by directly measurable quantities. The
inequality therefore becomes an identity (Theorem 4).
The NashGap of the weighted average strategy equals the weighted
external regret plus a signed value correction. Bounding the regret by the
running counterfactual-regret accumulator (Lemma 1)
gives a certificate whose per-checkpoint cost is linear in the number of
terminal histories.

The strongest solvers update players in alternation
(Tammelin, 2014; Brown and Sandholm, 2019; Burch et al., 2019). The regrets they
evaluate then refer to a partially updated opponent, while the averages
record the start-of-round profile. A second regret pass per iteration is
the usual remedy. The mismatch itself is one more measurable comparator
term, a signed linear functional maximized in one backward pass per player
with nonzero comparator weight, so no second regret pass is needed. The
certificate is therefore sound for any update
order and any number of players (Proposition 9). In
games with three or more players the same term is the coalition imbalance
that the correlation level is structurally blind to
(Remark 7). No bound on the coalition term vanishes with
the correlation level, so the Pinsker-type route fails beyond two players;
the comparator term measures it directly. The
certificate splits its bound into a regret term, a value correction and
comparator terms (Table 5).

The certificate turns the post-hoc protocol into an algorithm
(Figure 1). Run a portfolio of training-free
regret-matching solvers, weighted, predictive, discounted, scheduled and
stabilised variants
(Tammelin, 2014; Farina et al., 2021; Brown and Sandholm, 2019; Xu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026; Farina et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025),
and record the certificate at every checkpoint of every solver. Output the
iterate with the smallest certificate, so the selection rule and its budget
are explicit. The zero-best-response certificate ( $C^{0}$ ) reads accumulators
alone, and its exact-comparator refinement ( $C^{1}$ ) adds one signed backward
pass per player with nonzero comparator weight at each checkpoint. On biased
Leduc this is a single pass, costing about as much wall-clock as an exact gap
evaluation and less than one training iteration. The selected iterate can be
verified exactly in one further gap evaluation (Corollary 10).

Figure 1: Two selection protocols on the same $K$ solvers and $m$ 
checkpoints per solver. a, Exact evaluation scores every candidate
with $n$ best-response (BR) passes, costing $Kmn$ passes overall, and
outputs the minimum-gap strategy with its exact gap.
b, Online certification combines signed regret, value correction,
and comparator terms (Proposition 9). $C^{0}$ uses
accumulators alone; $C^{1}$ adds one signed backward pass per player with
nonzero comparator weight at each checkpoint. Either certificate selects
its own argmin across solvers and checkpoints and bounds the selected
strategy’s NashGap. Optional verification evaluates only that strategy,
with $n$ BR passes (Corollary 10). Nodes, trees and policy
glyphs are schematic; arrows on trees indicate backward traversal.

On the benchmarks of Sychrovský et al. (2026) this protocol
matches the trajectory-minimum rule with no exact-gap query during
selection; the cost it does pay is the accumulator bookkeeping
(Table 4). On biased
Leduc ( $64$ instances), certificate selection over sixteen training-free
solvers solves $89\%$ of instances at threshold $10^{-5}$ , the same fraction
as the trajectory-minimum union over the same solvers. The seven original
solvers alone reach $84\%$ , and the sixteen-solver
pool, extended by nine recent variants in a second pre-registered stage,
reaches $92\%$ on $64$ held-out instances. On a third instance set that no earlier stage
used, the protocol repeats at $89\%$ ( $57/64$ ).

The certificate itself is below the threshold on every in-sample solve, for
 $C^{0}$ read off accumulators alone and for $C^{1}$ with one signed backward
pass per checkpoint. Across the three sets $C^{1}$ certifies every solve, and
 $C^{0}$ all but one held-out solve. At the selected iterate $C^{1}$ is within a
median $1.4\times$ of the true gap over the $36$ instances whose selected gap
is above $10^{-12}$ . The aligned start-of-round certificate pays an extra
regret pass per player per iteration yet is looser ( $1.9\times$ ) and
certifies $86\%$ . On the single deterministic three-player Leduc game,
PDCFR+ reaches NashGap $1.17\times 10^{-6}$ while the certificate-selected
HS-PCFR+ run is certified at $2.83\times 10^{-6}$ , both below the reported
 $10^{-3}$ NPCFR+ comparator. Under our protocol the training-free
portfolio reaches $0.89$ against the reported $0.96$ . The certificate is
solver-agnostic and attaches to NPCFR+ or any other update sequence
unchanged. Our $7$ in-sample failures cluster in games with a low
tie-refund fraction (Section 7).

Our contributions are:

• 

Theory. We prove that in two-player games the NashGap of a
weighted average equals its weighted external regret plus a
signed value correction, an identity, not a bound
(Theorem 4). We build from it an online certificate whose
zero-best-response form reads accumulators alone and whose exact form
costs one signed backward pass per player with nonzero comparator
weight, sound for any update order and player count
(Proposition 9). We show that in games with three or
more players no correlation level controls the comparator term
(Remark 7), and the certificate measures it
directly. One exact gap evaluation verifies the selected iterate
(Corollary 10).

• 

Algorithm. We turn the certificate into the selection
rule: score every checkpoint of every solver, output the argmin, and
report the candidate with a stated budget and no exact-gap query
during selection. The argmin comes from accumulators alone under
 $C^{0}$ ; under $C^{1}$ it costs one signed backward pass per player with
nonzero comparator weight.

• 

Re-evaluation under a stated selection rule. On the NPCFR
benchmarks, we show that training-free certificate selection reaches
 $89\%$ in-sample, matching the trajectory-minimum union over the same
solvers, $92\%$ held-out and $89\%$ on a third, never-used set,
against the reported meta-trained $96\%$ . $C^{1}$ certifies every solve
in all three sets, and $C^{0}$ certifies all but one held-out solve.
The residual in-sample failures show the same lean.

## 2. Related Work

Meta-learning and steering.
Learning-not-to-regret meta-learns regret-minimizer internals for faster
convergence (Sychrovskỳ et al., 2024), following the general
meta-learning-in-games program of Harris et al. (2023). NPCFR
(Sychrovský et al., 2026) redirects this machinery at
general-sum Nash approximation by meta-learning a predictive bias, and is
the reference point for our re-evaluation;
Sychrovský et al. (2025) extends the line to self-play. An
alternative channel steers no-regret learners toward equilibria through
external payments (Zhang et al., 2024). Our core methods RM+ and
PRM+ are standard training-free algorithms; DPRM+ is also training-free
but modifies the PRM+ prediction with an analytic decorrelation term.
The portfolio-level selection among their iterates is new.

Certificates and gap evaluation.
Theorem 1 of Sychrovský et al. (2026) bounds the NashGap by a
regret term plus a term in the extensive-form marginalizability of the
empirical play distribution, via a Pinsker-type inequality, and states it
as an analysis tool. Our
Proposition 3 is its weighted-averaging analogue, and
Theorem 4 removes the distribution inequality entirely in
the two-player case. Outside these structural certificates, obtaining a NashGap means
computing it, one exact best-response pass per player. Small equilibrium
certificates exploit tree structure to compress the strategy witness
in large games
(Zhang and Sandholm, 2020), and accelerating the best-response computation
itself has long been an engineering goal there
(Johanson et al., 2011; Li and Huang, 2026b). Exploitability is likewise the
standard for judging deployed agents
(Davis et al., 2014; Lisỳ and Bowling, 2017; Lockhart et al., 2019; Balduzzi et al., 2018; Li et al., 2026a).

Regret-based certificates.
They survive only through zero-sum structure. There the
marginals of a coarse correlated equilibrium are $2\varepsilon$ -Nash
(MacQueen, 2023), and the average’s gap is bounded by total regret at
every step (Zinkevich et al., 2007). Since $u_{2}=-u_{1}$ forces
 $\Delta_{1}=-\Delta_{2}$ , that bound is the zero-sum case of
Theorem 4, in which the two signed value corrections cancel.
In general-sum play they do not, and the theorem measures the residual from
the running realized value. Faster regret rates, such as those of the $+$ and
predictive variants (Tammelin, 2014; Farina et al., 2021), shrink the
regret term and leave that residual untouched. AIVAT (Burch et al., 2018) estimates a fixed
agent’s value without bias, and anytime PSRO (McAleer et al., 2022) gates a growing
policy population on restricted-game exploitability.
None of these gives an online, best-response-free certificate
for iterate selection during training in general-sum extensive-form games.

Regret minimization and equilibria.

Counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) decomposes external regret over
infosets (Zinkevich et al., 2007). CFR+
(Tammelin, 2014; Tammelin et al., 2015) with alternating updates
(Burch et al., 2019; Li and Huang, 2026g) and linear averaging solved heads-up limit
poker (Bowling et al., 2015). Predictive regret matching+
(Farina et al., 2021), discounted regrets and weights
(Brown and Sandholm, 2019), their predictive combination PDCFR+
(Xu et al., 2024), hyperparameter schedules for the discount and
weight exponents (Zhang et al., 2026), the smooth, stable and
extragradient stabilisations of regret matching+ (Farina et al., 2023)
and scale-invariant IR-PRM+ (Zhang et al., 2025) are training-free
accelerants, and one configuration of each is in our pool. The last-iterate
linear convergence of the scale-invariant step is analyzed by
Li and Huang (2026h). All of
these guarantees concern regret, which
in general-sum games yields only (coarse) correlated equilibria
(Anagnostides et al., 2022; Celli et al., 2019). Even averaging with an
explicit approximation guarantee, as under fictitious play
(Conitzer, 2009), works only in restricted settings. Monte Carlo variants
(Lanctot et al., 2009; Li et al., 2026b) trade these exact terminal
distributions for sampling. Abstraction and pruning
(Li et al., 2024; Li and Huang, 2025; Li and Huang, 2026a; Li and Huang, 2026c) are a
complementary route to scale in
large games (Appendix F).

Portfolios and algorithm selection.
Running several solvers and selecting among their outputs is classical in
algorithm selection (Rice, 1976; Gomes and Selman, 2001; Xu et al., 2008).
Here the selection signal is a certificate with a soundness guarantee,
so the selected iterate comes with
a bound on its NashGap.
The task differs from optimizing a strategy portfolio, which is already NP-hard
in zero-sum games (Drabent et al., 2025), and from solver-dependent selection
among equal-value equilibria (Leal, 2026). Ours is a portfolio of no-regret
solvers, and the chosen iterate is scored by the certificate.

## 3. Preliminaries

Extensive-form games and sequence form.
We consider finite $n$ -player perfect-recall extensive-form games (EFGs).
Each has terminal set $\mathcal{Z}$ , information sets (infosets) $\mathcal{I}_{i}$ that group each
player’s decision points by what that player observes there, at most $A$

title: Latent space configuration for neural network finetuning, fast ranking, and embedding dimensionality reduction
abstract: Finding K most similar elements for a query in a large gallery of neural network (NN) embeddings is essential in various areas of computer science and industrial applications of artificial intelligence. This paper proposes search algorithms for structured latent spaces (LS) of NNs which allow to speed up top K item retrieval owing to O(1) complexity small candidate gallery subset search. ArcFace-pretrained IResNet50 models are finetuned using Latent Space Configuration (LSC) methodology to obtain new distribution of embeddings with desired geometric properties. Applying the proposed algorithms to embeddings obtained from finetuned models leads to several times speed-up over baseline exhaustive search. Specifically, we report up to 3 times speed-up on GPU and 40% speed-up on CPU compared to the baseline method GPU speed. These results are obtained for the original and reduced numbers of LS dimensions. The results show that LS dimensionality reduction allows to further accelerate the search and even improve rank-N metrics.

body_start:
Abstract

Finding K most similar elements for a query in
a large gallery of neural network (NN) embeddings is essential in
various areas of computer science and industrial applications of
artificial intelligence. This paper proposes search algorithms for
structured latent spaces (LS) of NNs which allow to speed up top
K item retrieval owing to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ complexity of a small candidate
gallery subset search routine. ArcFace-pretrained IResNet50 models are finetuned
using Latent Space Configuration (LSC) methodology to obtain
new distribution of embeddings with desired geometric
properties. The application of the proposed algorithms to embeddings obtained from
finetuned models leads to several times speed-up over baseline
exhaustive search. Specifically, we report up to 3 times speed-up on GPU
and 40% speed-up on CPU compared to the baseline method GPU speed.
These results are obtained for the original and reduced numbers of LS
dimensions. The results show that LS dimensionality reduction allows to
further accelerate the search and even improve rank-N metrics.

Keywords: Neural network finetuning, embedding gallery search, image
retrieval, vector systems, latent space configuration.

## 1 Introduction

Nowadays, various complex systems rely on efficient retrieval of
relevant information from extremely large databases. Often this requires
data ranking by asserting relevance of database data with the query and
returning K most relevant elements (top-K, or
top-k, or top-N) [1]. High-dimensional outputs
(embeddings) of neural networks (NNs) can directly be used as
description vectors that represent the data, so numerical similarity
between vectors becomes a measure of relevance [2]. This is widely
used in document analysis, recommendation systems, speech and audio
recognition [3, 4, 5]. In context of computer vision (CV),
this translates to finding K most relevant images in gallery
G for a query q. This is essential for e-commerce, face
recognition, biometrics, and security [6, 2, 7].

Exhaustive search has $\mathcal{O}(n\textsubscript{g})$ complexity since it
requires to compare queries with all embeddings in G with size
ng. This is not feasible for galleries of million
or billions of elements, so approximate methods are used instead. These
methods often require building indexing structures over the gallery for
fast retrieval of a smaller subset specific to the given query [8, 9, 10]. While indeed allowing sub-linear scaling, these methods are
still computationally expensive and can reduce complexity to
 $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n\textsubscript{g}})$ [11].

In this paper we take advantage of geometric properties of vector
systems used for NN latent space configuration (LSC) to find a small
subset in G and significantly accelerate top K retrieval.
LSC is a novel methodology which uses predefined class prototypes to
structure and add geometric properties to NN LS during training
 [12]. It has previously been shown that the complexity of the
search of mean vectors of class embeddings for classifier NNs with
preconfigured LS is $\mathcal{O}(1)$ , which can be realized with a single
sort operation performed on the embedding vector. In context of face
recognition this translates to the search of mean vectors of person
identity (id) embedding clusters with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ complexity.
Hence, the complete search complexity becomes $\mathcal{O}(n\textsubscript{c})$ 
where nc is
id cluster size which can be several orders of magnitude smaller
than ng. It is also important that
nc depends on the number of images per id
(which can differ for different ids) and not
ng.

The desired geometry of NN emebdding distribution can be achieved with
finetuning. NN pretraining on extremely large general purpose datasets
and finetuning on smaller target datasets using supervised or
self-supervied learning methods has proven to be very effective in
various CV areas [13, 7, 14]. It has recently been shown that
finetuning can also be performed using prototype-based training methods [15, 16].
However, most of them use trainable prototypes and
require loss functions which complexity grows linearly with the number
of clusters, classes, or ids in the gallery
nid [17, 15, 18]. On the
contrary, LSC chooses predefined non-trainable prototypes allowing to
avoid nid scaling, which is beneficial for
training and finetuning on datasets with extremely large
nid [12].

In this paper we propose two id cluster search algorithms which
allow to rapidly identify a small candidate subset of gallery embeddings
which similarity with the query needs to be assessed. These algorithms
require that NN LS possesses certain geometric properties, so
configuring LS during finetuning is essential for fast high-accuracy
retrieval. The application of the proposed algorithms to embeddings of
finetuned NN leads to several times speed-up on GPU and 40% speed-up on
CPU compared to exhaustive search performed on GPU. The latter is
particularly important for low computational budget and edge
applications where GPU resources are limited or unavailable.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 outlines the
LSC methodology for finetuning, Section 3 describes the proposed search
algorithms, Section 4 summarizes experimental results, Section 5
discusses potential application scenarios of proposed methods, and
Section 6 concludes the paper.

## 2 Configuring LS of NNs during training and finetuning

LSC training methodology is discussed in detail in [12, 19]. The
goal of LSC is to force mean vectors of embedding clusters to align with
vectors of some predefined vector system Vn with
desired geometric properties. To configure NN LS one needs to choose the
base Vn, to distribute mean vectors of embedding
clusters (corresponding to classes or ids) among them, and to
choose a loss function. It has been shown that cosine loss (which
maximizes cosine similarity between embeddings and prototype vectors)
performs best in high-dimensional cases [12]. Since cosine loss
values illustrate how close id embeddings are to their target
vectors, training naturally reduces cluster size while ensuring
separation of clusters determined by the Vn
vector distribution.

It has been shown that NN discriminative ability depends on properties
of the LS embedding distribution. Firstly, embeddings of similar inputs must
have high similarity and be close in LS, so clusters of embeddings
corresponding to one class or id are compact. Secondly,
embeddings of different classes or ids must have low similarity,
so embedding clusters are well-separated. This is achieved by
introducing loss functions that affect NN embedding distribution by
acting directly in LS [18, 20]. One of the most
important methods is ArcFace which has introduced an additive angular
margine penalty to standard softmax loss to improve cluster
compactization and separation [21]. This has led to significant
improvement in discriminative ability and the overall performance of
face recognition NNs.

However, ArcFace requires to use several complicated loss functions
which include id loss, which requires having an NN layer with
nid size. As previously mentioned, this limits
the application of this method when nid is
extremely large. On the contrary, LSC does not require creating
trainable objects of nid size and, by choosing
sparsely distributed prototypes, the inter- and intra-class (cluster)
distribution requirements mentioned above are automatically satisfied
when clusters formed around Vn vectors are
sufficiently compact.

In general, any system of vectors with some predefined set of desired
properties can be used for LSC. In this paper we use systems of vectors
 $V_{n}^{mk}$ such that all vectors in the system are obtained as
permutations of elements of a base vector which consists of m
ones, k negative ones, and ( $n-m-k)$ zeros [22, 23]. Specifically, we use $V_{n}^{11}$ system, meaning that all
Vn vectors have exactly one “1”, one “-1”,
and ( $n-2)$ zeros. These vectors coincide with root system $A_{n-1}$ 
vectors [24]. For NN training purposes
n coincides with the number of LS dimensions.

Figure 1: Pretrained model finetuning with LSC. Black arrows
indicate operations done once before finetuning. Blue arrows indicate
the parameter update loop.

## 2.1 Finetuning LS with the original number of dimensions

Figure 1 shows steps required to finetune a pretrained model using
LSC. Firstly, it is necessary to calculate class or id mean
embedding vectors on the target dataset. A classification layer should
be removed if it is present in the architecture. Secondly, mean
id embedding vectors should be paired with closest (with respect
to cosine similarity) unique vectors from the chosen
Vn. This allows to determine which id
corresponds to which Vn vector and use them as
the target cluster center vector C. Afterward the finetuning
process follows basic LSC training procedure described in Section 3.3 in [12].
Ids can be predicted in the same manner in which
labels are predicted in the original method, i.e. by checking the
id assigned to Vn vector closest to a
given embedding. Id prediction accuracy used in Section 4.1 is
the percentage of correct id predictions for all data points in
the dataset used for finetuning.

## 2.2 Finding Vn vectors closest to mean embedding vectors

It has been mentioned in Section 2.1 that each id should be
paired with the closest Vn vector. However, two
or more id clusters may share the same closest
Vn vector, which can be expected for classes or
ids of objects or persons with some degree of similarity.
Assigning the same Vn vector to several
ids will make these ids indistinguishable after
finetuning, which is not acceptable. Hence, all but one id should
be assigned different Vn vectors.

Fortunately, there exists a neat way of finding possible
Vn vectors owing to the structure of the proposed
vector systems. It has previously been shown that for an arbitrary
embedding m of its largest and k of its smallest elements
determine its cosine similarity with $V_{n}^{mk}$ vectors [23].
For $V_{n}^{11}$ this means that only maximum and minimum magnitude
elements in the embedding affect the similarity calculation results, and
one can find their indexes using argmax and argmin operations,
respectively. It should be mentioned that $V_{n}^{11}$ vectors can be
uniquely referred to using indexes of their positive and negative
elements. For example, a vector with elements [1,-1, 0 … 0] is
referred to as (0, 1), another one with elements [0,1, 0 … -1] is
referred to as (1, n-1), etc. This pair is hereafter referred to
as index of $V_{n}^{11}$ vector.

Large and small elements of embedding vectors, as well as their indexes,
can also be found by analyzing sorted embedding vectors. When the
closest vector, i.e., a vector with “1” in embedding’s argmax
position and “-1” in its argmin position, to some mean embedding
vector is already assigned an id, another close
Vn vector can be found by choosing pairs of
indexes as shown in Figure 2. This approach ensures that mean
embedding vectors are not paired with distant Vn
vectors and the original distribution of clusters is not disturbed.

Figure 2: Example of finding $V_{n}^{11}$ vectors close to some
mean embedding vector when the closest $V_{n}^{11}$ vector is already
assigned an id.

## 2.3 Finetuning LS with the reduced number of dimensions

Reducing the number of dimensions of NN embeddings can lead to faster
computations and storage space reduction [25, 26]. However, this
often leads to worse accuracy metrics, which indicates an important
trade-off. Hence, computation acceleration and accuracy metrics should
be carefully monitored to identify the optimal number of LS dimensions.

In this paper we use random projection to obtain low-dimensional NN
embeddings [27, 28]. Specifically, to obtain embeddings in
LS with reduced number of dimensions nred
(hereafter referred to as reduced LS) using known embeddings in LS
with the original number of dimensions norig, we
first construct a random uniform matrix with dimensions
[norig, nred]. We then
apply QR decomposition to this matrix [29] and use the
obtained matrix Q (with dimensions
[norig, nred]) for
embedding projection

 $z_{red}=z_{orig}\cdot Q,$ 

(1)

where zorig and zred are
NN embeddings in the original and reduced LS, respectively. It has
previously been shown that for specific nid,
nred should be chosen to be the smallest possible
when the number of vectors in Vn system
nvects $\geq$ nid [22].
In case of $V_{n}^{11}$ the number of vectors is

 $n_{vects}=n\cdot(n-1).$ 

(2)

Substituting nred for n,
nid for nvects, and
solving for nred yields

 $n_{red}=\frac{1+\sqrt{\left(1+{4\cdot n}_{id}\right)}}{2},$ 

(3)

which should be rounded up to the next integer. Figure 3 shows that
the projected embeddings are used to calculate mean vectors of embedding
clusters and to find closest vectors in Vn to use
them as vector C as discussed in Section 2.1. A projection layer
should also be included into NN architecture so output embeddings’

body_start:
Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), particularly through group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), has emerged as a central paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs). While RLVR is highly effective at enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, it commonly induces distribution sharpening, whereby the policy distribution becomes excessively peaked and rare-yet-correct trajectories are progressively suppressed, thus diminishing sample diversity. To this end, we promote flat-reward optima in RLVR to smooth the policy distribution.
We theoretically link flat reward RLVR to reduced distribution sharpening, and empirically show improved sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy. Our method, called Flat-RLVR, searches for flat reward regions via sharpness-aware minimization during LLM post-training, combining this with GRPO variants to achieve better trade-offs between sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.

Keywords: 
Distribution Sharpening, RLVR, Flatness, Reasoning Capability

## 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), especially through group-relative methods, has emerged as a predominant methodology for large language model (LLM) post-training (Shao et al., 2024; Lambert et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). Its prominence stems from two complementary strengths: first, rewarding only the correctness of the final answer is sufficient to elicit valid reasoning behaviors (Guo et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2026); and second, the group-relative method eliminates the value network required by proximal policy optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), substantially reducing the memory burden of maintaining a critic of comparable size to the policy (Shao et al., 2024). This critic-free design—first realized as group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) and subsequently extended in its variants—has rapidly become the de facto standard for RLVR.

Figure 1: RLVR and Flat-RLVR on LLM reasoning capacity. Gray nodes indicate paths that are unlikely to be sampled by the model, black nodes indicate paths that are likely to be sampled, i.e., each path consists of a sequence of outputs, later formulated by $o_{j}$ , where $j$ is the path index. Green nodes indicate correct solutions, and red nodes indicate incorrect.

However, a critical doubt has been raised, stemming from empirical observations that GRPO impairs its efficacy when evaluated across multiple samples by checking whether any one succeeds; so-called Pass@ $K$ performance metric (Shao et al., 2024). Specifically, base LLM models without post-training even surpass their RLVR-tuned counterparts under Pass@ $K$ with sufficiently large $K$ (Yue et al., 2025).
This misgiving has recently raised a hypothesis that RLVR merely improves sampling efficiency at the expense of the model’s underlying reasoning capacity driven by LLM’s sample diversity (Nguyen et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). Further evidence reinforces this view: RLVR has been shown to amplify only responses that already carry high probability mass while neglecting the long tail of rare-yet-correct samples, thereby reducing sample diversity (He et al., 2025); and to concentrate exclusively on regions already solvable by the base model, failing to acquire novel capabilities (Yue et al., 2025). Taken together, these findings further support the interpretation that the current RLVR mechanism induces distribution sharpening—a phenomenon in which the model reinforces only the easier, already-solved instances and loses its exploratory capacity.

This is particularly problematic in light of the emerging paradigm of inference-time compute scaling, which leverages sample diversity for effective LLM deployment (Wang et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2024; Chow et al., 2025; Handa et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). These strategies operate on a simple principle—generate many candidate solutions and rely on a verifier to identify the correct ones—and are particularly well aligned with RLVR’s domains of mathematics and code, where deterministic verifiers naturally enable reliable selection (Cobbe et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2024).
In this regard, distribution sharpening from RLVR, which is observed to trade output diversity for efficiency, directly undermines LLM’s benefits of inference-time computation. Figure 1 presents LLM-generated output trajectories (i.e., reasoning paths), the base model covers sometimes-incorrect but wide variety of answers, but RLVR narrows the path to a few answers discarding diversity.

In response to this growing need for sample diversity, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) to flatten the reward surface of the RLVR framework, thereby smoothing policy distributions and diversifying the generated candidate samples.
Recently, it has been shown that a flatter maximum on the reward surface implies a robust policy against uncertain perturbations on actions, states, and rewards (Lee and Yoon, 2025).
Motivated by the flat RL concept, our key insight is that, rather than updating the LLM toward steepest loss descent, steering it to flatten the surface may smooth the distribution sharpening.

In this paper, we find that sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) variants (Foret et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022; Hassan et al., 2025) applied to RL optimization within the RLVR paradigm indeed mitigate distribution sharpening by yielding a flatter reward
(as illustrated in Figure 1).
In addition, we formalize how the flat-search optimization mathematically lifts suboptimal candidates by smoothing the reward surface. Our contributions are highlighted as follows:
i) We propose a novel strategy to alleviate the distribution sharpening of GRPO by borrowing the concept of flat-minima search. ii) We provide a theoretical analysis of how a flat-inspired GRPO elevates suboptimal candidates, leading to the smoothed output distribution. iii) We suggest a Flat-RLVR framework by integrating SAM into GRPO methods. Flat-RLVR, instantiated by combining with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), and CISPO (Chen et al., 2025), consistently improves Pass@ $256$ mathematical reasoning capacity while preserving accuracy with our LLM post-training adaptations.

## 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Group-Relative RLVR

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a large language model on binary rewards provided by deterministic verifiers, eliciting strong reasoning behavior without human-preference data (Guo et al., 2025; Lambert et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2026). Within this paradigm, group-relative methods have become dominant, yielding computation benefits by normalizing rewards across a group of rollouts sampled from the same prompt and thereby removing the need for a separate value network (Shao et al., 2024). The original instance, GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), has since been extended in several directions. DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) introduces asymmetric clipping bounds that allow low-probability tokens to bring larger upward updates, together with dynamic sampling that discards groups whose advantages collapse to zero. CISPO (Chen et al., 2025) clips the importance-sampling weight to prevent dropping tokens that carry essential information.

Our work integrates a sharpness-aware optimization perspective into the reinforcement learning loop, showing a general applicability across the group-relative RLVR family.

## 2.2 Distribution Sharpening in RLVR

While the distribution sharpening phenomenon of RLVR is now well documented (Yue et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025), existing mitigation strategies all intervene at the level of the reward or token distribution. F-GRPO (Plyusov et al., 2026) applies a Focal Weight to down-weight easy prompts, the unlikeliness reward (He et al., 2025) amplifies signals from rare correct trajectories, and clipping-based variants such as DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) relax token-level updates to preserve low-probability tokens.

We address distribution sharpening via optimization geometry itself, biasing updates toward flat regions of the loss landscape via SAM—a direction is novel and orthogonal to the above approaches.

## 2.3 Advances in SAM

Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) has been improved as a primary driver of flat-minima search by addressing its drawbacks. The first concern is its sensitivity to parameter re-scaling: ASAM (Kwon et al., 2021) addresses this by introducing a scaling operator that adaptively adjusts the perturbation radius according to parameter magnitudes. The second issue is SAM’s vulnerability to noisy gradients, particularly during the early stages of training; GCSAM (Hassan et al., 2025) mitigates this through Gradient Centralization, which removes the mean of the gradient to yield a more reliable perturbation direction. The third concern is the computational overhead of SAM; LookSAM (Liu et al., 2022) amortizes this cost by computing the SAM update only periodically, while Momentum-SAM (Becker et al., 2025) integrates Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG) into SAM to directly improve computational efficiency. Lastly, the observation that SAM does not invariably converge to flat minima leads to GSAM (Zhuang et al., 2022) adopting a surrogate gap formulation for the sharpness metric.

Our work adopts the idea of several SAM-based variants to build the Flat-RLVR framework; applying the SAM update periodically, inspired by LookSAM (Liu et al., 2022) and Gradient Centralization, inspired by GCSAM (Hassan et al., 2025). Notably, Flat-RLVR is not limited to a certain type of SAM approaches.

## 2.4 Flat-Minima and Generalization

Flat minima have been studied as being linked to improved generalization (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997; Keskar et al., 2017) emphasized in domain generalization (Cha et al., 2021) and adversarial robustness (Wei et al., 2023) with underlying principles (Zhang et al., 2024; Yoo and Yoon, 2026).
Researchers have extended flat-minima toward various learning frameworks, including generative modeling (Lee et al., 2025), federated learning (Qu et al., 2022; Lee and Yoon, 2024), and reinforcement learning (RL) (Lee and Yoon, 2025).
Notably, RL with flatter reward yields more robust policies to action, state, and reward uncertainties (Lee and Yoon, 2025). Such flat reward insight makes us anticipate potential benefits in RLVR, but it is nontrivial to identify how flatness-aware RL steers LLM behavior.

Our work is the first attempt to employ SAM in LLM post-training, revealing its benefits in relieving distribution sharpening in RLVR.

## 3 Preliminaries

## 3.1 Group Relative Policy Optimization

GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) removes the value function, then instead calculates advantages relative to a group of sampled rollouts. For a prompt $q\sim Q$ with $G$ rollouts $\{o_{i}\}^{G}_{i=1}$ , and rewards $\{R_{i}\}^{G}_{i=1}$ , the group-relative advantage for $i$ -th rollout is

 $\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\bar{R}}{\sigma_{R}+\varepsilon},$ 

(1)

where $\bar{R}:=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i}R_{i}$ , $\sigma_{R}=\textrm{std}(\{R_{j}\})$ and $\varepsilon>0$ .

Let $o_{i}=(y_{i,1},...,y_{i,|o_{i}|})\in O$ denote the token sequence for rollout $i$ computed by the old policy $\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(O|q)$ from a prompt $q$ . GRPO optimizes policy $\pi_{\theta}$ to maximize the following clipped surrogate objective based on group-relative advantage $\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i,\tau}$ :

 $J_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim P(Q),\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(O|q)}\bigg[\\
\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|o_{i}|}\sum_{\tau=1}^{|o_{i}|}\min\Big\{\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,\tau}\mid q,o_{i,<\tau})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{i,\tau}\mid q,o_{i,<\tau})}\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i,\tau},\\
\mathrm{clip}\big(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,\tau}\mid q,o_{i,<\tau})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{i,\tau}\mid q,o_{i,<\tau})},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\big)\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i,\tau}\Big\}\bigg],\\
$ 

(2)

where $o_{i,\tau}=y_{i,\tau}$ , $o_{i,<\tau}=\{y_{i,1},\cdots,y_{i,\tau-1}\}$ , and $\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i,\tau}$ is the $i$ -th rollout advantage given with a set of partial sequences $\{o_{i,\leq\tau}\}_{i=1}^{G}$ . In RLVR, all tokens within the same rollout share an identical advantage value; $\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i,\tau}=\hat{\mathcal{A}_{i}}$ for all $\tau$ . $\mathrm{clip}(\cdot,a,b)$ clips input to be in interval $(a,b)$ , where $a<b\in\mathbb{R}$ .

We drop the Kullback-Leibler regularization term adopted by GRPO by following recent findings that the regularization hinders explorations in reasoning (Zhou et al., 2026).

Figure 2: Illustration of the loss landscape and reasoning capacity of RLVR and Flat-RLVR.
Flat-RLVR converges to a flatter minimum in the loss landscape by jointly optimizing for loss reduction and sharpness minimization, whereas RLVR is drawn to a sharper minimum driven solely by reward maximization.
As shown in the trees (see Figure 1), Flat-RLVR explores a broader reasoning tree, while RLVR collapses to a narrow set of paths.

## 3.2 Sharpness-Aware Minimization

SAM (Foret et al., 2021) seeks a minimum with both small loss and curvature, biasing optimization toward flat regions of the loss landscape. Formally, SAM solves the following min-max objective:

 $\underset{\theta}{\min}\ \underset{\|\epsilon\|_{2}\leq\rho}{\max}\ \mathcal{L}(\theta+\epsilon),$ 

(3)

where $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ is the loss function parametrized by $\theta$ , and $\epsilon$ is a parameter perturbation constrained to lie within an $\ell_{2}$ ball of radius $\rho>0$ . The inner maximization admits a first-order approximation so that the worst-case perturbation becomes

 $\epsilon^{*}=\rho{\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)}/{\lVert\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\rVert}.$ 

(4)

By minimizing the worst-case loss within this perturbation neighborhood, SAM penalizes sharp minima and encourages convergence to flat ones.

## 4 Analysis on Flatness in RLVR

Based on the GRPO and SAM objectives, we analyze how a sharpness-aware RLVR, so-called Flat-RLVR, affects distribution sharpening over LLM outputs. Without loss of generality, we use a local sequence-level unclipped surrogate induced by a fixed rollout group (Ge et al., 2026). For a prompt $q$ , let $J_{q}(\theta)$ denote the local RLVR objective, which drops the expectation and clipping in Eq. (2).
Set $\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta)=-J_{q}(\theta)$ ; maximizing RLVR objective is equivalent to minimizing $\mathcal{L}_{q}$ .
Figure 2 previews the key components of our analysis that follows.

Definition 4.1 ( $\rho$ -Flat-RLVR).

Given prompt $q$ and the computed local sequence-level RLVR loss $\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta)$ , let $\rho$ -sharpness of $\mathcal{L}_{q}$ at parameter $\theta$ be

 $\operatorname{Sharp}_{\rho}(\theta;q)=\max_{\|\epsilon\|_{2}\leq\rho}\left[\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta+\epsilon)-\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta)\right],$ 

(5)

where $\epsilon$ is a parameter perturbation and $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ is Euclidean norm.
Then, the $\rho$ -Flat RLVR objective is defined as the expected sharpness-aware loss:

 $\min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{q\sim Q}\left[\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta)+\operatorname{Sharp}_{\rho}(\theta;q)\right]\\
=\min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{q\sim Q}\left[\max_{\|\epsilon\|_{2}\leq\rho}\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta+\epsilon)\right].$ 

(6)

Following SAM, Flat-RLVR optimizes Eq. (6) by a two-step update at parameters $\theta_{t}$ , where $t$ is an update index: it first ascends to the worst-case perturbation $\epsilon_{t}^{*}=\rho\,\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta_{t})/\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta_{t})\|_{2}$ , then descends using the gradient at the perturbed point,

 $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\alpha\,\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q}(\theta_{t}+\epsilon_{t}^{*}).$ 

(7)

The perturbation $\epsilon_{t}^{*}$ is what distinguishes Flat-RLVR from the standard update, which cannot account for loss sensitivity to perturbations.

Definition 4.2 (Correct-set Distribution Sharpening).

Given prompt $q$ and policy distribution $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|q)$ over outputs $o\in O$ , let $\mathcal{C}_{q}=\{o:R(o)=1\}$ be a verifier-correct set, whose elements show $1$ -reward.
For two correct outputs $o_{h},o_{l}\in\mathcal{C}_{q}$ satisfying

 $\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(o_{h}|q)>\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(o_{l}|q),$ 

(8)

let us formulate their correct-set log-probability gap at parameter $\theta$ as

 $D_{h,l}(\theta;q)=\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{h}|q)}{\pi_{\theta}(o_{l}|q)}.$ 

(9)

An update from $\theta_{\mathrm{old}}$ to $\theta_{\mathrm{new}}$ is defined to sharpen the correct-set distribution on $(o_{h},o_{l})$ if

 $D_{h,l}(\theta_{\mathrm{new}};q)-D_{h,l}(\theta_{\mathrm{old}};q)>0.$ 

(10)

Here, $o_{h}$ denotes a correct reasoning path with higher probability under the old policy, while $o_{l}$ denotes a lower-probability but still correct reasoning path.
We now analyze how the policy update via $\rho$ -Flat-RLVR affects the confidence gap $D_{h,l}$ .

Lemma 4.3 ( $\rho$ -Flat-RLVR One-Step Decomposition).

The one-step update of Flat-RLVR from Definition 4.1 admits the following local expansion:

 $\theta_{t+1}^{\texttt{Flat}}=\theta_{t}+\alpha\Big(\underbrace{g_{t}}_{\textnormal{Score Part}}\underbrace{-\,\rho\,\frac{M_{t}g_{t}}{\|g_{t}\|_{2}}}_{\textnormal{Flatness Part}}\Big)+R_{t}.$ 

(11)

Here, for the sequence-level score is $s_{i,t}=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(o_{i}|q)|_{\theta_{t}}$ over rollouts $\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}$ , $g_{t}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i}s_{i,t}$ , $M_{t}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i}s_{i,t}s_{i,t}^{\top}$ .

The residual $R_{t}=-\alpha\rho\,B_{t}g_{t}/\|g_{t}\|_{2}-\alpha R_{T}$ collects the log-policy Hessian term $B_{t}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i}\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i}\nabla_{\theta}^{2}\log\pi_{\theta}(o_{i}|q)$ and the higher-order Taylor residual $R_{T}$ .

conclusion:
In this work, we present a way to mitigate the distribution sharpening in group-relative RLVR, by utilizing flatness-seeking optimization. Concretely, we provide a mathematical analysis of the one-step parameter update in RLVR, showing that flat-minima search dampens the abrupt increase in probability, thereby mitigating distribution sharpness of LLM post-training. We propose the Flat-RLVR framework by integrating sharpness-aware minimization into RLVR.
Throughout experiments, Flat-RLVR implemented as Flat-GRPO/DAPO/CISPO mitigates the distribution sharpening induced by RLVR, consistently improving the diversity of the output distribution while preserving accuracy with our LLM post-training adaptations. These imply flatness serves as the central catalyst to mitigate the distribution sharpening.

title: CRAB: Cuboid-based Representation for As-built BIM from Point Clouds
abstract: As-built BIM reconstruction from point clouds demands semantic, volumetric, parametric, and editable building components, beyond 2D layouts or planar abstractions. Yet existing scan-to-BIM pipelines often rely on handcrafted rules, heuristic optimization, or manual correction, while learning-based methods fall short of recovering wall thickness, opening geometry, and component-level BIM structure. We introduce CRAB, a BIM-ready cuboid reconstruction framework that encodes walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with IFC-compatible semantics and parameters. CRAB bridges point clouds and editable BIM by combining ProposalNet, which predicts coarse component cuboids, with AssemblyNet, a relation-aware Flow Matching model that refines geometry, predicts structural relationships, and enables automatic structural correction and human-guided editing. To address limited cuboid-level supervision, we extend Structured3D with component-wise cuboid annotations and construct cuboid-based procedural scenes. Experiments show CRAB surpasses floor plan and plane-based alternatives in component completeness, geometric accuracy, and generalization. For interior wall thickness estimation, CRAB achieves a mean error of 2.80 cm, with 79.50% of matched walls within 3 cm. The project page is available at https://vcc.tech/research/2026/CRAB.

body_start:
Abstract.

As-built BIM reconstruction from point clouds demands semantic, volumetric, parametric, and editable building components, beyond 2D layouts or planar abstractions.
Yet existing scan-to-BIM pipelines often rely on hand-crafted rules, heuristic optimization, or manual correction, while learning-based methods fall short of recovering wall thickness, opening geometry, and component-level BIM structure.
We introduce CRAB, a BIM-ready cuboid reconstruction framework that encodes walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with IFC-compatible semantics and parameters.
CRAB bridges point clouds and editable BIM by combining ProposalNet, which predicts coarse component cuboids, with AssemblyNet, a relation-aware Flow Matching model that refines geometry, predicts structural relationships, and enables automatic structural correction and human-guided editing.
To address limited cuboid-level supervision, we extend Structured3D with component-wise cuboid annotations and construct cuboid-based procedural scenes.
Experiments show CRAB surpasses floor plan and plane-based alternatives in component completeness, geometric accuracy, and generalization.
For interior wall thickness estimation, CRAB achieves a mean error of 2.80 cm, with 79.50% of matched walls within 3 cm.
The project page is available at https://vcc.tech/research/2026/CRAB.

Scan-to-BIM; Scene Reconstruction; Parametric Modeling; Cuboid Representation; Relation-aware Assembly.
