## 1. Introduction

3D scanning is widely used on construction sites to capture the geometric structure of real-world buildings and environments. The resulting point clouds often provide noisy, incomplete, and purely geometric surface measurements. In contrast, Building Information Modeling (BIM) represents buildings as structured collections of semantic component instances with volumetric geometry, parametric attributes, and explicit relationships(Zbirovský and Nežerka, 2025; Liu et al., 2025b). Consequently, BIM aims to reconstruct editable as-built architectural components rather than merely producing a geometric reconstruction of the scanned scene. For architectural components, this requires inferring wall thickness, wall-opening relationships, and editable instance identities that are not directly observable from raw scans.

Current methods rarely recover such BIM components directly from point clouds.
Manual modeling remains labor-intensive, while classical Scan-to-BIM pipelines rely on multi-stage processing, including segmentation, primitive fitting, plane extraction, and topology optimization, often requiring scene-specific assumptions and carefully tuned parameters (Zbirovský and Nežerka, 2025; Liu et al., 2025b).
Learning-based approaches improve automation, but most focus on intermediate geometric abstractions such as floor plans, room polygons (Yue et al., 2023), or 3D planes (Mao et al., 2025).
Although these representations support spatial understanding, they describe
layouts or surfaces rather than explicit volumetric component instances.
They do not directly couple component geometry, limiting their
extensibility to other BIM attributes such as load-bearing status and
materials.
A reconstruction representation should therefore expose these attributes as primary variables, rather than deriving them from layouts or planes after prediction.

This mismatch calls for a volumetric, component-aware representation.
Cuboid and primitive assemblies are a natural candidate because they encode compact solids with interpretable parameters and support editable 3D modeling.
However, existing cuboid-based methods primarily target object decomposition(Ye et al., 2025b), shape generation (Jones et al., 2020), or furniture arrangement (Feng et al., 2025), rather than architectural reconstruction from incomplete scene-level point clouds with ambiguous component boundaries.
Moreover, their generic cuboid parameterizations are not tailored to highly
elongated architectural components. This motivates a BIM-oriented volumetric
representation that explicitly models parametric component geometry and
architectural relations.

To this end, we introduce CRAB (Cuboid-based Representation for As-built BIM), a BIM-ready proposal-and-assembly framework for indoor point clouds. CRAB is designed precisely to move
beyond layout and plane abstractions toward volumetric BIM components,
thereby demonstrating the value of a BIM-oriented cuboid representation for
AI-based Scan-to-BIM. It reconstructs walls, doors, windows, beams, and
columns in single-floor scenes and represents each scene as centerline-based
semantic cuboids and explicit topological relationships, jointly encoding
parametric component geometry, semantics, wall adjacency, and opening-wall
affiliation.

To recover these cuboids and relationships from noisy and incomplete point
clouds, CRAB adopts a two-stage design. ProposalNet first generates coarse semantic cuboids from point cloud features, while AssemblyNet further refines their geometry and predicts inter-component relationships through relation-aware Flow Matching. This refinement improves structural consistency while preserving editable cuboid parameters for user-guided modification. The resulting components can be directly instantiated as Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) elements, enabling compatibility with the open BIM data-exchange standard.

A further challenge is the lack of cuboid-level supervision for scan-to-BIM learning.
Existing indoor datasets typically provide floor plans, meshes, semantic labels, or layout annotations, but lack component-wise volumetric cuboids aligned with BIM elements.
To support training and evaluation, we extend the public Structured3D (Zheng et al., 2020) dataset with cuboid annotations for architectural components, and further construct a cuboid-based synthetic dataset with procedurally generated scenes and simulated point cloud acquisition.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

• 

We recast scan-based indoor BIM reconstruction as semantic cuboid assembly, using centerline-based cuboid parameters to explicitly model component semantics, wall thickness, opening height, and editable volumetric geometry.

• 

We construct CrabSet, a scalable cuboid-level supervision dataset for Scan-to-BIM, by enriching Structured3D with component-wise cuboid annotations and procedurally synthesizing diverse architectural scenes with simulated point-cloud acquisition.

• 

We introduce CRAB, a proposal-and-assembly framework that couples ProposalNet for semantic cuboid generation with AssemblyNet for relation-aware flow-matching refinement, producing accurate, structurally coherent, and editable BIM-ready models.

## 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Structured Indoor Modeling

Indoor structural modeling is often cast as floor plan or layout estimation.
Existing methods reconstruct 2D graphs, room polygons, or polygonal loops from RGB-D scans and point-density maps (Chen et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2022a; Stekovic et al., 2021; Yue et al., 2023), with recent variants improving polygon generation, room representation, graph reasoning, segmentation, and edge continuity (Chen et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025a).
While compact, these floorplan-oriented outputs do not directly specify wall thickness, vertical extent, opening height, or component volume, which are required by CAD/BIM workflows.

Recent 3D structured modeling methods move beyond 2D layouts by predicting walls, openings, oriented boxes, or parametric layout quads from images or point clouds (Avetisyan et al., 2024; Mao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2022b; Bieri et al., 2025).
For planar representations, recovering volumetric semantic component
instances from predicted paired parallel planes requires additional plane
pairing and instance association to infer wall thickness, opening affiliation,
and component identity. Such associations can be ambiguous when a single
plane spans multiple walls, limiting extensions to instance-specific BIM
attributes such as materials and load-bearing status.
We instead reconstruct cuboid assemblies for walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns, with explicit centerline, thickness, height.

## 2.2. BIM-Ready Cuboid Reconstruction

Scan-to-BIM converts sensed geometry into editable building models.
Existing systems recover walls, slabs, openings, rooms, and IFC-compatible outputs from point clouds (Murali et al., 2017; Ochmann et al., 2019; Zbirovský and Nežerka, 2025), and BIMNet highlights the need for domain-specific data and BIM-aware geometric and topological evaluation (Liu et al., 2025b).
Yet many pipelines still rely on geometric rules, segmentation, optimization, or software-specific workflows, making them sensitive to clutter, occlusion, and incomplete scans (Wu et al., 2023; Han et al., 2023; Wong et al., 2025).
Moreover, they primarily recover final component geometry without explicitly modeling relations, limiting coordinated refinement.

Cuboid and primitive assemblies offer compact, editable structures.
ShapeAssembly represents shapes as programs over cuboid parts (Jones et al., 2020), while recent primitive and procedural methods learn structured decompositions or editable programs from data (Ye et al., 2025b; Raji et al., 2026).
CASAGPT uses cuboid primitives for indoor scene synthesis to reduce mesh-level collisions (Feng et al., 2025).
Existing methods mainly target object decomposition, shape generation, or
furnished scene synthesis rather than architectural reconstruction from
incomplete scene-level point clouds. They typically use generic cuboids
parameterized by center, size, and orientation, which are not tailored to
highly elongated architectural components. CRAB instead adopts
centerline-based semantic cuboids and explicit relations, supporting coordinated refinement and
editable component reconstruction.

## 2.3. Local Structural Refinement

Recent LLM/VLM agents have moved generation and editing from one-shot prompting to closed-loop planning, tool use, evaluation, and revision.
SceneCraft refines Blender-code scenes with rendered feedback (Hu et al., 2024), and VIGA reconstructs editable graphics programs through a code-render-inspect loop (Yin et al., 2026).
Similar feedback-driven loops appear in visual editing (Yao et al., 2026), while BIM agents invoke APIs, manipulate IFC data, or operate authoring software (Du et al., 2026; Nithyanantham et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025).
Xie et al. (Xie et al., 2025) further show the value of local correction for missed or misplaced 3D layout elements.
Motivated by these local correction paradigms, our cuboid representation and AssemblyNet support user-guided refinement, enabling controllable local edits and global correction for improved structural consistency.

## 3. CrabSet Construction

Learning BIM-ready cuboid reconstruction requires component-level volumetric supervision, including the geometry and relations of walls, doors, windows, and other elements.
However, as summarized in Table 1, most existing indoor datasets are designed for scene understanding, embodied AI, or layout estimation, and mainly provide 2D floor plans, room layouts, semantic labels, or structured planar annotations.
Only a few datasets contain explicit volumetric building components, and they are limited in scale or scene diversity.

To this end, we construct CrabSet, a cuboid-level dataset for indoor BIM reconstruction from point clouds.
Each sample contains an input point cloud, component-wise volumetric cuboid annotations, and pairwise relations among architectural components.
Each cuboid records its semantic category, instance identity, position, orientation, and dimensions.
As shown in Fig. 2, CrabSet combines component-wise cuboid annotations derived from Structured3D with procedurally synthesized scenes, covering both residential layouts and broader architectural configurations. For synthetic scenes, point clouds are generated through virtual scanning.

Representative samples from CrabSet, combining S3D-derived residential and procedurally synthesized scenes for cuboid-level supervision.
The synthesized subsets vary boundaries, scales, and corridor-centered layouts, covering non-uniform wall thicknesses, non-Manhattan contours, service shafts, and diverse circulation patterns.

## S3D-derived.

This subset is derived from Structured3D, which provides diverse residential layouts with room partitions, openings, non-Manhattan structures, and occlusions.
Using its planar faces, normals, semantic labels, and outer contours, we convert walls, doors, and windows into component-wise volumetric cuboids.
This subset anchors CrabSet to a public residential benchmark.

## Boundary-varied.

This subset increases local geometric diversity by varying outer contours, wall thicknesses, and non-Manhattan wall configurations.
It encourages the model to recover accurate cuboid geometry and wall thickness.

## Scale-varied.

This subset expands spatial scale and component complexity through large architectural spaces with service shafts, columns, and multi-layer window configurations.
It improves the model’s ability to handle dense non-residential scenes with large variations in component size and spatial extent.

## Corridor-centered.

This subset focuses on circulation-driven layouts, including straight, bent, notched, H-shaped, T-shaped, and ring-like corridors.
Rooms and openings are arranged along corridor boundaries, covering large building configurations that are rarely represented in residential datasets.

Figure 3. 
Overview of CRAB.
Given a raw indoor point cloud, ProposalNet encodes the scan and autoregressively predicts an initial set of semantic cuboids for walls, doors, and windows.
AssemblyNet represents each proposal with centerline-based cuboid tokens augmented by semantic, relation, and edit-control flags, and refines them through intra-cuboid, inter-cuboid, and cuboid–point attention.
A velocity head performs relation-aware flow-matching refinement of cuboid geometry, while a relation head infers structural dependencies such as wall adjacency and door/window affiliation.
The refined cuboids and relations are finally instantiated as editable BIM-ready components, converting unstructured scans into component-level architectural models.

## 4. Methodology

## 4.1. Problem Formulation

Our goal is to reconstruct as-built BIM components, such as walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns, from an input point cloud. We represent them as parameterized semantic cuboids along with their explicit topological relationships.

Formally, we define the input point cloud as $P=\{p_{i}\}$ , where each point feature $p_{i}$ contains spatial coordinates and color information. The reconstructed architectural components are represented by a set of semantic cuboids

 $C=\{c_{i}\},\quad c_{i}=[g_{i},s_{i}],\quad g_{i}=[x_{1},y_{1},z_{1},x_{2},y_{2},z_{2},w,h],$ 

where the geometric parameters $g_{i}$ define the bottom central axis connecting endpoints $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})$ and $(x_{2},y_{2},z_{2})$ , together with cuboid thickness $w$ and height $h$ , while $s_{i}$ denotes the semantic category.

The relationships between cuboids are further represented by:

 $R=\{r_{ij}\mid c_{i},c_{j}\in C\},$ 

where $r_{ij}$ encodes structural interactions between components, including attachment relationships (e.g., doors or windows belonging to a wall) and adjacency relationships between neighboring walls.

The overall reconstruction task is therefore formulated as

 $(C,R)=\mathcal{F}(P),$ 

where $\mathcal{F}$ denotes the proposed mapping function that reconstructs cuboids and their relationships from the input point cloud.

## 4.2. ProposalNet

We argue that the primary objective of the first stage is to generate accurate individual architectural components, since reliable prediction of each cuboid forms the foundation for subsequent relationship reasoning and structural assembly. Therefore, this module focuses exclusively on cuboid geometry and semantic prediction. Formally, we aim to learn the conditional distribution $p_{\theta}(C\mid P)$ , from which the initial cuboid proposals are generated:

 $C_{\text{init}}\sim p_{\theta}(C\mid P).$ 

Specifically, we employ Sonata (Wu et al., 2025) as the point cloud encoder and Qwen2.5-0.5B (Yang et al., 2024) as the auto-regressive cuboid generator.
The Sonata encoder is initialized with pretrained weights and further trained on our point cloud and cuboid pairs.
For each input scene, we voxel-downsample the point cloud at $2.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ and randomly keep at most $800{,}000$ points for training and inference.

The point cloud encoder and autoregressive cuboid decoder are connected by a lightweight MLP Adapter, which maps point cloud features into the decoder token embedding space.
Conditioned on the adapted point cloud tokens, the decoder sequentially generates the initial semantic cuboids.

limitations:
CRAB still has several limitations.
(1) Missing component recovery.
CRAB can automatically correct continuous geometric errors, local misalignments, and redundant components, but entirely missing components may still require coarse user initialization. The supplementary material further shows AssemblyNet’s ability to correct geometric errors and local misalignments, while removing redundant components through component alignment.
(2) Irregular non-Manhattan geometry.
While CRAB handles standard Manhattan layouts and moderate non-Manhattan variations, highly irregular or curved structures remain challenging: cuboids can capture the dominant organization, but may oversimplify fine-scale deviations.
(3) Sparse infrequent components.
Beams, columns, stairs, and service shafts appear sparsely in current real-world test scenes, limiting comprehensive evaluation.
Although CRAB can model these elements in principle, robust reconstruction requires richer component-level supervision and broader BIM benchmarks.

conclusion:
We presented CRAB, a cuboid-based approach to indoor Scan-to-BIM reconstruction.
The key observation is that BIM reconstruction requires component-level volumetric structure, not only layout curves or planar surfaces.
Accordingly, CRAB represents walls, doors, windows, beams and columns as semantic cuboids with explicit centerline, thickness, height, and opening parameters.
This representation makes architectural components directly editable and provides a natural interface for downstream BIM conversion.

The proposed framework follows a proposal-and-assembly design.
ProposalNet predicts coarse architectural cuboids from point-cloud observations, while AssemblyNet refines their geometry and relationships through relation-aware Flow Matching. Together, the two-stage system is capable of correcting geometric errors and local misalignments while removing redundant components through component alignment.
To support learning and evaluation, we constructed CrabSet, which provides cuboid-level supervision from Structured3D-derived annotations and procedurally generated architectural scenes.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world scans show that cuboid assembly yields more accurate wall-thickness estimation, more stable refinement, and more flexible BIM instantiation than floor-plan- or plane-based alternatives. Importantly, these gains in volumetric reconstruction do not come at the expense of layout or plane quality, where CRAB remains competitive with representation-specific baselines.

To address the limitations discussed earlier, future work will primarily broaden CRAB’s practical capabilities and application scope. We will explore (1) complex non-Manhattan geometry and richer primitives, including cylinders and curved surfaces, (2) broader BIM categories and structural relations, together with semantic plane cues as auxiliary geometric evidence for robust reconstruction under real-scene domain shifts, and (3) interactive or agent-assisted workflows, reducing manual effort and enabling more automated Scan-to-BIM reconstruction.

title: Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization. Our evaluation shows that for the task of language generation on LM1B, HMDLM reduces perplexity by more than 1.5 points over Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM), a recently proposed strong diffusion baseline; on WikiHow, we see a drop in perplexity of up to 4.4 pts on ADLM and up to 7 pts against MDLM. An LLM judge on WikiHow prefers HMDLM generations (the two variants combined) more than $2\times$ as often as the baseline. On the task of solving Sudoku puzzles requiring multi-step reasoning, it improves solution accuracy by up to $8.6\%$ absolute points over existing diffusion baselines.

Abstract

Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization. Our evaluation shows that for the task of language generation on LM1B, HMDLM reduces perplexity by more than 1.5 points over Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM), a recently proposed strong diffusion baseline; on WikiHow, we see a drop in perplexity
of upto 4.4 pts on ADLM and upto 7 pts against MDLM (Masked Diffusion Language Model). A LLM judge on WikiHow, prefers HMDLM generations (the two variants combined) more than $2\times$ as often as the baseline.
On the task of solving Sudoku puzzles requiring multi-step reasoning, it improves solution accuracy by up to $8.6\%$ absolute points over existing diffusion baselines.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the AI space, from general-purpose text generation to solving complex problems such as mathematical reasoning and theorem proving. Despite their success, limitations remain. One of the criticisms of modern-day LLMs, which are largely auto-regressive in nature, is that they generate text only in a strictly left-to-right manner. It has been argued that this style of decoding has specific disadvantages, such as not being able to correct past mistakes, and involving large computational costs. As a remedy, recent literature has proposed another class of models, referred to as Diffusion Models (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025c), which do not subscribe to the left-to-right generation style, but rather generate multiple tokens in parallel. The formulation is based on a forward diffusion process, which translates the text into noise, and on learning the reverse process, can generate the desired text by iteratively denoising from complete noise. This line of work has shown significant promise for the future of language generation, both for increasing computational efficiency and solving complex tasks (e.g., solving Sudoku or generating structured text).

A key open question in masked diffusion language models is how to choose the order in which positions should be denoised. Standard masked diffusion treats token positions symmetrically: with a shared masking schedule and no task-dependent notion of priority. Recent work shows that token ordering and decoding strategies can substantially affect generation quality (Kim et al., 2025; Garg et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2026; Fox et al., 2026). Recent approaches address this by identifying important anchor tokens (Rout et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2026), or adding planning-aware training and decoding mechanisms (Peng et al., 2025; Israel et al., 2025). These methods suggest that not all positions should be treated equally, but none provides a general hierarchy-aware forward and backward diffusion process. Such priority is often available: many problems carry a natural hierarchy over positions. In document generation, titles and section headings or summary often provide high-level semantic structure before the surrounding body text. In Sudoku, more constrained cells are easier to fill first, and their priority belongs to the position, not the digit it will contain.

We introduce HMDLM, a hierarchical extension of masked diffusion language models that associates each token position with a hierarchy variable.
During the forward process, both the token and its hierarchy state are diffused toward a masked state. During the reverse process, the model first predicts the hierarchy for masked positions and then predicts token identities conditioned on the predicted hierarchy. This two-stage factorization allows the model to learn which hierarchy level each position belongs to before decoding its token value. Unlike anchor-based methods (Rout et al., 2025), which tie importance to token identities, HMDLM assigns hierarchy to positions, with a separate noise schedule per level to control how fast each level is unmasked (see Section 4.3.2). We also derive the negative evidence lower bound (NELBO) for this process which serves as our training objective 4.

We experimentally validate HMDLM across several benchmark domains. On language modeling benchmarks like LM1B, we train the model from scratch and compare with diffusion baselines (like MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024), SEDD (Lou et al., 2024), the Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM) (Rout et al., 2025), and DiffusionBERT (He et al., 2023)) on both perplexity and generation quality. On Wikihow, we fine-tune on pretrained checkpoints and compare with ADLM and MDLM on perplexity and qualitative generation. On Sudoku, we train from scratch, and more reliably produce accurate solutions than the diffusion baselines (like MGDM (Ye et al., 2025) and MDLM). These results demonstrate that explicitly modeling hierarchy over token positions can improve masked diffusion generation across both natural language and structured domains.

Our work makes the following contributions: (a) We present a novel formulation for incorporating the notion of hierarchy in the discrete diffusion models, referred to as HMDLM (b) We re-formulate the standard diffusion formulation to have a two stage training and inference process, where the first stage predicts distribution over hierarchy levels, and second one predicts token distribution given the hierarchy prediction. (c) We re-derive the ELBO to incorporate the notion of hierarchy in the forward and backward diffusion process. (d) We present experiments showing gains over masked diffusion baselines in perplexity and generation quality on LM1B and WikiHow, and report accuracy on Sudoku. We also plan to release the code for HMDLM on paper acceptance.

## 2 Related Work

Masked diffusion language models:

Diffusion models have recently been adapted to language generation as an alternative to left-to-right autoregressive modeling. Early approaches explored diffusion in continuous word-vector spaces, as in Diffusion-LM (Li et al., 2022), or directly over discrete tokens, as in D3PMs (Austin et al., 2021) with structured transition matrices and absorbing [MASK] states. More recent masked diffusion language models formulate generation as iterative denoising from partially masked sequences: the forward process gradually replaces tokens with [MASK], and the reverse model reconstructs the sequence from bidirectional context. SEDD (Lou et al., 2024), reparameterized discrete diffusion (Zheng et al., 2023), DiffusionBERT (He et al., 2023), MD4 (Shi et al., 2024) and MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) improve the objectives and sampling procedures for this setting, while large-scale systems such as MDM (Nie et al., 2025a), LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025b) and LLaDA2.0 (Bie et al., 2025) show that masked diffusion can support instruction-following LLMs. However, these models typically employ a uniform masking schedule, ignoring the inherent semantic or structural hierarchy of the task.

Generation order and decoding strategies:

Masked diffusion is attractive because generation need not proceed left-to-right; tokens can be revealed in arbitrary or partially parallel orders. This flexibility also makes the choice of denoising order important. Prior work shows that adaptive or learned ordering can significantly improve masked diffusion, through inference-time token ordering (Kim et al., 2025), planner-aware training (Peng et al., 2025), planned generation where the model first constructs a high-level plan and then denoises the planned spans in parallel (Israel et al., 2025), variational order learning (Fox et al., 2026), or unified learnable-order formulations (Hong et al., 2026). Other methods (Wang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025) modify sampling trajectories to address irreversibility or decoding bias. Our work is complementary: rather than learning a free-form position policy or adding an external planner, HMDLM encodes a task-dependent hierarchy in the diffusion state itself and uses per-level schedules to induce a controllable soft generation order.

Anchoring, planning, and structured priors:

Several recent works also argue that diffusion language models benefit from identifying important tokens or high-level structure before completing the full sequence. Anchored Diffusion Language Models (Rout et al., 2025) observe that masking important words early can remove useful context, and use a two-stage model that predicts anchor-token distributions before predicting missing tokens. Planned Diffusion (Israel et al., 2025) first constructs an explicit plan and then generates spans in parallel. In code generation, AnCoder (Xue et al., 2026) uses syntax-tree priors to prioritize keywords and identifiers, and code-focused diffusion models such as DiffuCoder and Dream-Coder further show the value of domain-specific structure (Gong et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025). These works share our motivation that not all sequence positions should be treated equally. However, HMDLM differs by attaching hierarchy to positions rather than only token identities, supporting multiple task-defined hierarchy levels, and using these levels to control both the forward corruption process and the reverse denoising dynamics through level-specific schedules.

## 3 Background

## 3.1 Notations

Let ${x}$ denote a sequence of discrete tokens each token $x^{i}$ is represented as one-hot column vector, and $\mathcal{V}=\{x^{i}\in\{0,1\}^{D}:\sum_{j=1}^{D}x^{i}[j]=1\}$ at position $i$ as the set of all such vectors. Define $Cat(.;\pi)$ as the categorical distribution over $\mathcal{V}$ classes, where $\pi\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ and $\sum_{d}\pi[d]=1$ . Also we assume a special $[MASK]$ token, $m\in\mathcal{V}$ and treat it as the $D^{th}$ category, i.e., $m[D]=1$ . Let $x_{t}$ denote the state of the diffusion process at time step $t$ . The following description follows the treatment provided in Sahoo et al. (2024).

## 3.2 Discrete Diffusion Models

Forward process.
Discrete diffusion process is defined using a forward process that gradually corrupts data over $T$ time steps, and replaces each token with a special MASK token. Let $t\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}$ , with $t=0$ corresponding to clean data and $t=T$ to fully masked data, and $x_{t}^{i}\in\mathcal{V}$ denote progressively noisier latent variables where the timestep $t$ ranges from $0$ (zero noise) to $T$ (maximum noise). The forward noising process $q$ at time $t$ and position $i$ is defined as:

 $q(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{0}^{i})=\mathrm{Cat}\!\left(x_{t}^{i};\alpha_{t}x_{0}^{i}+(1-\alpha_{t})m\right),$ 

(1)

where $x_{0}^{i}$ is the clean state, $\alpha_{t}$ is the masking schedule where $\alpha_{t}\in[0,1]$ is a strictly decreasing function in $t$ , with $\alpha_{0}=1$ and $\alpha_{T}=0$ controlling the proportion of unmasked tokens at time $t$ . The corresponding posterior transition with $\lambda_{t}=\frac{\alpha_{t-1}-\alpha_{t}}{1-\alpha_{t}}$ is:

 $q(x_{t-1}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{i},x_{0}^{i})=\begin{cases}\mathrm{Cat}(x_{t-1}^{i};x_{t}^{i}),&x_{t}^{i}\neq m,\\
\mathrm{Cat}\!\left(x_{t-1}^{i};(1-\lambda_{t})m+\lambda_{t}x_{0}^{i}\right),&x_{t}^{i}=m.\end{cases}$ 

(2)

Reverse process.
The reverse process iteratively denoises the data from timestep $t$ to $t-1$ until the sequence becomes fully unmasked. Diffusion model aims to approximate the reverse process by learning a backward model $p_{\theta}(x_{t-1}^{i}|x_{t}^{i})$ . Since the true posterior depends on the unknown clean token $x_{0}^{i}$ , it is approximated with a neural network $x^{i}_{\theta}(x_{t},t)\in\Delta^{\mathcal{V}}$ , which predicts the clean token distribution from the noisy input $x_{t}^{i}$ at time $t$ . During the reverse diffusion process, unmasked tokens stay fixed, and clean inputs are never masked:

 $p_{\theta}(x_{t-1}^{i}\mid x_{t})=\begin{cases}\mathrm{Cat}(x_{t-1}^{i};x_{t}^{i}),&x_{t}^{i}\neq m,\\
\mathrm{Cat}\!\left(x_{t-1}^{i};(1-\lambda_{t})m+\lambda_{t}\,x^{i}_{\theta}(x_{t},t)\right),&x_{t}^{i}=m.\end{cases}$ 

(3)

NELBO.
The denoising model $x_{\theta}({x_{t}},t)$ is trained using the following Negative ELBO:

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NELBO}}({x};\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q,t}\!\left[-\log p_{\theta}({x_{0}}\mid{x_{1}})+T\left(\frac{\alpha_{t}-\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\alpha_{t}}\log\langle x_{\theta}(x_{t},t),x_{0}\rangle\right)\right]$ 

(4)

## 4 Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model

In this section we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model
(HMDLM), which extends discrete diffusion models by incorporating a notion of
hierarchy into both the forward and backward processes. Our framework augments
each token position with a hierarchy level. Let $h_{0}^{i}$ denote the gold hierarchy at position $i$ , represented as a one-hot vector over $K$ levels, i.e., $h_{0}^{i}\in\{0,1\}^{K}$ . We introduce a distinct hierarchy mask state $h_{\mathrm{m}}$ , giving $K{+}1$ possible hierarchy states.
Positions to be unmasked at time step $t$ are governed by the level dependent masking schedule $\alpha_{k}(t)$ defined for time step $t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$ and level $k\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}$ which is a decreasing function. If a position $i$ at time step $t$ is sampled or is already unmasked, we then set $b_{t}^{i}=0$ and $b_{t}^{i}=1$ otherwise.

Since $b_{t}^{i}$ is shared, a token and its hierarchy level are always masked or

revealed level.

title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents
abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.

body_start:
Abstract

Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11–24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media—with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody—and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.

## 1 Introduction

Omni-modal assistants such as GPT-4o, Gemini, Qwen-Omni, and MiMo (OpenAI et al., 2024; Team et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2026; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026) are moving from single-turn demos to persistent, multi-session deployments. A user may share a product photo in January, leave a dietary voice note in March, and later expect both to inform a recommendation. Answering requires not only retrieving temporally scattered evidence, but chaining it across modalities (Figure 1). Prior conversational memory benchmarks omit video/audio, treat images as optional, or stop at text–image co-reference; none combine four-modality multi-session dialogue with a matched stage-diagnostic protocol (Table 1).

(causal validation is strongest for spatial detail; §6.2).

write (representation compression), retrieve (missed

Multi-hop text QA (Yang et al., 2018; Trivedi et al., 2022) likewise lacks this multimodal, temporal setting, and coupled system comparisons obscure where evidence is lost. We therefore cast the pipeline as four stages—write, retrieve, deliver, and read (Figure 2)—and diagnose them with matched interventions under a frozen reader, prompt, budget, and judge.

Each stage fails in its own way, motivating four research questions:

• 

RQ1 (Write). Does the stored representation keep the spatial,
temporal, and prosodic detail the answer will later depend on?

• 

RQ2 (Retrieve & Deliver). Is every required unit found,
and does it survive packing into the reader’s request? Media caps can
drop even top-ranked artefacts, so the two are measured separately.

• 

RQ3 (Read). Given the complete delivered chain, can the reader
integrate it across modalities and sessions?

• 

RQ4 (Abstain). Does the system abstain precisely when
required evidence is absent—and only then?

MOSAIC has 923 questions in 11–24-session haystacks with
construction-targeted modality gaps (§3.2). Headline
findings: textualization costs $\sim$ 9 points (spatial-heavy); retrieval costs
 $\sim$ 8 points and packing $\sim$ 4 at production budgets (far more under tight
media caps); $\sim$ 15 points remain under gold symbolic facts; abstention
remains weak on these controls. Under the matched protocol, each paired drop is
associated with the intervened stage; within-item carrier contrasts further
localize signal-specific loss, with the strongest causal validation for spatial
information and additional selector-level validation for annotated prosody
(§6.2).

## Contributions.

• 

MOSAIC, 923 persona-grounded omni-modal memory questions
with construction-targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals (strongest
causal validation for spatial information; selector-level validation for
annotated prosody), cross-modal multi-hop chains, and 139 refusal controls.

• 

A matched four-stage diagnostic protocol separating
write, retrieve, deliver, and read,
with fixed-reader and native end-to-end evaluation tracks.

• 

A validated public benchmark pipeline, including human
audits, media, filtering dispositions, manifests, and run configurations.

## 2 Related Work

## Conversational memory benchmarks.

From single-session persona grounding (Zhang et al., 2018) to multi-session suites, text-only benchmarks probe extraction, multi-session and temporal reasoning, knowledge updating, recall, and persona consistency (Zhong et al., 2023; Ou et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Du et al., 2025). Multimodal extensions remain limited: LoCoMo images are often non-essential (Maharana et al., 2024; Bei et al., 2026); Mem-Gallery and MemLens make images task-critical but stop at text+image and emphasise finding rather than cross-modal chaining (Bei et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026); ATM-Bench aggregates personal multi-source evidence rather than sequential conversational chaining (Mei et al., 2026); and MMRC, MMDU, MM-NIAH/MMNeedle, Mementos, and M3-Bench add image/video reasoning without multi-session dialogue structure (Xue et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024b; Zhou et al., 2026). MOSAIC is the first to require retrieving and chaining evidence across all four primary modalities in multi-session conversations (Table 1).

## Multi-hop and cross-modal reasoning.

HotpotQA, MuSiQue, MultiModalQA, WebQA, and CRIT target compositional multi-hop QA over text and images (Yang et al., 2018; Trivedi et al., 2022; Talmor et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2022; Sung et al., 2026); long-context suites such as BABILong, RULER, and MMLU-Reason chain facts in static corpora (Kuratov et al., 2024; Hsieh et al., 2024; Tie et al., 2025). MOSAIC combines multi-hop reasoning with session-scattered multimodal retrieval.

## Memory-augmented LLM systems.

Memory architectures virtualize or structure long context (Packer et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023; Sarthi et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a), integrate graphs with retrieval (Guo et al., 2025; Gutiérrez et al., 2025; Paul et al., 2026), or provide agentic/OS-inspired layers (Xu et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). They lack a standard omni-modal benchmark for controlled comparison—the role MOSAIC fills.

## RAG and memory diagnosis.

Prior work localizes failures via claim-level RAG diagnostics (Ru et al., 2024), tests of visual evidence use (Hu et al., 2025), controlled document pools (Peng et al., 2026), AMemGym’s write/read/utilization split (Jiayang et al., 2026), and MemFail’s text-memory stages (Garg et al., 2026); localization itself is not novel. We differ in how stages are separated: instead of stressing a still-coupled pipeline, MOSAIC makes each stage substitutable under a frozen reader, prompt, packer, budget, and judge. This measures deliver apart from retrieve and attributes loss to carrier-level signals—to our knowledge the first substitutable four-stage protocol for omni-modal conversational memory.

## 3 Preliminaries

Every MOSAIC item is a persona-grounded, multi-modal query embedded in a chronological haystack of user–assistant sessions. Three orthogonal axes define it, each worked through end-to-end in Appendix A: the question type fixes the reasoning skeleton (§3.1), the modality gap defines what each non-text modality must contribute (§3.2), and the reasoning chain composes Narrower, Selector, and Answer facts into a deterministic retrieval path (§3.3).

## 3.1 Question Types

MOSAIC covers six types: single-session information extraction;
cross-session selection and bridging; knowledge updates; temporal-plan
disruptions; and refusal after evidence removal. Questions require one to
three facts; Appendix A defines each type, and
Appendix D reports per-type counts.

## 3.2 Modality Gaps

A modality gap is information that survives only because its native
modality preserves it, while a text-only or caption-based agent would lose it.
Required non-text facts are assigned a gap strategy
(Appendix A): image (background detail, fine-grained
attribute, spatial configuration), video (action ordering, state
transition, repetition count), or audio (happy/unhappy prosody with
neutral wording over $\geq 2$ candidates); Appendix D
breaks down tag coverage. Audio prosody is the most frequent
annotated strategy (450 facts / 399 of 784 answerable items), so Caption-Text /
ASR write paths lose the tone discriminator by design—a pipeline exposure,
not a gold-delivery perception cost (§6.2).

## Challenge by construction.

A media attachment is insufficient to establish multimodal reasoning,
since a caption or transcript may preserve the entire answer. MOSAIC therefore
assigns a challenge before dialogue and media realization, specifying the
native relation that carries a fact together with constraints that keep that
relation out of the surrounding text; every answerable item contains at least
one required challenge-bearing fact (Table 2). Action
Repetition Count is representative: a fixed-camera clip repeats one action with
no cuts and no on-screen counter, and the dialogue says only “a few times,” so
a generic caption preserves the event but loses the selector
needed to continue the chain (per-challenge specifications:
Appendix A).

## 3.3 Reasoning Chains and Fact Roles

Every answerable item has a reasoning chain of required facts with roles
Narrower (NAR; reduces candidates), Selector (SEL; identifies
an entity), and Answer (ANS; carries the final value), in the pattern
 $\text{NAR}^{*}\;\text{SEL}^{*}\;\text{ANS}$ .
Valid chains are bridge-entity-linked and deletion-tested
(§4): removing any required fact makes the
question unanswerable, and audio/video discriminators choose among
 $\geq 2$ same-type entities. A chain is cross-modal when required
facts span at least two modalities; gap-bearing detail usually sits in a
Narrower or Selector, and the Answer’s final
value is always a short text-expressible string (enabling judge
scoring), though the fact carrying it may itself be multimodal (full
constraints and templates: Appendix A).

## 4 The MOSAIC Generation Pipeline

MOSAIC is produced by a fully automated, config-driven four-stage pipeline
(Figure 7; details in Appendix B). Each item
is grounded in a Nemotron-Personas persona (Meyer and Corneil, 2025).
An LLM designs a caption-distinct primary entity, then builds the chain
question-first under the bridge-entity and entity-pair constraints
(§3.3). A validate-and-repair loop combines programmatic checks
with a per-fact deletion test against twelve failure modes; unrepaired chains
are discarded, and Answer Refusal items strip required facts after
auditing. Surviving facts become chronological evidence and filler sessions
under leak guards. Stage 4 synthesises media (FLUX-2-pro / Kling–Seedance /
Qwen3-TTS). Filtering then yields the exact lineage
 $1{,}050\!\rightarrow\!1{,}004\!\rightarrow\!879$ (automated) before a
three-annotator audit of 100 items (94.3% well-posed) rescues 44 probe false
negatives, giving MOSAIC-Eval: 923 items (784 answerable +
139 refusal). Reweighting that audit with a 100-item probe-YES follow-up
estimates $\approx$ 97.8% gold-correct and $\approx$ 96.6% evidence-sufficient
on the 784 answerable releases (Appendix I); the 784/864
(90.7%) figure remains a filtering retention rate, not a human
answerability ceiling (Appendix E).

The release spans 70 personas (11–24 sessions, mean 17.5), 10,765 multimodal
artefacts (Table 10), and $\sim$ 18.8M tokens
( $\sim$ 269K/persona). Among answerable items, 85.2% need $\geq$ 2 facts and
75.0% need $\geq$ 2 modalities; required evidence appears in image, audio,
video, and text for 99.5%, 54.1%, 23.5%, and 35.3% of items (overlapping),
so we report per-challenge strata rather than claiming uniform modality
balance; Appendix D collects the remaining haystack
statistics.

## 5 Diagnostic Evaluation Protocol

of the pipeline separately substitutable under a frozen reader, prompt, and
budget. For history $H$ , question $q$ , and delivery budget $B$ , let

We run seven matched conditions on the same 784 answerable QIDs
(Table 3), changing only representation, retrieval, or
delivery under one reader, prompt, packer, and judge. These are
interventions rather than an assumed ranking: native evidence may remain
perceptually difficult, and retrieved context may include useful evidence

The main paired contrasts are symbolic versus native (perception cost),
structured versus generic text (avoidable write-time compression), gold native
versus retrieved-all-delivered (retrieval loss), and all-delivered versus
production-capped requests (delivery loss). Delivery is additionally traced as a
budget curve over tighter packer allowances (top-10 units; top-5 with one
media item per modality). Residual errors under gold symbolic facts bound

## Frozen configuration.

Matched conditions use Gemini 3.5 as the fixed omni-modal reader (temperature 0;
extended thinking disabled), held out from dataset construction: MiMo-V2.5 is
the answerability probe, so using it as the primary reader would couple
selection with evaluation. The trade-off is disclosed—gold-native failures
mix perception error with bounded item noise
(§6.1). Retrieval replays a frozen top-50 ranked
manifest; the production budget delivers the top 20 units with at most three
items per modality under a 100 MB media cap. E
limitations:
MOSAIC’s personas, evidence sessions, and media are synthetic; evaluation on
organically collected multimodal histories remains future work. The primary
reader is held out from filtering, and stage contrasts are paired, but stage
labels are matched-protocol associations rather than fully isolated mechanisms.
Video nulls are underpowered (Appendix F). The raw-audio versus
ASR gap is inconclusive for this reader, and textualized audio carriers often
retain paralinguistic lexical cues while other gold hops already expose the
answer value—so gold-delivery audio nulls do not establish acoustic recovery
(Appendix G). Swapped gold prosody tags
nonetheless show selector-level sensitivity
(Appendix K.4). RQ4 uses length-matched refusal
controls with residual form cues (Appendix H).
Further caveats on modality coverage and backend scope are in
Appendix G.
conclusion:
MOSAIC separates omni-modal memory failures into write,
retrieve, deliver, and read. Under the matched
protocol and fixed reader, reading accounts for the largest residual loss
under gold facts; retrieval and delivery constrain native pipelines, textualization text-derived ones. These are protocol associations, not universal bottlenecks. Spatial structure has the
clearest causal validation and no adequate text surrogate; annotated prosody
tags show selector-level sensitivity, while temporal and raw-audio versus ASR
contrasts remain inconclusive. No system both answers and refuses reliably:
progress requires preserving modality-specific signal, delivering complete
chains, and reading them faithfully.

title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

headings: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
Two-Dimensional Assessment of Safety and Usefulness.
body_start:
Abstract

Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment.
To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a
bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive
84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets:
DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts
with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and
DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex
instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations—substantially higher than the 69%–87% achieved by the baselines—and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen’s $\kappa$ = 0.864).
Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

## 1 Introduction

As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into real-world applications, they pose potential risks that make evaluating their safety crucial for responsible deployment. To systematically quantify these risks, the research community has developed various safety benchmarks. Recent efforts, including SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024b), Do-Not-Answer (Wang et al., 2024), DecodingTrust (Wang et al., 2023), AIR-Bench (Zeng et al., 2024), and SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024), have made significant progress by introducing finer taxonomies, supporting multilingual prompts, and broadening attack coverage.

Figure 1: DiagSafe Evaluation Overview (1) Prompt-level rubric: The rubric includes harmful, exempt, and useful entries specific to this prompt, which serve as the basis for the Judge’s evaluation. (2) Reliability of evaluation: The rubric shows a high degree of consistency between LLM Judge results and human annotations, and demonstrates robustness across different LLMs. LLMs using a generic prompt and the security classifier both exhibit low agreement rates. (3) Fine-grained diagnostics: DiagSafe can diagnose the specific performance of individual models and uncover information hidden within security binary classification metrics.

Despite these advancements, existing benchmarks face three primary limitations. First, their evaluation granularity is often too coarse. Reducing responses to binary safe or unsafe labels lacks explanatory depth, leaving developers without actionable insights for targeted improvements. Second, current evaluation methods suffer from low consistency. Prior work shows that swapping the evaluation classifier can shift attack success rates by nearly 30 percentage points, with inter-judge agreement dropping to 22% in certain categories (Liu et al., 2026b). Third, data diversity remains restricted. No existing benchmark systematically integrates multilingual prompts, single- and multi-turn dialogues, and different attack types across a generalized and comprehensive taxonomy, resulting in unsystematic and incomplete safety evaluation (see Table 1).

To address these limitations, we introduce DiagSafe, a comprehensive and diagnostic safety benchmark. It comprises two core components: a novel evaluation framework (Figure 1) and a highly diverse dataset.
First, inspired by the domain-specific rubrics in FORTRESS (Knight et al., 2025), our diagnostic evaluation framework moves beyond traditional binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Instead of relying on generic instructions, we designed a dedicated rubric for every prompt with explicit, item-level criteria for both safety and usefulness. This dual-dimensional approach transforms subjective binary judgments into objective, explainable assessments.

Second, to ensure robust and realistic evaluation, the DiagSafe dataset is grounded in a comprehensive safety taxonomy. By systematically collecting and coding AI safety policies and regulations from various countries, we developed a three-level taxonomy comprising 84 safety labels, each with a detailed policy specifying its definition and boundaries. Built upon this rigorous foundation, the dataset is designed to capture a wide spectrum of real-world scenarios and adversarial threats. It consists of two bilingual
(English and Chinese) subsets. DiagBase covers single- and multi-turn prompts, including both direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks. DiagAttack further embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks, forming instruction attacks (Jiang et al., 2023).

Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotators and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen’s $\kappa=0.864$ ). Applying our benchmark to a series of LLMs (8B to 1.6T parameters) reveals critical vulnerabilities. While unsafe rates on DiagBase range from 2% to 33%, 8 of the 11 models exceed 40% on DiagAttack. In addition, models are generally more susceptible to unsafe behaviors in Chinese contexts and during multi-turn interactions. Furthermore, the fine-grained analysis effectively exposes the unique safety blind spots of each evaluated model. In summary, our main contributions are three-fold:

• 

Prompt-Level Rubric Evaluation: We propose a novel paradigm that shifts safety evaluation from generic binary classification to fine-grained, item-by-item assessment. By independently evaluating safety and usefulness, this approach yields highly consistent and explainable judgments.

• 

Comprehensive Safety Benchmark: We construct a diverse dataset grounded in a rigorous three-tier 84-label taxonomy. It integrates bilingual prompts, multi-turn dialogues, and various attack strategies to ensure realistic threat evaluation.

• 

Actionable Model Diagnostics: We conduct extensive evaluations on leading LLMs, uncovering specific vulnerabilities obscured by aggregate metrics. Our findings provide concrete guidance for LLM alignment.

## 2 Related Work

Safety benchmarks are a crucial component of large language model evaluation (Gehman et al., 2020; Hartvigsen et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2022). Recent advancements have evolved along two primary dimensions: taxonomic scope and scenario diversity. To broaden taxonomic scope, benchmarks like SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024) and S-Eval (Yuan et al., 2025) introduce hierarchical risk categories, AIR-Bench (Zeng et al., 2024) designs risk categories based on actual regulatory documents, and Safety-Prompts (Sun et al., 2023) significantly scales up the data volume. To enhance scenario diversity, recent datasets incorporate adversarial jailbreak attacks (Mazeika et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024), multilingual contexts (Deng et al., 2024), and multi-turn dialogues (Cao et al., 2026). Despite these expansions, most existing benchmarks lack precise, policy-level boundary definitions for their labels and rarely integrate these diverse elements into a single framework. DiagSafe bridges this gap by unifying diverse evaluation scenarios under a comprehensive taxonomy, providing a unified diagnostic resource with explicit, instance-specific rubrics (Table 1).

Regarding the evaluation methods, existing work mainly falls into
three categories. The first category uses multiple-choice questions (MCQs) to assess safety, enabling
fully automatic and reproducible scoring, as in SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024b) and CHiSafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024a). However, this paradigm measures a model’s ability to recognize harmful content rather than the safety of its actual generations. The second relies on trained safety
classifiers, such as open-weight models (e.g.,
LlamaGuard4 (Meta AI, 2025)) and benchmark-specific evaluators
(e.g., SALAD-Bench’s MD-Judge (Li et al., 2024)). Although fast, these classifiers provide only binary labels without evidence trails or actionable
diagnostics. The third employs general-purpose LLM judges with
generic prompts, as seen in EasyJailbreak (Zhou et al., 2024), but
such judges are highly susceptible to stylistic
variations (Eiras et al., 2025) and degrade on adversarial or
multilingual inputs (Liu et al., 2024).
Classifiers and LLM judges with generic prompts suffer from
significant inconsistency (Liu et al., 2026b) because their scoring
rules are either implicit or globally generic. To address this limitation, recent work by Knight et al. (2025) demonstrated that employing instance-specific rubrics can achieve high human alignment in specific high-risk domains (e.g., national security and public safety). Building upon this insight, DiagSafe scales and generalizes this prompt-level rubric paradigm to a comprehensive safety evaluation. Whereas Knight et al. (2025) directly pair each prompt with a dedicated rubric, DiagSafe introduces an explicit and reusable intermediate layer, following a safety provisions $\rightarrow$ label specification $\rightarrow$ prompt-level rubric pipeline. Through systematic experiments, we provide the first evidence that automatically synthesized prompt-level rubrics are highly effective in safety scenarios. By providing explicit, per-sample criteria across a broad taxonomy, our approach effectively constrains judge behavior to yield highly consistent, explainable, and reliable judgments (§4.2).

Figure 2: Leaf-level comparison of the DiagSafe taxonomy (11/34/84) with four public benchmarks (SALAD-Bench, S-Eval, Do-Not-Answer, CHiSafetyBench); outer-leaf arc width is proportional to prompt count. Red leaves are unique (no counterpart in any compared benchmark), orange leaves are finer (prior benchmarks lack a matching leaf and cover them only by a parent category), and gray leaves are shared coverage. The inset card shows the label specification for the “adult product” label as an example.

## 3 The DiagSafe Benchmark

We present a diagnostic safety evaluation method that relies on prompt-level rubrics to conduct fine-grained evaluation of LLMs. The rubrics are grounded in a three-level taxonomy comprising 84 safety labels. To instantiate this method, we construct two subsets, DiagBase and DiagAttack (Section 3.2).

## 3.1 The Diagnostic Evaluation Framework

DiagSafe is built on an intuitive idea: reliable safety judgments depend on explicit evaluation criteria. Rather than relying on generic instructions to classify responses as “safe” or “unsafe,” we equip each prompt with a dedicated, prompt-specific rubric. These rubrics contain verifiable items across two dimensions: safety and usefulness. Since both are fundamental requirements for deployed models, evaluating them jointly provides a more comprehensive picture of model behavior than assessing safety in isolation.

## Safety dimension.

The safety dimension is made of S-items, each naming a concrete behavior. A rubric contains multiple S-items, each corresponding to one type of harm that the response to this specific prompt may produce. Each S-item also carries its own exemptions: behaviors under that same risk that must not be judged unsafe, such as objective conceptual discussion, an explicit refusal, or legal and common-sense knowledge. These exemptions delimit the legitimate boundary for that item and suppress false positives.

Figure 3: The DiagSafe data synthesis pipeline. (1) Prompt synthesis: an LLM generator, conditioned on the per-label specification and three orthogonal attributes (language, dialogue turns, and attack form), produces DiagBase; its single-turn normal prompts are then rewritten into instruction attacks using task shells from an external instruction-following dataset, yielding DiagAttack. (2) Rubric synthesis: each synthesized prompt, together with the same label specification, is passed to a rubric-writer LLM to produce a prompt-level rubric comprising safety items ( $S_{1}\dots S_{n}$ ) and an independent usefulness item ( $U$ ).

## Usefulness dimension.

The usefulness dimension consists of U-items, which independently assess whether a response fulfills the given instruction. These items fall into three categories: instruction following, information quality (e.g., factual correctness and internal consistency), and response patterns (e.g., bare refusals or the provision of alternatives). This dimension comprises eight fixed U-items whose binary (Yes/No) answers map to a 0–3 score via a deterministic rule. For example, a score of 3 requires a direct, factually consistent answer, whereas a bare refusal scores 1.

In summary, this rubric forms the foundation of DiagSafe’s fine-grained and reliable evaluation, converting subjective “is this safe?” judgments into objective, item-level criteria. Furthermore, by treating safety and usefulness as independent dimensions, the rubric enables a more comprehensive assessment of LLM behavior than a single safety label can provide.

Figure 4: Unsafe rates (%) of the 11 evaluated models on DiagBase and DiagAttack.

## 3.2 Label System of DiagSafe

We build the dataset around a hierarchical label taxonomy. To ensure that the labels are scientifically grounded and complete, we collect a broad set of public safety standards as the basis for label design, and equip each label with a detailed definition and explicit criteria that delimit its boundary.

## Safety guidelines collection.

We collect public safety guidelines from countries and regions such as the European Union, the United States, and China, covering ethical principles, risk frameworks, industry taxonomies, and national technical policies. From these documents we extract and consolidate 204 safety provisions. Drawing on this multi-source, cross-jurisdictional base, rather than a single company’s internal policy, keeps the taxonomy from inheriting any one vendor’s blind spots.

## Label and label specification construction.

We use an LLM agent to merge the collected provisions and expand them into individual safety labels, each accompanied by a detailed label specification. Safety-team experts then review and revise the draft, verifying source traceability, rule accuracy, and boundary clarity, and removing safety-irrelevant labels. Each label specification explicitly specifies four components: (1) a precise definition of the label, (2) value principles grounded in public safety standards, (3) dangerous behaviors that constitute violations, and (4) safe behaviors that are permitted. Compared with the taxonomies of existing benchmarks, ours offers broader coverage and finer granularity, as shown in Figure 2.

headings: Huayu-Global: Skillful real-time quasi-global precipitation retrieval
body_start:
Abstract

Satellite precipitation products face a persistent trade-off: real-time estimates are timely but less accurate, whereas the most reliable products are often released months after observation. This delay keeps high-quality precipitation information outside the decision window for flood warning and disaster response. Here we report Huayu-Global, a cross-constellation deep-learning system that combines three geostationary sensor streams from five satellites through a common retrieval framework and generates coherent quasi-global precipitation fields every thirty minutes. Across more than a million independent station records from two periods outside the training years, Huayu-Global improves event detection and precipitation-amount estimation relative to the real-time products evaluated and reaches delayed-product-level skill in key metrics. Huayu-Global therefore turns operational geostationary observations into a timely, high-skill precipitation layer for flood forecasting, water management and disaster response. Its cross-constellation design also provides a scalable foundation for incorporating future geostationary missions into hydrological and weather-prediction systems.

keywords
Huayu-Global, Real-time precipitation monitoring, Machine learning-based retrieval, Geostationary satellites

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Data processing workflow for the Huayu-Global precipitation monitoring framework. Representative Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES), Meteosat, and FengYun-4B (FY-4B) sector views are transformed into Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), Spinning Enhanced Visible and Infrared Imager (SEVIRI), and Advanced Geostationary Radiation Imager (AGRI) cloud-feature sequences, then passed through the Huayu models for the Americas, Europe-Africa, and Asia-Pacific domains. Sector outputs are merged to generate coherent quasi-global grid precipitation products using only satellite inputs available at the inference time.

Precipitation is a primary driver of the water cycle, flood hazard, agricultural risk, and hydrological extremes. Operational monitoring therefore requires products that are both timely and quantitatively reliable. Ground gauges, weather radar, and gauge–satellite merged analyses provide essential constraints on precipitation fields, but their global operational use is limited by uneven station density, radar-network gaps, terrain blockage, oceanic coverage gaps, and differences in data-sharing conditions (Shen et al., 2014; Fulton et al., 1998; Sun et al., 2018; Kirschbaum et al., 2017). These limitations are most acute when precipitation information is needed rapidly and consistently across continents and ocean-adjacent regions.

Satellite precipitation products have reduced this coverage gap, but operational users still face a hard choice between speed and accuracy. Real-time streams such as Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation NOW (GSMaP_NOW) and Precipitation Estimation from Remotely Sensed Information using Artificial Neural Networks–Cloud Classification System (PERSIANN-CCS) provide prompt coverage but show lower detection and quantitative skill (real-time products achieve critical success index (CSI) values between 0.23 and 0.33 in our evaluation, whereas the gauge-adjusted Final Run of Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG FR), released 3.5 months after observation, reaches 0.42) (Kubota et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2018; Hong et al., 2004). More extensively processed products such as the Climate Prediction Center morphing technique (CMORPH) and IMERG can improve accuracy, but their highest-quality streams may arrive months later (Joyce et al., 2004; Huffman et al., 2015; Kidd et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2019; Huffman et al., 2023). Global IMERG assessments also show that residual errors remain dependent on region, season, and precipitation regime, even after multi-sensor merging and gauge adjustment (Tan et al., 2016; Pradhan et al., 2022). Information delivered after the decision window cannot support flood warning or other time-critical action. A useful quasi-global system must therefore combine real-time availability with delayed-product-level precipitation skill.

High-frequency geostationary observations offer a route to this goal because they continuously sample cloud evolution across broad domains. Decades of geostationary meteorological satellite development, from early operational systems to modern multispectral imagers, have increased the temporal and spectral information available for rainfall inference (Blersch and
Probert, 1991; Schmit et al., 2005; Bessho et al., 2016). The difficulty is that cloud-top radiances do not map uniquely to surface rainfall, and the relationship varies with region, season, terrain, storm type, and sensor geometry. The challenge is compounded across satellite platforms: the GOES ABI, Meteosat SEVIRI, and FY-4B AGRI differ in spectral coverage, native spatial resolution, and full-disk scan cadence, yet an operational quasi-global product must seamlessly combine their outputs. Recent studies have shown that nonlinear and multispectral models can improve geostationary precipitation retrieval in regional settings (Song et al., 2026; Kühnlein
et al., 2014; Sehad et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2022a; Ma et al., 2022b; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2025). The remaining challenge is to extend this idea from single-sensor or regional retrievals to a cross-constellation system that can operate across the Americas, Europe-Africa, and Asia-Pacific sectors while preserving a common output grid.

Here we present Huayu-Global, a cross-constellation framework for real-time quasi-global precipitation retrieval. Extending the earlier regional Huayu framework (Song et al., 2026), it coordinates sensor-adapted models for GOES ABI, Meteosat SEVIRI, and FY-4B AGRI within a common architecture and merges their outputs on a unified 0.05∘ grid (Fig. 1). Huayu-Global thereby converts operational geostationary observations into coherent precipitation fields every 30 minutes across most low- and mid-latitude regions. The system is developed from 59.7 TB of satellite data and evaluated against 5,395 independent ground stations contributing 1.85 million matched three-hourly records from July–December 2022 and January–June 2025, both outside the 2023–2024 training years. It leads the evaluated real-time products in event detection and error magnitude and reaches delayed-product-level skill in key station-based metrics. By moving high-skill precipitation information from retrospective archives into the operational decision window, Huayu-Global establishes a scalable observation layer for flood forecasting, water management, disaster response and future satellite-enabled weather prediction.

The full-sample metrics in Table 1 show the same pattern across complementary diagnostics. Across 1,847,967 matched 3-hour station-product records, Huayu-Global achieves the highest CSI (0.441) and coefficient of determination (R2, 0.362), and the lowest root-mean-square error (RMSE, 1.961 mm). Huayu-Global also exceeds the 3.5-month IMERG FR product in CSI, R2, and RMSE in this independent station comparison. Its overall accuracy (ACC, 0.896) is close to the highest value from CMORPH (0.904), and its correlation coefficient (CC, 0.605) is close to the highest value from IMERG FR (0.613). Daily-scale diagnostics (Extended Data Fig. 2) show that this aggregate advantage is not confined to a small number of validation dates, while also indicating that the strongest non-Huayu baseline varies by metric and day.

## 2.2 Representative spatial case

Figure 3: Representative spatial comparison of precipitation estimates for one selected evaluation case. Panels show (a) GSMaP_NOW, (b) PERSIANN-CCS, (c) PERSIANN, (d) CMORPH, (e) IMERG FR, and (f) Huayu-Global. Each panel presents a quasi-global precipitation field with four enlarged regional views; station markers indicate the validation locations in the zoomed regions. The annotations report case-specific CSI, CC, R2, and RMSE for the displayed case only and should not be interpreted as the full-sample scores in Table 1.

The selected case in Fig. 3 illustrates the spatial character of the retrievals. All six products locate the main precipitation systems in broadly similar areas, but Huayu-Global preserves connected rain bands and internal intensity gradients across the mosaic, whereas several baselines produce fragmented, block-like, or isolated features. The four enlarged regions show the same contrast for both elongated rain bands and localized precipitation centres.

The case-specific metrics are consistent with the visual result: Huayu-Global has the highest CSI (0.595), CC (0.686), and R2 (0.455), together with the lowest RMSE (1.528 mm), among the six displayed products. Because this is a single selected scene and some uncertainty ranges overlap, it illustrates rather than establishes the product-wide ranking; that conclusion rests on the full-sample evaluation in Table 1.
