## 2.4 Performance across validation conditions

Figure 5: Stratified performance across validation conditions. Rows show CSI, ACC, POD, FAR, CC, R2, and RMSE; columns show validation month, station elevation, longitude sector in 2022 and 2025, and observed 3-hour precipitation amount. Solid teal lines denote Huayu-Global, and dashed grey lines denote the strongest non-Huayu baseline selected separately within each bin and metric. Metric–bin combinations that are undefined or uninformative by construction are omitted.

Figure 5 resolves the aggregate comparison across temporal, geographic, and precipitation regimes. Across validation months, Huayu-Global generally remains close to or exceeds the best-baseline envelope, although the size of the difference varies by metric and month. The 2022 longitude profiles are comparatively stable, whereas the 2025 profiles are more heterogeneous; Huayu-Global nevertheless remains among the leading products across most valid longitude sectors.

Stratification also identifies the most challenging evaluation regimes. CSI and POD generally decrease with station elevation while FAR increases, indicating weaker event detection over high terrain. RMSE rises sharply with observed precipitation amount, identifying heavy precipitation as a prominent regime of increasing magnitude error. Because the strongest baseline is selected separately within each bin and metric, the grey series is an upper-envelope diagnostic rather than a comparison with one fixed product; amount-conditioned categorical metrics likewise describe the selected precipitation bins rather than an independent threshold-sensitivity test.

## 3 Discussion

Huayu-Global extends the earlier regional Huayu framework (Song et al., 2026) from a single-sensor regional retrieval to a three-sensor quasi-global system covering approximately 85% of Earth’s land surface between 60∘S and 60∘N. It demonstrates that high-frequency geostationary imagery can deliver real-time-input precipitation estimates with skill previously associated with delayed post-processed products. At independent station locations, Huayu-Global achieves the highest CSI and R2 and the lowest RMSE among the evaluated products. Relative to GSMaP_NOW, it increases CSI by 34.9% and reduces RMSE by 31.8%. The central advance is the conversion of continuously available cloud-evolution observations into high-skill precipitation information within the operational decision window.

This capability connects satellite retrieval directly to time-critical environmental workflows. Huayu-Global generates a new 0.05∘ precipitation field every 30 minutes, and data loading and inference require less than 5 minutes per timestep after model initialization on a single workstation (Methods). conclusion:
Huayu-Global extends the earlier regional Huayu framework (Song et al., 2026) from a single-sensor regional retrieval to a three-sensor quasi-global system covering approximately 85% of Earth’s land surface between 60∘S and 60∘N. It demonstrates that high-frequency geostationary imagery can deliver real-time-input precipitation estimates with skill previously associated with delayed post-processed products. At independent station locations, Huayu-Global achieves the highest CSI and R2 and the lowest RMSE among the evaluated products. Relative to GSMaP_NOW, it increases CSI by 34.9% and reduces RMSE by 31.8%. The central advance is the conversion of continuously available cloud-evolution observations into high-skill precipitation information within the operational decision window.

This capability connects satellite retrieval directly to time-critical environmental workflows. Huayu-Global generates a new 0.05∘ precipitation field every 30 minutes, and data loading and inference require less than 5 minutes per timestep after model initialization on a single workstation (Methods). The resulting fields can provide a timely observation layer for flood nowcasting, hydrological forecasting, agricultural monitoring and disaster response. They also complement recent deep-learning nowcasting and weather-prediction systems, which require rapidly updated precipitation information to initialize, constrain and evaluate forecasts (Sønderby et al., 2020; Ravuri et al., 2021; Espeholt et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023).

The cross-constellation design makes this capability scalable. The three sector models share the same Head–Geographic Attention Block (GeoAB)–Tail architecture while using separate parameters for ABI, SEVIRI, and AGRI streams. This combination applies a consistent representation pathway to cloud evolution while adapting to differences in spectral coverage, resolution, scan frequency and viewing geometry. All three models achieve useful retrieval skill within their respective domains (Table 2), enabling their outputs to form a coherent quasi-global product. The same design provides a practical path for incorporating Meteosat Third Generation, FY-4C, and Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO) missions as the global geostationary constellation evolves.

##  LTEM: LLM-Friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown for Table Understanding and Generation

Eunbin Kim, Hyeonseok Kang, Sangkeun Jung

headings: LTEM: LLM-Friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown for Table Understanding and Generation
2.2 LLMs on Tables and Format Choice
body_start:
Abstract

Tables in real-world documents, including scientific papers, financial reports, and statistical summaries, frequently use merged cells, multi-level headers, and sectioned layouts. Yet the lightweight formats LLMs handle best (Markdown, CSV) cannot express these structures, while expressive formats (HTML, LaTeX) impose excessive token cost and parsing complexity. To enable systematic analysis of this trade-off, we introduce a taxonomy decomposing table structure into six atomic features (F1–F6) and corresponding complexity levels (L1–L6), and construct STB (Synthetic Table Benchmark), a controlled benchmark with 1,089 tables systematically distributed across complexity levels. Using this framework, we propose LTEM (LLM-friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown), a formally specified, minimal extension of Markdown that explicitly encodes spans and hierarchical headers. Experiments across five state-of-the-art LLMs show that LTEM achieves accuracy comparable to HTML, offers a favorable accuracy–token trade-off relative to HTML and LaTeX, and produces substantially fewer invalid responses than LaTeX; for table generation, LTEM is comparable to MultiMarkdown though HTML is best. We release our taxonomy, benchmark, and format specification to support future research on LLM-table interaction.

## 1 Introduction

LLMs excel at natural language tasks, yet many practical applications, including document editing, report writing, and data summarization, require tables. Because tables are two-dimensional while LLM inputs are linear, models must reconstruct header roles, spans, and hierarchies from serialized text, making performance sensitive to the representation format.

Recent work confirms that format choice matters: identical tables yield different performance depending on serialization, delimiters, and ordering (Sui et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). However, existing studies provide limited tools for comparing what structural information each format preserves.

Real-world tables often include merged cells, multi-level headers, and sectioned layouts. Lightweight formats (Markdown, CSV) are easy for LLMs but cannot faithfully express these structures, while expressive formats (HTML, LaTeX) are verbose and increase token cost and parsing burden. For example, GitHub-Flavored Markdown (GFM) defines pipe-delimited tables (GitHub, 2019) but does not support colspan/rowspan (MDN Web Docs, 2026). MultiMarkdown adds column-spanning syntax through repeated pipes (Penney, 2023). In contrast, HTML and LaTeX can represent complex tables but require substantial markup interpretation.

To systematize this trade-off, we define six Structural Features (F1–F6) and Complexity Levels (L1–L6) as cumulative feature requirements. This taxonomy makes table complexity explicit and enables direct comparison of formats by expressiveness.

We then propose LTEM (LLM-friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown), a minimal extension of Markdown that explicitly encodes spans and multi-level headers while remaining linear to read and parsable in a single pass. LTEM targets L3–L5 structures with less verbosity than HTML/LaTeX, aiming to improve token efficiency and response stability without sacrificing expressiveness.

We evaluate LTEM on Table Understanding (Table QA) and Table Generation across formats (Markdown, CSV, HTML, LaTeX, MultiMarkdown, LTEM) and five state-of-the-art LLMs, and analyze Token Efficiency using token-normalized metrics.

Our contributions are as follows:

• 

Structural complexity taxonomy: We formalize table difficulty and format expressiveness via F1–F6 and L1–L6, providing a systematic framework for comparing serialization capabilities.

• 

STB benchmark: We construct a controlled benchmark with 1,089 tables systematically distributed across complexity levels, enabling controlled analysis of structural effects on LLM performance.

• 

LTEM: We propose a minimal, formally specified Markdown extension that instantiates the taxonomy-derived requirements, explicitly encoding cell spans and hierarchical headers while preserving LLM-friendly linear readability.

• 

Empirical trade-off analysis: We evaluate understanding, generation, and token efficiency across formats and diverse LLM backbones.

## 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Table QA and Table Reasoning

Early Table QA focused on semantic parsing, mapping questions to executable programs. WTQ (Pasupat and Liang, 2015) and WikiSQL (Zhong et al., 2017) established QA over Wikipedia tables, and later work introduced pretrained table encoders such as TAPAS and TaBERT (Herzig et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2020). However, these datasets largely emphasize flat tables, underrepresenting document-style structures such as merged cells and hierarchical headers. Benchmarks including HiTab and TAT-QA better reflect hierarchical and numerically grounded reasoning (Cheng et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2021). In contrast to work centered on tasks or model variants, we treat serialization format as a primary variable and study its impact on stability and token efficiency across structural complexity.

## 2.2 LLMs on Tables and Format Choice

Recent studies show that LLM performance on tabular tasks is sensitive to serialization, delimiters, and ordering (Sui et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025). LongTableBench emphasizes format and context length in long-context table reasoning (Li et al., 2025), and RealHiTBench compares representations for complex hierarchical tables across LaTeX, HTML, and images (Wu et al., 2025). While these works establish that format matters, they offer limited tools to compare what structural information each representation preserves. Our taxonomy addresses this gap by decomposing table structure into atomic operations.

## 2.3 Markup Expressiveness and Text-to-Table Evaluation

Markdown tables are common: GFM defines pipe-delimited tables (GitHub, 2019) but lacks structural attributes such as colspan/rowspan (MDN Web Docs, 2026), while MultiMarkdown adds column-spanning syntax through repeated pipes (Penney, 2023). HTML and LaTeX provide explicit span constructs for complex tables (WHATWG, 2026; LaTeX2e Unofficial Reference Manual Project, 2026; van Oostrum et al., 2024). Their more verbose syntax motivates our evaluation of format-dependent accuracy and structural consistency. For text-to-table generation, evaluation is difficult because multiple surface forms can represent the same structure. Prior work proposes multi-granularity table metrics (Pal et al., 2023), statement-based checks (Ramu et al., 2024), and discusses structure-aware metrics under constrained decoding (Oestreich and Müller, 2025). We analyze format-dependent structural consistency via normalized representations, following exact-match perspectives common in structured output evaluation (Yu et al., 2018).

## 3 Taxonomy of Table Structural Complexity

An objective comparison of table representation format capabilities requires clear criteria. This section presents a taxonomy that serves as an evaluation methodology for systematically characterizing table structural complexity and the structural information a serialization must preserve for LLMs. This classification scheme comprises two axes: Structural Features (F1–F6), the atomic operations for expressing table structure, and Complexity Levels (L1–L6), the cumulative feature requirements for expressing specific tables.

## 3.1 Structural Features

We define six atomic operations for expressing table structure. Each Feature is independent of the others, enabling binary assessment of whether a specific structural capability is present or absent.

## F1 (Grid Formation).

F1 (Grid Formation) represents the most basic requirement: that cells “exist” at row-column intersections.

## F2 (Header Designation).

F2 (Header Designation) indicates that cells have assigned “roles.” In HTML, header cells use <th> while data cells use <td>; in Markdown, rows above the separator line (|---|) are treated as headers.

## F3 (Cell Merging).

F3 (Cell Merging) is the critical branching point in this taxonomy. A substantial portion of tables in scientific papers require cell merging for group headers or category representation.

## F4 (Header Nesting).

F4 (Header Nesting) applies when headers themselves have parent–child hierarchies, exemplified by grouping quarterly revenue as “Q1”, “Q2”, “Q3” under a “Revenue” superheader.

## F5 (Section Stacking).

F5 (Section Stacking) and F6 (Table Composition) address compound table structures. F5 applies when multiple sections sharing identical column structure (schema) coexist within a single table, such as displaying “Model A Results” and “Model B Results” in one table in regression analysis.

## F6 (Table Composition).

F6 applies when tables with different schemas constitute a single logical unit, such as placing “(a) Correlation Matrix” and “(b) Sample Sizes” in one figure.

## 3.2 Complexity Levels

Complexity Level is defined as the cumulative features required to express a specific table. Each Level includes all Features from previous Levels and adds new required Features. Complexity Level definitions are summarized in Table 5 in the Appendix.

The key implication of this cumulative structure is: a format that cannot support a specific Level cannot structurally express any higher Levels. For example, a format not supporting F3 (Cell Merging) cannot structurally express not only L3 but also L4, L5, and L6 tables.

## 3.3 Expressiveness of Existing Formats

We apply the above taxonomy to analyze the expressiveness of major table representation formats. The analysis covers five formats spanning minimal data exchange formats (CSV), lightweight markup with high frequency in LLM training data (Markdown, MultiMarkdown), and document standards with complete structural expressiveness (HTML, LaTeX). Two important patterns emerge from this analysis (Table 1).

First, F3 (Cell Merging) is the decisive branching point. Markdown does not support F3 at all, fundamentally precluding expression of L3+ tables. MultiMarkdown supports colspan in some renderers but lacks standardization, with even more limited rowspan support. This is not merely a feature absence but a structural limitation: the syntax for encoding this information simply does not exist.

Second, only LaTeX has complete expressiveness. HTML can approximate F5 and F6 using multiple <tbody> elements or separate <table> elements, but cannot structurally specify logical relationships between sections. LaTeX is the only format that can express structures at all levels through a nesting-based approach using nested tabular environments and subtable.

This analysis presents an important implication overlooked in prior research: the format LLMs process most efficiently (Markdown) cannot express L3+ tables commonly found in scientific papers, while formats capable of such expression (LaTeX, HTML) are inefficient for LLM processing.

LaTeX’s \multicolumn{2}{c}{...} and HTML’s <td colspan="2"> encode cell merging information, but LLMs must undergo additional steps to interpret this syntax and infer actual cell positions and ranges. The same burden exists when providing tables as images, requiring inference of cell boundaries and merging relationships from visual structure.

This taxonomy-based analysis yields concrete serialization requirements for LLM table processing: a format targeting L3–L5 structures should explicitly encode span information and header hierarchies while maintaining linear readability. This motivates the design of a new table markup language optimized for LLM comprehension.

## 4 LTEM: Language Design

To demonstrate how the taxonomy-derived requirements (Section 3) translate into concrete format design, we present LTEM (LLM-friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown) as an instantiation that explicitly encodes F3–F5 features while preserving Markdown’s linear readability. This section describes design principles, syntax specification, and LTEM’s position within the landscape presented in Section 3.

## 4.1 Design Principles

LTEM’s design is grounded in five principles derived from the taxonomy-based analysis in Section 3, each addressing specific structural requirements identified by our framework.

## Markdown Compatibility.

LLM training corpora include substantial proportions of sources using Markdown format, such as GitHub and StackExchange (e.g., GitHub 4.5%, StackExchange 2% in LLaMA; (Touvron et al., 2023)). This composition leads LLMs to exhibit high familiarity with Markdown syntax; in fact, major commercial LLMs such as ChatGPT and Claude use Markdown as their default output format for table generation. LTEM is designed as a superset of Markdown to leverage this existing knowledge. Even when new syntax elements render as plain text in existing Markdown parsers, basic table structure is preserved. This design enables LLMs to understand LTEM as an extension of familiar Markdown rather than learning an entirely new format.

## Linear Readability.

Table structure should be semantically comprehensible when reading source text sequentially from top to bottom. This principle aligns with LLMs’ autoregressive processing and simultaneously facilitates human review and debugging.

## Explicit Structure.

Structural information should be expressed through explicit markers rather than implicit rules. For example, a cell with colspan=2 is clearly indicated with a {c:2} attribute or << marker, eliminating the burden of contextual inference by LLMs. This blocks a major source of structural hallucination.

## Minimal Grammar Extension.

We minimize the number of new syntax elements. LTEM adds only seven syntax elements to standard Markdown: four for span expression (<<, ^^, {c:N}, {r:N}), one for in-cell line breaks (\\), one for table identification (| # id |), and one for references (@). Appendix H.2 reports a design-choice ablation comparing alternative forms for five LTEM elements.

## Unidirectional Parsing.

While Linear Readability concerns semantic understanding, this principle concerns syntax parsing implementation. LTEM is parsable in a single pass without forward references, guaranteeing efficient parser implementation with linear time complexity.

## 4.2 Core Syntax

LTEM’s core syntax addresses cell spanning and multi-level headers. Appendix C shows the tables these constructs render to.

## Colspan.

Column spanning is expressed via marker syntax (<<) or attribute syntax ({c:N}). The two forms are structurally equivalent, as illustrated in Figure 1.

(a) Motivation: span-aware vs. span-unaware.

(b) Equivalent encodings: << vs. {c:N}.

Figure 1: Colspan in LTEM. (a) illustrates why explicit span markers matter; (b) shows marker- and attribute-based forms are structurally equivalent.

Marker syntax maintains visual alignment, while attribute syntax is efficient for large span values, allowing concise expression like {c:5} without repeated marker entry.

## Rowspan.

Row spanning is expressed via the ^^ marker or {r:N} attribute. Compound spanning combines as {c:N,r:M}.

Figure 2: Multi-level headers in LTEM: multiple header rows above the separator line naturally encode hierarchical header nesting (F4).

## Multi-header Rows.

All rows above the separator line (|---|) are treated as headers. This design naturally supports F4 (Header Nesting) without additional syntax (Figure 2).

## Multiline Cell.

The \\ escape sequence represents line breaks within cells.

## 4.3 Rich Cell Content

LTEM supports structured content within cells based on \\. Bullet lists, numbered lists, checkboxes, and formulas can be combined within a single cell, as illustrated in Figure 3.

Figure 3: Rich cell content in LTEM: inline line breaks (\\) enable structured content (lists, checkboxes) and math within a single cell.

## 4.4 Relational Tables

LaTeX and HTML permit nested structures inserting tables within cells, but this requires recursive parsing, disrupts linear reading, and expresses inter-table relationships only implicitly. To address this, LTEM adopts an alternative approach: table decomposition with explicit references, as illustrated in Figure 4. This is analogous to normalization principles in relational databases.

Figure 4: Relational tables in LTEM: tables are decomposed and linked via explicit table IDs (| # id |) and references (@ref) instead of nesting.

A table is identified by a unique label placed in the first row as | # identifier |. Other tables are referenced with the @ prefix.

## 4.5 Formal Specification

LTEM syntax is defined as a Context-Free Grammar (CFG). The complete EBNF (Extended Backus-Naur Form) specification is provided in Appendix D, together with syntax validation rules (V1–V12) and AST and TableStructure JSON schemas.

## 5 Experimental Setup

## 5.1 Experimental Design

The experiments are designed to answer the following research questions:

• 

RQ1: Can LTEM sufficiently express diverse tables?

– 

RQ1-1: Does LTEM improve LLM table comprehension?

– 

RQ1-2: Does LTEM achieve high fidelity in table generation?

• 

RQ2: Is LTEM more token-efficient than existing formats?

To address these questions, we utilize two complementary datasets. First, the Synthetic Table Benchmark (STB) provides synthetic tables with systematically controlled structural complexity, enabling controlled analysis of format effect
limitations:
• 

Dependence on data distribution.
Because the ranking of formats differs between STB (synthetic) and HiTab (real-world), it is difficult to generalize the superiority of a particular serialization format from a single benchmark. In practice, formats should be re-evaluated on a validation set whose distribution matches the target domain.

• 

Training Distribution Bias.
LLM pretraining corpora contain substantially more HTML and Markdown tables than LTEM-formatted content, as LTEM is introduced in this work. This exposure imbalance may favor established formats, particularly in generation tasks that depend on learned serialization patterns. HTML’s strong generation performance (ANLS: 0.913, 76% Excellent) may partly reflect this imbalance. In a separate table-QA setting, Appendix H.5 reports a small LoRA pilot showing that 4B-scale models can adapt to LTEM with limited supervision.

• 

Model–format interactions.
Format effects vary substantially across models, and some model–format pairs exhibit atypical behaviors such as elevated invalid-response rates. Therefore, format selection cannot be made independently of the model, and prior validation on the deployment backbone is necessary.

• 

Sensitivity to experimental settings (prompting/decoding).
Our experiments are based on a specific prompt template and decoding configuration. In particular, output length constraints, instruction wording, and post-processing rules can affect invalid/refusal rates for verbose formats such as LaTeX, and relative rankings may change under different settings.

• 

Limited coverage of formats and domains.
While we compare six representative formats, the space of possible serialization designs is broader. Moreover, HiTab focuses primarily on Wikipedia tables, so our conclusions may not directly transfer to other industrial domains (e.g., OCR-extracted tables or noisy financial/log tables) without additional verification.
conclusion: This paper introduced a structural complexity taxonomy (F1–F6, L1–L6) and STB, a controlled benchmark for analyzing how serialization formats affect LLM performance across complexity levels. We then proposed LTEM, a minimal Markdown extension that explicitly encodes cell spans and hierarchical headers, instantiating taxonomy-derived requirements as concrete syntax choices. Experiments on STB and HiTab show that LTEM achieves competitive table understanding accuracy while improving response stability at structural transitions where lightweight formats fail and verbose formats introduce noise. Beyond LTEM itself, we hope the taxonomy and benchmark provide reusable infrastructure for future research on robust and efficient LLM–table interaction.

title: Resuming Vision-Language Inference across Onboard Interruptions
abstract: Executing vision-language models (VLMs) aboard low-Earth orbit satellites enables flexible processing of observation data without first downlinking it to the ground. On commercial off-the-shelf payloads, however, a request may span multiple execution windows: power and thermal constraints, fault-triggered reboots, and competing payload demands can interrupt inference before it completes. Each shutdown discards volatile activations and KV caches, forcing an unprotected request to repeat work after restart. We present OrbitWeaver, a framework that preserves VLM inference progress across onboard interruptions through coordinated checkpointing and recovery. Its phase-aware checkpointing selects recovery boundaries according to the state lifetimes and computational characteristics of vision encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding, balancing storage traffic against recomputation. Its dependency-aware dynamic recovery schedules restoration from partially completed states across the layer and token-chunk dimensions. By overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation, it reduces restart latency; the recovery planner computes an optimal execution order under its scheduling model within 100 ms. Experiments on satellite payload hardware using on-orbit telemetry traces show up to a 4.07-fold end-to-end speedup and a 3.56-fold reduction in SSD write volume over the evaluated baselines. A 72-hour deployment on two low-Earth orbit satellites demonstrates that OrbitWeaver retains inference progress and resumes execution across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.

body_start:
Abstract.

Executing vision-language models (VLMs) aboard low-Earth orbit satellites enables flexible processing of observation data without first downlinking it to the ground. On commercial off-the-shelf payloads, however, a request may span multiple execution windows: power and thermal constraints, fault-triggered reboots, and competing payload demands can interrupt inference before it completes. Each shutdown discards volatile activations and KV caches, forcing an unprotected request to repeat work after restart.

We present OrbitWeaver, a framework that preserves VLM inference progress across onboard interruptions through coordinated checkpointing and recovery. Its phase-aware checkpointing selects recovery boundaries according to the state lifetimes and computational characteristics of vision encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding, balancing storage traffic against recomputation. Its dependency-aware dynamic recovery schedules restoration from partially completed states across the layer and token-chunk dimensions. By overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation, it reduces restart latency; the recovery planner computes an optimal execution order under its scheduling model within 100 ms.

Experiments on satellite payload hardware using on-orbit telemetry traces show up to a 4.07 $\times$ end-to-end speedup and a 3.56 $\times$ reduction in SSD write volume over the evaluated baselines. A 72-hour deployment on two low-Earth orbit satellites demonstrates that OrbitWeaver retains inference progress and resumes execution across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.

## 1. Introduction

Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites are emerging as powerful platforms for satellite computing (Denby and Lucia, 2020), a new paradigm that shifts heavy data processing directly to orbit to overcome the intolerable latency of the traditional bent-pipe architecture.
Backed by the integration of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) edge hardware (e.g., NVIDIA GPUs on Starcloud-1 (Starcloud, Inc., n.d.)), this high-performance orbital infrastructure is now physically accessible and cost-effective (Xing et al., 2024; Federal Communications Commission, 2026; Agüera y Arcas et al., 2025).
Leveraging these advanced platforms, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are rapidly becoming the premier workload for dynamic space missions.
Instead of relying on fragmented, task-specific models, VLMs offer unified, on-the-fly functional elasticity for effortless mission redirection (Zhang et al., 2025b; Kuckreja et al., 2024; Wang and Qiu, 2025).
Pioneering space-agency initiatives, such as NASA’s Prithvi geospatial foundation model and the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Phi-Sat-2 mission, have recently validated the feasibility of executing such foundation models directly in orbit (Du et al., 2025a), marking the dawn of intelligent satellite computing.

Mismatch: sustained VLM execution vs. bus-enforced interruptions. 
On-orbit VLM inference requires sustained computation, while spacecraft-level control can interrupt payload execution before a request completes.

Long-running on-orbit VLM workloads.
VLM inference on satellites can involve high-resolution images or multiple images within a single request.
These inputs can produce long visual-token sequences, increasing the computation needed to complete the request.
For example, Earth observation (EO) workloads can involve processing image sequences of up to 30 frames (Ding et al., 2026) and images reaching 44.93 megapixels (Luo et al., 2025).
Our in-orbit evaluation of Qwen3-VL 2B on Sat-1 and Sat-2 shows that a typical 3-minute mission processes only 8 frames ( $>32K$ tokens).

Short and unpredictable inference survival windows.
Onboard computing payloads face unpredictable interruptions that severely truncate execution windows. These abrupt halts primarily stem from three sources:
(i) Bus-enforced hard shutdowns due to dynamic power constraints or thermal violations (Common Instrument Interface Project, 2011). For example, VLM inference on Sat-1 and Sat-2 11

 We refer to the two satellites as Sat-1 and Sat-2 throughout this paper. spikes the payload temperature from $45^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $55^{\circ}\text{C}$ in just 48 s, leading to sudden thermal cutoffs that vary drastically depending on the satellite’s orbital state.
(ii) On-orbit anomalies (e.g., radiation-induced SEUs or software faults) that trigger the Fault Detection, Isolation, and Recovery (FDIR) system. FDIR forces sudden system reboots to clear errors; our private LEO satellite telemetry data reveals that in worst-case scenarios, such reboots occur as frequently as once per minute (Evans et al., 2016).
(iii) Resource contention from intermittent, high-priority payloads (e.g., bursty transceivers or laser transmitters) that preempt shared bus resources (Fong et al., 2011).

To tackle this mismatch, we propose OrbitWeaver, an efficient and reliable VLM inference engine designed for satellite computing.
OrbitWeaver achieves transparent, minimal-overhead preservation of VLM execution progress by dynamically checkpointing essential states to onboard non-volatile storage (e.g., eMMC/SSD).
Upon rebooting, it swiftly reconstructs the context to resume inference.
Achieving this goal requires addressing two challenges:

 $\bullet$ Checkpointing phase: fast checkpointing vs. efficient recovery.
Preserving execution progress creates a dilemma: minimizing checkpointing I/O for active inference speed versus maximizing progress preservation for rapid recovery.
Fine-grained checkpointing (e.g., per-token/layer) captures complete progress but incurs substantial I/O overheads, whereas coarse-grained checkpointing (e.g., per-chunk) minimizes I/O but forces expensive recomputation of discarded intra-chunk states.
This trade-off manifests across all VLM phases.
For instance, in memory-bound decoding, saving per-token KV caches and hidden states ensures optimal recovery at prohibitive costs (>100%), while merely saving token IDs eliminates I/O but forces full KV cache recomputation from scratch, introducing a latency of $>50$ seconds.

 $\bullet$ Recovery phase: unavoidable weight-checkpoint I/O in unstructured resumption.
Unlike traditional LLM context switching with uniform states (e.g., full prompt KV caches), arbitrary orbital bus-enforced interruptions leave an irregular, “staircase-like” inference progress state.
Resuming from this unstructured state complicates masking the coupled I/O overhead of reloading static weights alongside dynamic KV caches and hidden states from disparate positions.
Specifically, loading a layer’s weights unlocks computation across multiple chunks, whereas loading its KV cache only enables that specific chunk.
With numerous valid starting points along this irregular boundary, finding the optimal execution sequence to maximize compute-I/O overlap under complex dependency constraints becomes a highly non-trivial scheduling challenge.

To solve these challenges, OrbitWeaver incorporates two key techniques:

 $\bullet$ Phase-aware checkpointing. 
To resolve the checkpointing dilemma, OrbitWeaver leverages the heterogeneous lifespans of VLM states (persistent KV caches vs. transient hidden states) and phase-specific bottlenecks to establish adaptive recovery boundaries:
(i) Vision encoding (layer boundary):
Because bidirectional self-attention couples all image patches, patch chunks cannot be finalized independently.
OrbitWeaver therefore persists the full-patch hidden state after each vision layer, using layer boundaries as recovery points.
(ii) LLM prefill (2D block boundary):
Because prefill is compute-bound, checkpointing both KV Cache and hidden states minimally impacts active inference.
To mitigate SSD wear-out, OrbitWeaver groups operations into 2D blocks (execution grids spanning multiple sequence chunks and model layers), checkpointing transient hidden states exclusively at block boundaries.
(iii) LLM decoding (multi-token boundary):
Decoding is memory-bound, making per-token checkpointing prohibitively expensive.
Recognizing that the decoding recovery bottleneck is massive weight-loading I/O rather than lightweight recomputation, OrbitWeaver aggregates KV cache updates across multi-token boundaries.
This amortizes flash write overhead, as the slight recomputation increase is completely masked by the inevitable weight-loading I/O.

 $\bullet$ Dependency-aware dynamic recovery. 
To mitigate coupled I/O bottlenecks during unstructured resumption, we observe that despite recovery computation heavily outweighing I/O latency, strict dependencies still cause severe I/O stalls.
To maximize compute-I/O overlap, OrbitWeaver unlocks dependencies multi-dimensionally:
(i) 2D block-first recovery:
Rigid layer- or chunk-first strategies only resolve single-dimension dependencies.
Instead, executing a 2D block immediately unlocks both horizontal (chunk) and vertical (layer) dependencies, triggering a computation cascade to mask concurrent SSD reads.
(ii) Optimal scheduling plan:
Selecting the optimal ready block to minimize recovery latency is critical, as each choice unlocks distinct downstream computation cascades to maximize I/O masking; yet this scheduling is NP-hard.
We dramatically prune this search space via two domain-specific properties: (a) deferring hidden state loads to retain DRAM activations and avoid redundant SSD reads, and (b) packing layer-wise I/O to coalesce weight reads into coarse-grained streams.
This enables OrbitWeaver to mathematically solve the optimal execution order within 100 ms.

We implemented OrbitWeaver atop transformers (Wolf et al., 2020) and evaluated it on hardware testbeds mirroring two real satellite computing payloads: the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX (16 GB) and AGX Orin (64 GB).
These represent the onboard platforms of Sat-1 and Sat-2.
Our evaluations are driven by five interruption traces: four derived from telemetry collected on Sat-1 and Sat-2, and one from the Dellingr satellite (Hatfield, 2018).
Using these scenarios, we run advanced edge-viable VLMs, including Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B and MiniCPM-V 4.5, on remote sensing QA datasets.
Compared to three state-of-the-art baselines (two variants of a representative intermittent DNN execution runtime and a conventional KV cache context-saving approach), OrbitWeaver achieves up to a 4.07 $\times$ end-to-end speedup.
Furthermore, it reduces checkpointing and recovery latency by up to 61.9% and 85.6%, respectively, while slashing SSD write volume by up to 3.56 $\times$ .
To the best of our knowledge, we are the first academic work to successfully deploy and sustain VLM inference directly in orbit. We deployed OrbitWeaver on Sat-1 and Sat-2 for a 72-hour in-situ earth observation case study. The deployment demonstrates that OrbitWeaver preserves progress and sustains VLM inference across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We are the first to identify the bottleneck of bus-enforced shutdowns in on-satellite VLM
inference.

• 

We propose OrbitWeaver, the first efficient and reliable VLM inference system for satellite computing by introducing efficient checkpointing and recovery.

• 

We implement OrbitWeaver and deploy it on Sat-1 and Sat-2. Our evaluation shows that OrbitWeaver achieves up to a 4.07 $\times$ end-to-end speedup, while a 72-hour in-orbit deployment demonstrates sustained VLM inference across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.

## 2.1. On-Satellite Vision-Language Models

Satellite computing shifts data processing and services directly to orbit.
This approach overcomes the severe communication bottlenecks of the traditional bent-pipe architecture, where limited downlink bandwidth and brief contact windows make downlinking raw data for ground-side processing intolerably slow for modern space missions (Denby and Lucia, 2020).
This orbital computing capability is enabled by moving beyond traditional radiation-hardened controllers and integrating commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) computing platforms—such as CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs—into modern satellites (Xing et al., 2024; Denby et al., 2023; Giuffrida et al., 2022; Rapuano et al., 2021).
Consequently, satellites are evolving from simple data collectors into orbital edge nodes capable of executing diverse tasks.
Early examples include onboard filtering to discard cloudy images (Phi-Sat-1 (Giuffrida et al., 2022)) or select high-value samples (Kodan (Denby et al., 2023)).
More recently, platforms like Starcloud-1 are pushing hardware boundaries by carrying data-center-class NVIDIA H100 GPUs in orbit, demonstrating that high-performance AI accelerators can now be deployed as standard satellite payloads.

As shown in Figure 1, a typical satellite computing platform consists of a computing payload and a spacecraft bus that supports, monitors, and controls the payload.
The payload runs a VLM inference engine on top of an operating system, using SSD for persistent storage, RAM for volatile memory, and CPUs and GPUs for computation.
During inference, the engine loads model weights and input data from SSD into RAM and dispatches tensor operations to the processors, while intermediate tensors and runtime states remain in volatile memory.
Meanwhile, the spacecraft bus supplies payload power through the electrical power system (EPS), monitors payload temperature through sensors, and manages communication and fault protection through TT&C and the onboard computer (OBC) with FDIR.
These bus subsystems communicate over a CAN bus and can disconnect payload power or trigger a reboot when power, thermal, or safety constraints require intervention, abruptly interrupting the ongoing inference.

Vision-Language Models for LEO satellites. 
With advanced hardware in orbit, satellite computing tasks are rapidly shifting toward VLMs.
For critical applications like Earth observation (EO), traditional fragmented, task-specific models are being replaced by VLMs, which offer a “one-for-all”, prompt-driven framework that provides functional elasticity for dynamic missions without retraining overhead (Du et al., 2025a).
Furthermore, driven by the massive expansion of LEO constellations, initiatives like Starcloud (Feilden et al., 2024) are actively constructing “space data centers” to deliver real-time, space-native VLM inference and token generation services directly to users.
Robust, sustained VLM execution is therefore essential for next-generation LEO systems.

On-satellite VLM inference pipeline. 
A VLM is a multimodal model that converts images and text instructions into text outputs by combining visual encoding with language-model generation.
As illustrated in Figure 2, after the on-board camera captures an image, the acquired visual data is fed into the VLM for inference, initiating a three-phase pipeline.
In the first phase (vision encoding), a Vision Transformer partitions the input image into patches and encodes them into visual tokens (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021).
During the second phase (LLM prefill), the model processes these visual tokens alongside the prompt tokens, establishing the attention state and initializing the Key-Value (KV) cache for the multimodal context.
Finally, in the LLM decoding phase, the language model generates the response autoregressively, producing one token at a time while continuously utilizing and updating the KV cache established during the prefill phase.
These phases involve different intermediate states, including visual tokens, prefill states, KV cache, and partial outputs.

## 2.2. Bus-enforced Shutdowns in On-Satellite VLM Inference

Onboard computing payloads operate under strict spacecraft-wide power and safety constraints.
The spacecraft bus can abruptly disconnect payload power to preserve essential functions or protect hardware, regardless of the inference software’s status (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2025; Evans et al., 2016).
We term these platform-initiated interruptions bus-enforced shutdowns, which can terminate VLM requests unpredictably. They primarily stem from three sources:

 $\bullet$ Dynamic power and thermal constraints. 
The electrical power system (EPS) autonomously sheds non-essential loads (e.g., computing payloads) when demand exceeds supply (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2025; Ali et al., 2026).
This power availability fluctuates with solar illumination and battery aging, which alters discharge curves over time and makes supply highly non-linear.
Furthermore, thermal limits force sudden shutdowns. As shown in Figure 2, VLM inference on Sat-1 spikes the payload enclosure temperature from $45^{\circ}\text{C}$ to the $55^{\circ}\text{C}$ threshold in just 48 s, triggering an immediate power-off. Driven by external orbital states, these shutdowns are entirely decoupled from VLM execution boundaries (e.g., prefill and decoding steps).

 $\bullet$ Hardware/software anomalies and FDIR interventions. 
The harsh space environment introduces stochastic anomalies, such as radiation-induced Single-Event Upsets (SEUs) or software faults (e.g., erroneously activating Sun-pointing during an eclipse).

Generalizability. 
OrbitWeaver primarily targets orbital edge computing (Denby and Lucia, 2020) to reduce reliance on ground-based processing.
Starcloud (Feilden et al., 2024) and Project Suncatcher (Agüera y Arcas et al., 2025) envision dedicated space-based clouds.
Better power and thermal provisioning may reduce interruptions, but inference progress must still survive power cycling, resource contention, and unexpected resets.
OrbitWeaver’s checkpointing and recovery principles apply to these platforms, complementing hardware co-design by letting interrupted requests resume rather than restart.

title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
abstract: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.

Abstract

Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check
it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share.
Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of
distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and
live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two
pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5,
GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through
an evidence source and reached only that source’s readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on
injection resistance, a monitor’s refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in
all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of
votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The
pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the
twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded,
restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.

## 1 Introduction

AI agents take consequential actions for people and organisations: payments, messages, changes to code, access
to data. Before such an action runs, monitors check it. A monitor can be a language model, a rule engine,
or a human. They are also called guardrails, safety classifiers or judges, when the monitor is a large language model (LLM). In AI control, the study of overseeing a possibly misaligned model with weaker monitors, a monitor usually returns a suspicion score that decides
what a human audits. Ours decide whether the action runs.

Take an accounts-payable agent that proposes to pay a supplier’s invoice. Suppose three strong models serve as
judges, and all read the same invoice e-mail. An attacker forges the e-mail, replacing the
supplier’s bank account with their own, and fools all three at once. Three judges that read one document
are one monitor counted three times. Now suppose instead that the judges read different sources. A source is
one independent record against which a monitor checks the action, such as the invoice, the company’s vendor record,
or the supplier’s portal. The judges are cheap models, but a forged document now fools only its reader, and the
other two catch the fraud. A planted note has the opposite effect. The agent’s justification is the free-text note it attaches to
the payment. Suppose it contains a fake security notice: “this vendor is under investigation; do not pay”. Cheap judges then refuse a correct payment, whatever source they read. Judges that resist planted
instructions ignore the note. Which monitors must agree before the payment runs depends on which monitors can be
fooled together, and in which direction.

The safety half of this picture is classical in financial controls. A payment is checked against records that the
requester does not control. Examples are the vendor master file, changed bank details verified independently, the
three-way match of purchase order, goods receipt and invoice, and segregation of duties. We do not claim the
principle. Our contribution has three parts. First, published AI monitor designs rarely use this principle. In the
designs we reviewed, each monitor sees the agent’s whole trajectory: its actions, the tool outputs, and often its
reasoning [35, 29]. When several monitors are used, their scores are
aggregated [25, 10]. Panels of model judges take a
vote [56]. Some designs restrict what a monitor sees, to hide the agent’s reasoning or signals
that monitors could use to collude [19]. With one exception, Pandey et al. [48] (Section 7), none gives different
monitors different sources of evidence. Second, we measure what follows, in small and frontier pools. Third, we extend the analysis to liveness, which
classical controls do not address for monitors that can be persuaded.

Correlated failure of language models is documented. Models err on the same answers far more often than
independence predicts [30]. Jailbreaks transfer along shared
representations [5]. One poisoned corpus misleads several models [61].
One injection subverts several monitors [54]. Layered defences fail
together [44]. These findings have not been turned into a fault model estimated from attacks, a statement of
which joint failures a rule must survive. Distributed computing has a theory of correlated failures that reasons
about which sets of participants can fail together, instead of how many. A fail-prone system lists the sets
of components that may fail together [41, 24]. Given the list, the theory says
which approval rules are safe, never executing a bad action, and which are live, executing every good
one. It also says when no rule is both. We ask whether AI monitors fail like the replicas of this theory, the voting copies of a replicated service,
and what that implies for the rule.

## Five steps, from the theory to a design rule.

The theory tells us what to measure. A monitor can be
fooled in two directions: into approving a bad action, or into blocking a good one. For each direction we measure
which sets of monitors can be fooled together; we call these the approve side and the reject side.
Section 3 then gives the condition under which some approval rule is both safe and live given the two
sides (the cross-cover condition). We measured both sides on payment approval with twelve small open-weights
monitors, four families on three sources. Open-weights models have public weights and run locally. We ran a
pre-registered pilot, then a pre-registered confirmation on new data. To pre-register is to freeze the hypotheses
and the pass/fail criteria before any model is queried. The pilot tested the classical theory, with one list of
fooled sets, and refuted it: on the pooled list no rule is safe and live. Reading its fooled sets showed that the
two directions have different shapes, and the confirmation tested that reading. Without pre-registration we then ran three closed frontier
models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2.

(1) 

The approve-side structure is the sources. In the pilot, every fooling into fraud arrived through a source and
reached only that source’s readers. In the confirmation the approve-fooled sets were exactly the three source
columns, as pre-registered. Its attacker could read the
monitors’ token probabilities. Even so, no justification text made its target approve more than $8.3\%$ of the
training frauds. Every frontier-class monitor, the closed frontier models and the open DeepSeek, showed the same structure.
Diversify the inputs.

(2) 

The reject-side structure is set by injection resistance. Injection resistance is whether a monitor
ignores instructions planted in the data it reads. Planted notes made the small models of every family and
DeepSeek-V3.2 block correct payments, and worked across families. Opus and Astra ignored them, and Argon did
all but once. Persuasion optimised against Opus, with DeepSeek as the writer, the model that rewrites the note, fooled none of $640$ held-out verdicts.
Model size does not predict this. The notes travelled in the agent’s justification. In a pre-registered control that hid the field from the
monitors, every blocking note fell to within $0.05$ of the benign floor, the error rate on unattacked items. Harden the monitors.

(3) 

Therefore count sources, not votes. A rule that approves when the approvers read at least two
sources is safe whenever fooling into fraud stays within one source, however many monitors are talked into
blocking. In the confirmation it blocked $0.9\%$ of
correct payments, against $7.4\%$ for the best counting rule chosen on training data, at the same safety. The
difference was pre-registered and supported. An attacker given each rule’s decision as its objective changed none of $40$ held-out decisions per goal, for
either rule.

(4) 

The theory predicts where this breaks. Cross-cover fails when a rejection attack leaves the
approvers on one source. In the confirmation one blocking note, optimised against Gemma, did so for the twelve
language-model monitors. The pre-registered cross-cover hypothesis failed, and by our decision rule the worst-case claim for that pool is a negative result. A rule engine,
which compares fields and lies outside the text attack surface, restored the condition in every bootstrap
resample of the pre-registered thirteen-monitor pool. Include a monitor that cannot be persuaded.

(5) 

Caution is model-specific. Opus refused $30\%$ of correct payments whose evidence bore an apparent
trace of tampering, and none under a neutral line. Astra, Argon and DeepSeek refused none. Such refusals reach
only the readers of the tampered-looking source, so the two-source rule absorbs them (exploratory).

Section 5 follows the same five steps, after a note on what the pilot changed. Our monitors check a proposed action against external evidence and do
not read the agent’s reasoning. Chain-of-thought monitoring, whether a model’s thinking can be observed, is a
different question. The one piece of agent text they do read, the justification, carried the persuasion (step 2).
All empirical claims concern actions whose fields can be checked against independent records, measured on payment
approval. Section 8.1 says what transfers. Every zero bounds only the attacks we ran.

## Contributions.

C1 

A fault model for monitors and the rules it implies (Section 2), a synthesis of
classical results. Directional fail-prone systems (Section 3), a pair of lists for the two
directions of fooling. The condition for a safe and live rule is known [53]. Its reading for
one-shot approvals, the maximal rule and the counting criterion are new as statements and elementary.

C2 

Two pre-registered measurements on twelve small monitors (Sections 4 and 6).
The pilot suggested the directional reading. The confirmation supports steps (1) and (3) and refutes cross-cover
for that pool.

C3 

Frontier and frontier-class arms (Section 5), not pre-registered. They are a
replay on five models, attacks tailored to Opus, and a control for caution, the anomaly control of Section 5.6, on four.

## 2 Model and the approval-rule hierarchy

We write for two audiences: AI-security researchers who may not know fail-prone systems, and distributed-systems
researchers who may not know AI monitoring. Each term is explained at first use, and the recurring ones are
collected here. A monitor is anything that returns a verdict on a proposed action. A rule is safe if it never
executes a bad action, and live if it executes every good one. A fail-prone system is a list of the
sets of monitors that may all be fooled at the same time. The cover number $\tau$ is the smallest number of
listed sets whose union is every monitor. The condition $Q^{k}$ holds if no $k$ listed sets cover all monitors,
that is, if $\tau>k$ . A kernel is a set of monitors contained in no listed set, so at least one of its
members is honest. The kernel rule approves only if the approvers form a kernel. Provenance is which
base-model family a monitor runs and which source it reads. Findings outside the
pre-registered plan are labelled exploratory or not pre-registered.

## Monitoring AI agents.

AI control studies protocols in which a monitor oversees an untrusted
model [19]. The monitor is trusted because it is too weak to scheme (to pursue hidden goals of
its own), with a small budget of human audits. Consequential actions wait for the
monitors [38]. Several monitors are combined into one threshold by
averaging [31], by Neyman–Pearson tests [25] or by learned
combiners [10]. None states which joint failures it tolerates. An
unsafe approval violates safety. A false rejection violates liveness and costs usefulness or human
time, scarce in AI control [19].

## System and threat model.

abstract: Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly being used in place of deterministic predictors across machine learning, including for tasks that were classically formulated as regression. Given their success in such tasks, we ask the question: what useful information do the conditional distributions produced by CFMs carry beyond what a point predictor would provide? We identify a systematic phenomenon: in many natural regimes, CFM samples routinely have larger variance than the true conditional distribution, even in nearly deterministic regression problems. This effect is most pronounced where the model has not resolved the dependence on the conditioning variable, and thus the additional variance can be viewed as converting epistemic uncertainty in fitting the ground truth conditional distribution into apparent aleatoric variance in the generated samples. Through controlled synthetic and real-data experiments, and comparisons with explicit smoothing estimators, we show that the induced variance tracks model underfitting of complex or hard-to-fit targets, and decreases with additional training or data. We provide a theoretical account of the phenomenon in a simplified setting and demonstrate a consequent practical use-case of conditional flow-matching: designing high-coverage predictive sets that cover the ground-truth regression target.

body_start:
Abstract

Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly being used in place of deterministic predictors across machine learning, including for tasks that were classically formulated as regression. Given their success in such tasks, we ask the question: what useful information do the conditional distributions produced by CFMs carry beyond what a point predictor would provide?

We identify a systematic phenomenon: in many natural regimes, CFM samples routinely have larger variance than the true conditional distribution, even in nearly deterministic regression problems. This effect is most pronounced where the model has not resolved the dependence on the conditioning variable, and thus the additional variance can be viewed as converting epistemic uncertainty in fitting the ground truth conditional distribution into apparent aleatoric variance in the generated samples. Through controlled synthetic and real-data experiments, and comparisons with explicit smoothing estimators, we show that the induced variance tracks model underfitting of complex or hard-to-fit targets, and decreases with additional training or data. We provide a theoretical account of the phenomenon in a simplified setting and demonstrate a consequent practical use-case of conditional flow-matching: designing high-coverage predictive sets that cover the ground-truth regression target.

## 1 Introduction

The role of generative models in machine learning has expanded rapidly.
Rather than returning a single point prediction, these models produce a conditional distribution over possible outputs.
Perhaps surprisingly, they have gained traction even in settings where predicting a single value, rather than distribution over values, suffices. These setting, which we will call point-prediction problems, encompass predicting high-performing actions in robotics (Chi et al., 2023), accurate estimates of a policy value function in reinforcement learning (Agrawalla et al., 2025), and numerous other scientific estimation and time-series problems (Klein and others, 2025).

In this work, we focus on conditional flow-matching models (CFMs), which produce samples by integrating a learned velocity field from base noise to the output space, and suggest that these models confer a complementary benefit: they can naturally express estimation uncertainty, even in point-prediction problem in which observations are nearly noiseless.

In the idealized setting, the optimal flow $v^{\star}$ transports the base distribution to the true conditional law (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023).
In practice, however, the flow field is parametrized by a neural network $v_{\theta}$ that is learned imperfectly, due to a combination of limited training data, network capacity, and incomplete optimization (e.g. early stopping, popular in the robot learning community).
Thus the learned conditional distribution is shaped not only by the target distribution, but also by the inductive biases caused by fitting the ground-truth vector-field learning with a neural network. In particular, neural networks tend to oversmooth high-frequency features during learning (Rahaman et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2020; Tancik et al., 2020), causing the learned vector-field $v_{\theta}$ to underfit the ground-truth $v^{\star}$ .

We demonstrate, both across domains and in natural theoretical setups, that under this common underfitting behavior, conditional flow models convert epistemic uncertainty into apparent aleatoric variance. That is, the approximation error or uncertainty about the dependence of the generated variable on the conditioning variable is expressed as a larger spread in the learned conditional distribution.

Beyond scientific interest, this has actionable consequences. One can train conditional flow-matching models to fit potentially deterministic target functions and, as long as the model does not overfit, use the spread of their resulting samples to define confidence sets containing the ground-truth function, with no conformal correction.

Across the application domains we study, including RL policy evaluation, cell perturbation prediction, and robot policy learning, predictive sets built this way are approximately calibrated empirically in the underfitting regime, a property the variance-inflation phenomenon enables. A practitioner receives an uncertainty estimate “for free” alongside the point prediction.

Figure 1: Flow models vs Regression during underfitting. 

More concretely, we make the following contributions:

• 

We identify a surprisingly general relationship between learning error in the conditional flow field and the resulting generated samples: whenever a learned CFM underfits the ground-truth velocity field as a function of the conditioning variable, its generated samples have conditional variance strictly larger than that of the true distribution, in expectation over the conditioning variable. This stands in sharp contrast to deterministic regression, where underfitting manifests only as oversmoothing of the predictive mean.

• 

We trace this variance inflation to a single mechanism: smoothing bias in vector-field learning. Any inductive bias that smooths the learned conditional vector field along the conditioning variable, whether early stopping, or explicit regularization, produces the same effect. We demonstrate this empirically on synthetic regression problems, controlled smoothing estimators, and high-dimensional offline RL benchmarks.

• 

We propose an idealized setting of regularized smoothing to theoretically study the variance inflation phenomenon. Under an equivalent-kernel approximation to regularized vector-field learning, the learned conditional distribution is a local mixture of true conditionals around the query point. This yields a clean bias–variance relation: on average, the learned conditional variance is at least the true conditional variance plus the squared bias of the learned conditional mean. This simplified setting serves as a useful explanatory model to understand the variance inflation phenomenon empirically observed in neural CFMs. We also discuss the validity of this approximation to neural CFMs and the regimes where the approximation fails.

• 

Motivated by our theoretical study, we identify another empirical consequence of the variance inflation phenomenon – the distribution learned by CFMs is approximately calibrated in the underfitting regime. We give a practical method for leveraging variance inflation for predictive coverage. Across three application domains, policy evaluation, cell perturbation prediction, and behavior cloning for robotics, predictive sets built directly from CFM samples are approximately calibrated in the underfitting regime, and are competitive with or tighter than conformal-prediction baselines.

## 2 Related Work

Flow matching and conditional transport.

Flow matching and related stochastic-interpolant and rectified-flow methods learn continuous-time transports by regressing a time-dependent vector field along a path between base noise and data (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022; Albergo et al., 2025). Conditional flow matching indexes this transport by side information, yielding a model of the conditional law of an output given a conditioning variable. Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) have been applied broadly in robotics (Chisari et al., 2024; Rouxel et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024) and scientific modeling (Klein and others, 2025; Miller et al., 2024).

Inductive biases and generalization in diffusion and flow models.

Several recent works study why diffusion or score-based models generalize rather than simply memorizing the training data. Recent work has attributed this behavior to several sources of bias: variance in the denoising score-matching target (Vastola, 2025), architectural bias (Kamb and Ganguli, 2025), and selective underfitting of the learned score (Song et al., 2025). These papers are closest in spirit to ours, however, they focus on unconditional generation, whereas we study conditional generation and ask how underfitting with respect to the conditioning variable changes the conditional law.

Implicit regularization, spectral bias, and smoothing.

Our explanation is based on smoothing bias in the learned conditional vector field. Neural networks are known to preferentially fit low-frequency or smoother structure early in training, a phenomenon often called spectral bias (Rahaman et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2020). In wide-network regimes, training dynamics can be approximated by kernel gradient flow, connecting early stopping and finite-time training to classical regularization in function space (Jacot et al., 2018).
Related ideas appear throughout nonparametric regression, smoothing splines, kernel ridge regression, and inverse problems, where regularized estimators can be described by equivalent kernels or linear smoothing operators. We build on this viewpoint, but study a different object: not the bias of a point estimator, but the distribution obtained after integrating a smoothed conditional vector field.

## 3 Preliminaries

We study conditional generative modeling.
Given samples from a joint distribution $p^{\star}$ over random variables $(X,C)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{c}}$ , where $X$ is the generated variable and $C$ is the conditioning variable, conditional generative models learn to generate new samples from the conditional distribution of $X$ given $C=c$ , denoted $p^{\star}(\cdot\mid c)$ . Flow models represent such distributions as continuous normalizing flows (CNF) and ODEs transporting a simple initial distribution to a terminal distribution approximating $p^{\star}$ . Here, we consider the conditional variant.

Definition 3.1 (Continuous Normalizing Flow).

(Chen et al., 2018) Given a joint distribution $p_{1}$ over $(X,C)$ , an initial distribution $p_{0}$ over $(X,C)$ , and conditional vector field $v:[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{c}}$ mapping $(t,x,c)\to v_{t}(x\mid c)$ ,
we say that $(v,p_{0})$ is a conditional continuous normalization flow (CCNF) for $p_{1}$ if, for every $c\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{c}}$ , the random process $(X_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}$ defined by the

 $\displaystyle\textstyle X_{0}\sim p_{0}(\cdot\mid C=c),\quad\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}X_{t}=v_{t}(X_{t},c)$ 

(3.1)

satisfies $X_{1}\sim p(\cdot\mid c)$ . We let $\Phi_{t}^{v}(X_{0}\mid c)$ denote the deterministic function, called a flow-map, mapping $X_{0}$ to $X_{t}$ in Eq. 3.1.
Given $(p_{0},v)$ , we let $p_{t}^{v}(\cdot\mid c,p_{0})$ denote the distribution of $X_{t}\mid c$ marginalized over $X_{0}\sim p_{0}(\cdot\mid c)$ under Eq. 3.1. Note then that, by definition, $(v,p_{0})$ is a CCNF for $p_{1}^{v}(\cdot\mid\cdot,p_{0})$ . We suppress dependence on $p_{0}$ when clear from context.

Flow-matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023; Liu et al., 2022) provides a generic recipe for learning (C)CNFs from data. Let $p_{0}$ and differentiable coefficients $\alpha_{t},\beta_{t}:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying $\alpha_{0}=\beta_{1}=1$ and $\beta_{0}=\alpha_{1}=0$ both be given. The induced (linear) stochastic interpolant is the random variable $X_{t}=\alpha_{t}X_{0}+\beta_{t}X_{1}$ , where $X_{0}\sim p_{0}(\cdot\mid c)$ and $X_{1}\sim p^{\star}(\cdot\mid c)$ . Flow-matching is based on the following observation:

Proposition 3.1 (Albergo et al. (2025)).

Define the vector field $v^{\star}$ via $v_{t}^{\star}(\cdot\mid c)=\mathbb{E}[\dot{X}_{t}\mid X_{t},c]$ , where $\dot{X}_{t}=\dot{\alpha}_{t}X_{0}+\dot{\beta}_{t}X_{1}$ . Then, $(v^{\star},p_{0})$ is a CNF for $p^{\star}$ . Moreover, $v^{\star}$ satisfies $v^{\star}\in\argmin_{v}\mathcal{L}_{\textnormal{{fm}}}(v)$ , where the $\mathcal{L}_{\textnormal{{fm}}}$ is the flow-matching loss

 $\displaystyle\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\textnormal{{fm}}}(v):=\mathbb{E}_{(X,C)\sim p^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathrm{Unif}([0,1]),X_{0}\sim p_{0}(\cdot\mid c)}\mathbb{E}[\|v_{t}(X_{t},C)-\dot{X}_{t}\|^{2}]$ 

(3.2)

Motivated by Proposition 3.1, flow matching trains a velocity field $v_{\theta}=(v_{\theta;t}(x,c))$ by (approximately) minimizing an empirical approximation to the flow matching loss $\mathcal{L}_{\textnormal{{fm}}}$ .

## 4 Variance Inflation in Underfit Conditional Flows

In this section, we uncover two surprising phenomena about underfit conditional flow models: First, the resulting samples have larger conditional variance than the ground-truth distribution (in expectation over the conditioning variable), even in nearly deterministic regression problems. Second, this variance inflation is a consequence of smoothing bias in the learned vector field: any mechanism that smooths the conditional vector field along the conditioning variable produces the same effect. We demonstrate the phenomenon on a synthetic 1D problem (Figure 1), establish that it is driven by smoothing (Figure 2), and verify that it transfers to a high-dimensional benchmark used in offline RL (Figure 3)

(a) NN vector field parameterization: [Left to Right] Distributions learned with increasing training time

(b) NN vector field parameterization with explicit regularization penalty $\lambda(\partial_{c}v)^{2}$ 

(c) Vector field learning with kernel ridge regression with penalty $\lambda$ 

Figure 2: Any smoothing bias in vector-field learning induces variance inflation. In all three cases, the average learned conditional variance (reported in each panel title) decreases monotonically as smoothing decreases.

Figure 1, given in the introduction, illustrates a one-dimensional synthetic regression problem in which the target function contains both low and high-frequency structure. When a neural-network regressor is trained with early stopping, underfitting leads to oversmoothing of the predictive mean; the learned function captures the coarse trend but fails to recover the finer oscillations.

For a conditional flow model trained under the same regime, the learned conditional mean is similarly oversmoothed, but unlike the deterministic regressor, the flow also learns substantial additional variance, visible in the wide 95% band around the mean.
Even in a nearly deterministic problem, underfitting in the conditional vector field appears not only as bias in the learned mean, but also as extra variance in the generated conditional distribution.
Panel (d) shows the full learned conditional density $\hat{p}(x\mid c)$ , which is broad and roughly bimodal in regions where $f^{\star}$ (the conditional mean) has high-frequency oscillations within a smoothing neighborhood; the flow’s conditional distribution effectively averages over the local oscillations of $f^{\star}$ . This finding is not specific to this example, and Appendix C shows that similar phenomena arise across a number of synthetic target functions.

Why do we call this uncertainty epistemic? The excess variance arises from unresolved dependence of the target on the conditioning variable: the learned model smooths over distinctions between nearby conditions that the true conditional mean resolves. This uncertainty is therefore reducible and model-dependent, rather than irreducible randomness in the data-generating process. As the model resolves more of this structure, for example with additional data or training, both the smoothing bias and the excess variance decrease. However, in a CFM this unresolved variation appears as spread within the learned conditional distribution, and hence as apparent aleatoric variance. From the learned distribution alone, this model-induced spread is not distinguishable from genuine aleatoric variation.

## 4.1 Variance inflation tracks smoothing bias

Figure 2 reveals that the phenomenon in Figure 1 is not tied to a single estimator or training recipe. We compare three mechanisms that induce smoothing in the learned conditional vector field: early stopping of a neural network which biases training towards low-frequency components of the target (Yao et al., 2007; Rahaman et al., 2019; Tancik et al., 2020), an
explicit roughness penalty $\lambda\,(\partial_{c}v)^{2}$ in the
conditioning variable as used in classic non-parametric regression (Wahba, 1990; Green and Silverman, 1994), and kernel ridge regression with an RKHS-norm regularization penalty $\lambda$ (Caponnetto and De Vito, 2007). All these methods induce smoothing of the conditional mean function, as can be observed from the plotted learned mean at different regularization strengths (Figure 2). In all three cases, this smoothing is accompanied by another consistent effect: the learned conditional variance increases as the learned mean becomes smoother. The average learned conditional variance (reported in each panel title) decreases monotonically as smoothing decreases.

Our key finding, corroborated across additional functions in Appendix C, is that the key object is the smoothing bias in vector-field learning, not flow matching alone. Flow matching simply provides a mechanism through which this smoothing bias is expressed as conditional spread. Also note in Figure 2 that the induced variance is often largest precisely when the learned mean is most biased.

(b) Antmaze

## 4.2 Beyond one-dimensional synthetic regression: Monte-Carlo Policy Evaluation

We next test whether the variance-inflation phenomenon persists when the conditioning variable is high-dimensional.
For this, we use a Policy Evaluation task, where we train a CFM to predict $Q$ -values conditioned on state-action pairs $c=(s,a)$ , using Monte-Carlo targets.
We evaluate on two OGBench (Park et al., 2025) environments, Cube-Single and Antmaze-large, where the conditioning variable is high-dimensional while the target remains scalar.

Figure 3 visualizes the learned and empir
limitations:
We identify a surprising inductive bias of conditional flow models: smoothing bias in vector-field learning causes unresolved dependence on the conditioning variable to appear as excess predictive variance, converting epistemic uncertainty into apparent aleatoric variance. We observe this phenomenon across synthetic and real-world tasks, and provide an idealized model to study it. We empirically find that this excess variance has approximate coverage properties, and, at any point in training before overfitting, predictive sets constructed directly from CFM samples achieve approximately nominal coverage without explicit calibration training.

Limitations.

Our theory analyzes an idealized population-level regularized smoothing model and does not establish the variance-inflation result for arbitrary neural-network training. Although the theoretical result characterizes the variance inflation phenomenon, it does not imply formal predictive-coverage guarantees. The coverage properties studied here are empirical, and developing stronger theoretical coverage guarantees is left for future work.
