title: TrainBridge: Agentic NPU Training Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
abstract: We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.

headings: TrainBridge: Agentic NPU Training Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
2 NPU Training: Compilation Gaps and Optimization Challenges
3.2 Stage 1: NPU Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
body_start:
Abstract

We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error.
To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training.
TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling.
Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that
TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7× speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0× across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.11
 1

 Our code is available at https://github.com/YChen-zzz/NPU_optimal_reference_skills.

## 1 Introduction

Efficient training on modern accelerators can benefit from framework-level compilation that optimizes computation across operators. Such compilation is mature on NVIDIA GPU backends. However, in the Ascend NPU training programs we study, these optimizations are partially applied by the available compilation stack (Yu, 2026).
As a result, the execution of the training algorithm involves fragmented computation, redundant operations, and materialized intermediates, leaving space for NPU-specific program tuning.

Such NPU-specific tuning is often manual and expert-driven. Providing a tuning agent with
task-specific knowledge, such as NPU profiling results
(Zhang et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2025), enables it to diagnose bottlenecks and improve the NPU program. However, even with profiling guidance, the agent still needs to iteratively analyze, modify, execute, and validate the program, making the
optimization process time-consuming under a limited tuning budget. This motivates us to seek
additional guidance that can make the tuning process more efficient.

To provide this additional guidance, we introduce TrainBridge, a two-stage agentic
framework for NPU-specific optimization. We observe that the corresponding GPU
training programs already benefit from substantial optimization by mature compilation stacks.
The differences between the eager and compiled GPU execution reveal optimization decisions already made for the same workload.
Therefore, we think the differences are useful guidance on NPU execution.
In Stage 1, TrainBridge extracts the underlying optimization intents from the differences and
constructs NPU-specific rewrites when corresponding inefficient computation patterns are present
in the NPU program. In Stage 2, it iteratively profiles the updated program to identify remaining bottlenecks, addresses them, and updates the profile.

We evaluate TrainBridge in a GPU-to-NPU migration setting on training workloads spanning LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training.

In addition, we introduce an NPU version of the
Modded-NanoGPT speedrun (Jordan et al., 2024), a highly optimized community benchmark for end-to-end
language-model pretraining efficiency under a fixed validation target. We adapt its historical
GPU implementations to Ascend NPUs and release an open
leaderboard22
 2

 https://github.com/zhaoyiyidan/modded-nanogpt-npu and evaluation
environment to support further NPU training optimization.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We identify compilation-related optimization gaps in NPU training programs. To narrow these gaps, we present TrainBridge, a two-stage agentic approach. TrainBridge first extracts optimization intents from the differences between eager and compiled GPU implementations and uses them to guide NPU program rewrites, then iteratively profiles the rewritten program to address residual bottlenecks.

• 

We evaluate TrainBridge across multiple NPU training workloads. It achieves average
speedups of 1.7× across four training workloads and nearly 2.0× across 27
historical speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations, relative to the initial
NPU implementations. On the four additional workloads, it reduces the average NPU-to-GPU
training-time ratio from 2.8× to 1.5×.

## 2 NPU Training: Compilation Gaps and Optimization Challenges

## 2.1 Training Workloads and Migration Setting

We study GPU-to-NPU training migration across five workloads: Modded-NanoGPT, CIFAR-10 AirBench33
 3

 https://github.com/KellerJordan/cifar10-airbench,
Qwen3-0.6B training with Hugging Face Trainer, ViT training with TIMM44
 4

 https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models, and nanoVLM55
 5

 https://github.com/huggingface/nanoVLM. These workloads
cover language-model pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training. We evaluate them using one to eight devices.

Modded-NanoGPT builds on NanoGPT66
 6

 https://github.com/KellerJordan/Modded-NanoGPT,
a language-model pretraining codebase widely used for studying the architectural properties of
LLMs (Zhang et al., 2024) and training algorithms
(Yuan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025a). The original GPU speedrun requires participants to train a language model on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs and achieve a validation loss below 3.28
(Jordan et al., 2024). The speedrun contains the GPT-2 small, GPT-2 Medium, and
optimization tracks. We study the GPT-2 small track, which contains a sequence of
high-performance implementations developed over time. These implementations use different
training and kernel optimizations and therefore provide diverse migration tasks. We use
record to denote a valid historical leaderboard implementation that reaches the required
loss target; a larger record number indicates a later and faster implementation with a
shorter end-to-end training time.

For all workloads, we first use Kerminal77
 7

 https://kerminal.cn/ to perform the
initial functional migration from GPU to Ascend 910C NPUs. For Modded-NanoGPT, we preserve
the original training schedule, hyperparameters, and model dynamics, and require the migrated
program to reach validation loss below 3.28 at the same training step. The corresponding correctness criteria for the
other workloads are described in Appendix A.1.

## 2.2 Compilation Gaps in NPU Training

Across the four additional workloads besides Modded-NanoGPT, the initial NPU-to-GPU end-to-end
training-time ratio averages 2.8 $\times$ .
For Record 50, the compiled GPU implementation takes 128 seconds and the initial NPU
implementation takes 563 seconds, giving a ratio of 4.40 $\times$ . These measurements reflect
differences in both hardware capability and software optimization. Reported
compute-throughput figures88
 8

 https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/
(Zuo et al., 2025) suggest that the Ascend 910C provides roughly 76% of the H100 SXM’s peak
dense BF16/FP16 compute throughput. These end-to-end gaps cannot be fully explained by hardware capability alone and motivate us to investigate software-level optimization opportunities in the migrated NPU programs.

## 2.3 Challenges in Agentic Performance Tuning

We first tried using a generic coding agent with GPT-5.6-SOL in the Codex agent harness to tune the initial NPU program. It produced valid changes, but many candidates failed to improve end-to-end training time. Without task-specific knowledge, the agent often struggles to identify which regions have substantial
optimization potential and what changes are likely to improve training efficiency.

NPU profiling provides useful task-specific guidance by identifying expensive operators and
timeline intervals. However, high runtime alone does not indicate how much a region can be accelerated or which optimization should be applied. The agent therefore needs repeated cycles
of analysis, modification, execution, and validation to discover effective changes. While this
process can improve performance, it can be time-consuming and inefficient under a limited tuning
budget. This motivates complementary guidance that can narrow the optimization search space.

## 2.4 GPU Compilation as Optimization Evidence

GPU training ecosystems combine expert-designed implementations with mature framework-level compilation. For the same workload, differences between eager and compiled GPU execution reveal concrete changes that eliminate, fuse, or reorganize computation. Modded-NanoGPT Record 50 provides a representative example. Table 1 shows that, on eight NVIDIA H100 SXM GPUs, framework-level compilation through
torch.compile reduces the end-to-end training time of Record 50 from around 338 seconds
to 128 seconds, demonstrating its contribution to training efficiency.

We next examine whether the computation patterns addressed by the GPU-side compilation stack remain in the migrated NPU implementation. In our evaluated NPU training programs, some corresponding patterns remain despite the available compilation support, leaving fragmented computation and materialized intermediates that provide concrete opportunities for NPU-specific optimization.

Modded-NanoGPT Record 50
provides one example. Its KeyShift operation shifts half of each attention head’s key features by
one token along the sequence dimension. The original overlapping-slice assignment remains and produces a sequence of ViewCopy operations. Consistent with prior reports of compilation limitations on Ascend (Yu, 2026), the Ascend NPU compilation stack did not successfully produce a runnable end-to-end compiled program in our migrated training setting, leaving this inefficiency in the executed NPU implementation. The same inefficiency is present in eager GPU execution, whereas the compiled GPU execution eliminates it through functionalization and kernel fusion. Then, the agent extracts the intent of avoiding overlapping view updates and proposes an NPU-specific expression that realizes this intent. Table 2 reports the performance improvement from the NPU-specific rewrite.

Table 2: Local NPU latency of KeyShift operation in Record 50 of Modded-NanoGPT speedrun before
and after GPU-compilation-evidence-guided agent rewriting. The input shape is [1, 24576, 6, 128], and
we use BF16 precision.

This case illustrates that, when a computation pattern eliminated by mature GPU compilation remains in the NPU program, the underlying optimization intent can guide an effective NPU-specific rewrite and improve the efficiency of the corresponding NPU computation.

## 3 TrainBridge

## 3.1 Problem Formulation

We first formalize how source-side framework-level compilation provides optimization evidence for NPU tuning. In our source GPU setting, this compilation is implemented through PyTorch torch.compile. Such compilation may transform computation graphs and execution schedules, introduce fused regions, modify compiler IR, and generate specialized kernels. For clarity, we use computation-graph changes as a representative view to formulate the optimization problem; TrainBridge itself is not restricted to graph-level transformations. Our goal is to improve the end-to-end training time of the migrated NPU program while preserving its correctness requirements under a limited tuning budget.

At the graph level, let $G_{e}$ and $G_{c}$ denote representative computation graphs before and after source-side GPU compilation, respectively. From the computation-graph perspective, we summarize the changes as

 $G_{c}=\tau_{G}(G_{e}),$ 

where $\tau_{G}$ denotes only the graph-level changes observed during compilation. The difference between $G_{e}$ and $G_{c}$ therefore provides evidence of computation that the source stack found beneficial to eliminate, fuse, or reorganize.

Within $G_{e}$ , let $r_{e}\subseteq G_{e}$ denote a computation region before GPU compilation, and let $r_{c}$ denote its compiled counterpart. Suppose an inefficient computation pattern $p$ is present in $r_{e}$ but is eliminated or reorganized in $r_{c}$ . The difference between $r_{e}$ and $r_{c}$ therefore provides evidence about the optimization intent applied to this region.

Migration preserves the high-level computation of the source program but does not automatically reproduce the optimizations introduced by GPU compilation. When the available NPU compilation stack does not eliminate the corresponding inefficiency, the inefficient pattern $p$ may remain in a semantically corresponding NPU region $r_{n}$ .

In such cases, the agent can use the eager-to-compiled GPU difference to infer the underlying optimization intent and derive an NPU-specific rewrite that removes or reduces the corresponding inefficiency while preserving the original computation semantics. Applying such rewrites across applicable regions can improve the training efficiency of the migrated NPU program.

However, GPU evidence cannot address all inefficiencies in the migrated NPU program. Some GPU
transformations may not be beneficial on the NPU because of backend-specific execution
characteristics, and GPU evidence does not expose NPU-specific overheads in host scheduling,
communication, or memory management. These limitations motivate the two stages below.

## 3.2 Stage 1: NPU Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence

Figure 1: Overview of TrainBridge. Stage 1 aligns eager-to-compiled GPU changes with
the migrated NPU program, and uses the resulting optimization evidence to guide NPU
implementation optimization. Stage 2 iteratively profiles the updated NPU program and
addresses residual bottlenecks.

For the same training program, we collect GPU compilation artifacts, including pre-compilation graphs, post-fusion IR, generated kernels, and profiling summaries, together with the corresponding GPU and migrated NPU sources. Based on this evidence, TrainBridge groups related GPU operations into semantic supernodes. A semantic supernode represents a common high-level computation and provides a unit for relating source-side compilation changes to the migrated NPU program.

For each supernode, the agent first examines the eager-to-compiled GPU changes to identify what computation was eliminated, fused, or reorganized. These changes provide evidence of an inefficient computation pattern in the eager execution and the optimization intent used to address it. The agent then locates the NPU region implementing the same high-level computation and checks whether the corresponding inefficiency remains, using differences in operators, dtypes, layouts, materialized intermediates, and kernel boundaries as evidence.

When the inefficiency remains on the NPU, the agent uses the inferred optimization intent to propose an NPU-specific rewrite that removes or reduces it while preserving the original computation semantics. Candidate rewrites include API parameter changes, redundant-operation removal, fused NPU operators, and selective compilation of supported local subgraphs. Stage 1 ends after all semantic supernodes have been examined and applicable GPU-evidence-guided rewrites have been validated.

## 3.3 Stage 2: Profiling-Guided Residual Optimization

Stage 2 profiles the NPU program produced by Stage 1 to identify residual bottlenecks that are not captured by source-side GPU compilation evidence. The agent
combines operator statistics, host and device timelines, communication events, memory activity,
and source inspection to identify the remaining bottlenecks.

The agent considers several common optimization classes: eliminating redundant work, reusing computed
values or buffers, hiding latency through overlap, and replacing an implementation with an
equivalent NPU-native alternative. After each candidate modification, TrainBridge revalidates
correctness and performance and updates the profile when the bottleneck shifts. The agent repeats this process until no further performance improvement is observed or the tuning budget is exhausted.

## 4 Experimental Setup

## 4.1 Tasks and Migration Protocol

As described in Section 2.1, our evaluation covers five training workloads:
CIFAR-10 AirBench99
 9

 https://github.com/KellerJordan/cifar10-airbench,
Qwen3-0.6B pretraining with Hugging Face Trainer,
ViT training with TIMM1010
 10

 https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models,
nanoVLM1111
 11

 https://github.com/huggingface/nanoVLM,
and Modded-NanoGPT.
We migrate each workload to Ascend 910C NPUs and tune the migrated NPU implementation.
For Modded-NanoGPT, we randomly sample and evaluate 27 historical records from the first 50 leaderboard records,
treating each record as a separate tuning task.
A valid optimization must preserve the original training schedule and reach a validation loss
below 3.28 at the same training step.
The correctness criteria for the other workloads are described in Appendix A.1.

## 4.2 Hardware and Software

For GPU experiments, we use up to eight NVIDIA H100 SXM GPUs with PyTorch 2.7.0 and CUDA 12.8. For NPU experiments,
we use up to eight Ascend 910C NPUs with PyTorch 2.7.1, CANN 8.5.0, and torch-npu 2.7.1.post2. We report
end-to-end training time, excluding tuning time.
For Modded-NanoGPT, we use eight GPUs and eight NPUs in the respective experiments. Device counts for the other workloads are detailed in Appendix
limitations:
Our current tuning setting focuses on single-node training. Multi-node training introduces
additional performance factors from network topology, cross-node communication, and parallelization
strategy. Future work will evaluate TrainBridge in multi-node settings using large-scale training frameworks such as MindSpeed-LLM and Megatron-LM.

TrainBridge requires a source GPU implementation from which useful framework-level compilation evidence can be obtained. This
requirement provides task-specific optimization guidance but limits the method to workloads supported by a
mature source stack. A natural extension is to store source-side optimization evidence produced by the GPU compilation stack, together with validated NPU implementations, in a retrieval database.
Such a database could provide reusable knowledge about source-side optimization intents and their successful NPU implementations, helping agents prioritize promising rewrites for new workloads.
conclusion:
We study compilation-related optimization inefficiencies in NPU training and investigate how evidence from mature GPU compilation stacks can guide NPU-specific program optimization. TrainBridge extracts
optimization intents from differences between eager and compiled GPU implementations, constructs NPU-specific rewrites,
and profiles the updated program to address residual bottlenecks. It achieves a $2.0\times$ NPU speedup
across Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records and a $1.7\times$ speedup across four additional
workloads. These results show that GPU compilation evidence can guide NPU-specific program
optimization and help address compilation-related inefficiencies in NPU training.

title: How Representational Priors Shape Generalization in World Action Models
abstract: World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones. We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it. Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy. We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold. Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models. In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy. Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.

## How Representational Priors Shape 

Generalization in World Action Models

Junha Chun

Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Seoul National University

Youngjoon Jeong

Taesup Kim

headings: 3.1.1 Why image editing could be beneficial for generalization
3.1.2 Representational prior is more than pretraining objective
body_start:
Abstract

World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones.
We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it.
Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy.
We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold.
Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models.
In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy.
Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.

## 1 Introduction

World action models (WAMs) have recently become a major paradigm for a robotic foundation model (Kim et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Pai et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2026).
They inherit the representations and rich spatiotemporal knowledge from generative backbones with scalable pretraining, predict the future with world modeling objective, and generate actions from the features from the reasoning process.
It has been shown that they improve generalization to out-of-distribution scenes by predicting how the world changes.

However, recent researches question whether the capabilities of WAMs come from explicit test-time prediction or enriched representations from the world modeling, and whether video prediction is a good representational prior or objective for world modeling.
FastWAM finds that representational gains from world modeling, rather than explicit future generation at test time, is the main contributor of WAM’s performance (Yuan et al., 2026).
Furthermore, ImageWAM shows image editors as backbones led to significant improvements to the policy generalization from edit-aware representation which contain task-relevant visual changes and is evidenced by attention maps (Zhang et al., 2026b). We therefore ask:

Which geometric structure makes a backbone’s representational prior useful for WAM generalization, and how does policy adaptation transform that structure?

Understanding this question is necessary to explain why some inherited representations support stronger generalization. Inspired by the baseline WAMs and fundamental questions about their representations and performances, we start by analyzing the representational geometry of in- and out-of-distribution observations.

Throughout the paper, we introduce nuisance orthogonality, which characterized the geometric separation between feature displacement from visual variations and the empirical in-distribution manifold.
High nuisance orthogonality therefore measures a potential for disentangled representational prior which presents in the generative backbones before policy training.
We show that nuisance orthogonality is highly related to the generalization performance of WAMs, across visual variations and models, allowing prospective diagnostics of world models.
Furthermore, we present nuisance suppression after policy training, a suppressing behavior of residual displacement so that the policy can remove nuisance information, improve scene retrieval, and enable robust action generation.

Our contributions are as follows:

• 

A geometric characterization of representational priors: Nuisance orthogonality, the fraction of feature displacement orthogonal to the empirical span of in-distribution data, quantifying whether a backbone separates action preserving visual changes from directions that distinguish clean scenes.

• 

An evidence from nuisance orthogonality to policy robustness: Across world model comparisons, higher nuisance orthogonality is associated with stronger downstream visual robustness motivating a diagnostic for assessing world model backbones before WAM policy training.

• 

An analysis on how representations reshape after policy adaptation: We introduce nuisance suppression to measure how representation space change after adaptation, showing that more robust policy exhibits stronger and more consistent nuisance suppression.

Figure 1: Nuisance orthogonality and suppression lead to generalization of WAM. We show that orthogonality of feature displacement with respect to in-distribution data manifold is related to generalization of WAM. This arises from the reorganization of representations during policy adaptation, which we explain through nuisance suppression. Since adaptation reshapes the representation space, the figure provides a conceptual illustration.

## 2 Related Work

World Action Models.

World action models (WAMs) are emerging as a major paradigm for robot foundation models by action generation with predictive modeling of future visual observations (Kim et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Pai et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2026).
Their appeal lies in transferring spatiotemporal priors from generative pretraining to robotics control, while future prediction provides supervision linking actions to their visual consequences.
Empirical studies report improved data efficiency and generalization to unseen objects, tasks, and environments, with strong robustness under visual perturbations (Zhang et al., 2026c).
Beyond direct policy execution, predictive world modeling can help test-time planning by evaluating the consequences of candidate actions (Kim et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026).

Recent work further shows that video prediction co-training is necessary to improve world representation, but explicit test-time generation contributes only to trivial improvements of downstream tasks (Yuan et al., 2026).
In addition, some offer an alternative to video generation backbones showing that pretrained image editing representations are helpful for visual generalization (Zhang et al., 2026b; Labs, 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025).
These researches motivate examining the representational priors of generative backbones and their underlying generalization performance.
Our study investigates which geometric properties inherited from visual pretraining are related with robustness and how they reshape after policy adaptation.

Nuisance separation and representation geometry.

Nuisance invariance and disentanglement provide a foundation for separating task information from irrelevant variation (Achille and Soatto, 2018), although unsupervised disentanglement is not identifiable without inductive biases or supervision (Locatello et al., 2019).
Related objectives remove nuisance factors adversarially (Ganin et al., 2016), separate shared from domain-specific features, or encourage orthogonality between task and nuisance representations (Bousmalis et al., 2016; Sarhan et al., 2020), with applications in domain adaptation and fair representation learning.

In robot manipulation, prior work has decomposed generalization failures into factors of variation and studied which properties of pretrained visual representations predict robustness to distribution shift (Xie et al., 2023; Burns et al., 2023).
In visual reinforcement learning, similar ideas enable transfer across visual domains and robustness to task-irrelevant distractors (Higgins et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021).
More recent work disentangles nuisance factors through explicit or implicit separation in latent action pretraining (Bu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Jeong et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a).
Our diagnostic instead measures nuisance separation in pretrained representations and relates it empirically to policy robustness.

## 3 Experimental Setup

## 3.1 Motivation

Figure 2: Zero-shot editing on LIBERO.
Image editing models are already capable of zero-shot editing LIBERO data with visual variations.

## 3.1.1 Why image editing could be beneficial for generalization

Prior work have shown that WAMs from image editing models tend to generalize better than video prediction models (Zhang et al., 2026b).
From scalable pretraining, image editors learn to follow instructions so that they can zero-shot inference image editing even in out-of-domain images as shown in Figure 2.

During the denoising process, image editors are conditioned on a reference scene and a noisy target image that contains editing modifications, which allow the model to understand the relationship between the source image and edited target image from the early transformer blocks.
General knowledge and representational relationships of background modification, illumination, texture, or blurring are more efficiently learnable through scalable image editing pretraining.
Video generation models, in contrast, are biased more towards temporal continuity, motion, and dynamics rather than counterfactual changes of the world.
This motivates the hypothesis that the generative backbones for robust policy would have more rich representations under domain shift even before policy adaptation.

## 3.1.2 Representational prior is more than pretraining objective

The generalization performance of ImageWAM has shown significant improvements for using image editing models over video prediction models.
Howver, as in Table 1, when training ImageWAM from scratch initialization of FLUX.2 ( $63.9\%$ ), its advantage over Wan2.2 and FastWAM ( $46.5\%$ ) shows that prior knowledge of image editing alone cannot fully explain this comparison.
Thus, we assume that representational priors for WAMs are not just what the generative backbone has learned through the pretraining objective, but is affected by collection of all design choices including vision and language tokenizers, architecture and initialization, language injection pipeline, pretraining datasets.
To analyze this, we start by analyzing the geometry of internal representations of generative backbones when various observations are encoded as a conditioned frame.

## 3.2 Experimental Setting

Diagnostic dataset and visual shifts.

We construct a diagnostic dataset from LIBERO-Plus using paired observations that share the same underlying simulator state but differ in visual appearance (Liu et al., 2023; Fei et al., 2025). The dataset covers four categories of visual shift: lighting, background, sensor noise, and camera viewpoint, each evaluated at multiple strengths. We use 40 clean reference observations to estimate the empirical in-distribution feature subspace introduced in Section 4. For these reference states, we collect 1,200 corresponding out-of-distribution observations and use the resulting pairs to measure variation-induced feature displacement. Generalization requiring changes in language understanding, task composition, or action semantics is outside the scope of this study.

Generative backbones and WAMs.

The experiments use Wan2.2, FLUX.2, OmniGen2 and Ovis-U1 from the prior works and scratch FLUX.2 as generative backbones (Wan et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026; Labs, 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b). Generalization performances are presented with their policy success rates in LIBERO-Plus trained with LIBERO dataset under the configurations from FastWAM and ImageWAM, with total of $5,418$ evaluation trajectories.

In addition, to show that our work is generalizable to other generative backbones, we extend FlashMotion, Kiwi-Edit, SANA-Video 2.0 5B, and MAGI-1 4.5B with a comparable model capacity scale and extend them to a generative backbone for WAMs (Li et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; ai et al., 2025). ## 4 Nuisance Orthogonality

With the above motivation, we analyze the displacement of world model representations caused by the visual variations from the clean image. We hypothesize that displacement direction and their orthogonality from the in-distribution manifold would measure disentanglement of information from the generative backbones, which would be geometrically easier to remove nuisance information and less suffer from shortcut learning during policy adaptation.

## 4.1 Definition

Let $h_{\ell}$ be intermediate representations from transformer block at layer $\ell$ of generative backbone before WAM training.
We extract $h_{\ell}(x)$ spatially averaged with the clean observation $x$ .
With mean of the reference features $\mu_{\ell}=\frac{1}{n}\Sigma_{i=1}^{n}h_{\ell}(x_{i})$ , define

 $H_{\ell}=\begin{bmatrix}(h_{\ell}(x_{1})-\mu_{\ell})^{\top}\\
\cdots\\
(h_{\ell}(x_{n})-\mu_{\ell})^{\top}\end{bmatrix},\qquad P_{\ell}=V_{r}V_{r}^{\top}$ 

(1)

where $V_{r}$ contains the retained right singular vectors of $H_{\ell}=U\Sigma V^{\top}$ with retained rank $r$ , $P_{\ell}$ becoming a projection matrix to the empirical representation subspace at layer $\ell$ .

Then, we extract $h_{\ell}(Tx)$ which are features of corresponding sample and action-preserving transformation $T$ as a condition frame. Computing the orthogonality of the displacement vector

 $\qquad d_{\ell}(x,T)=h_{\ell}(Tx)-h_{\ell}(x),\qquad q_{\ell}(x,T)=1-\frac{\|Pd_{\ell}(x,T)\|^{2}}{\|d_{\ell}(x,T)\|^{2}}$ 

(2)

which can be aggregated over model layers and our diagnosis dataset, resulting the nuisance orthogonality of generative model under transformation $T$ .

 $\mathcal{O}(T)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{x}[q_{\ell}(x,T)].$ 

(3)

A high orthogonality score means that the displacement is mostly orthogonal to sampled in-distribution subspace.

## 4.2 Analysis

## 4.2.1 Nuisance Orthogonality Aligns with Generalization

If nuisance orthogonality is a useful inherited prior, generative backbones with higher orthogonality should tend to become more robust policies.
We test this on the baseline models with an average success rate of LIBERO-Plus tasks as a generalization performance after WAM training.
We retain full rank $r=39$ for 40 reference scenes preserving all nonzero empirical singular directions.

Figure 4: Rank ablation.
Nuisnace orthogonality is consistent to retained rank changes.

Table 1 presents the results with nuisance orthogonality compared to the evaluation success rate.
Figure 3 further shows that there is a strong tendency for the orthogonality to the downstream WAM generalization performance in general, while the sensitivity differs between visual variation types and difficulties.
We further ablate this by the retained rank in Figure 4, showing that the nuisance orthogonality is consistent with the changes in the retained rank. We note the value for the orthogonality increases as retained rank decreases because fewer directions contribute to the projected displacement.

## 4.2.2 Implications for model selection

To show that this tendency is generalized to other generative backbones, we conduct identical analysis to world models including FlashMotion, Kiwi-Edit, SANA-Video 2.0 5B and MAGI-1 4.5B (Li et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; ai et al., 2025).
Each model is trained as a WAM policy respecting their architecture and action expert designs in FastWAM and ImageWAM, with video prediction loss from the original backbones and flow matching loss for action prediction.
Specific designs are in the Appendix A.1.

The results in Table 1 and Figure 3 show that we could predict the performance in advance of WAM training by measuring the nuisance orthogonality.
Moreover, video models being capable of high generalization performance supports the hypothesis that any model with rich representation regardless of their pretraining objective could have a useful representational prior.

## 5 Nuisance Suppression

A useful representational prior for generalization should support policy adaptation that preserves task-relevant scene distinctions while reducing sensitivity to action-preserving appearance changes.
We therefore measure how displacements within and outside the empirical in-distribution manifold change after WAM training.

conclusion:
We studied how the representational geometry of generative backbones relates to visual generalization in world action models.
Nuisance orthogonality measures whether action-preserving visual variations displace features outside the empirical subspace of in-distribution observations, providing a diagnostic before computation intensive policy training.
Across the evaluations, higher orthogonality is generally related with stronger policy robustness in LIBERO-Plus, with further evaluations of additional world models support examining representational geometry beyond the distinction between image and video pretraining.
After adaptation, ImageWAM capable of robust action generation exhibits consistent nuisance suppression of displacement, whereas FastWAM shows less consistent and weak suppression.
Together, these findings suggest that useful representational priors separate visual nuisance from in-distribution samples and that policy adaptation reduces its relative influence.

Limitations

Our evidence is restricted to simulated LIBERO manipulation and the visual shifts evaluated in LIBERO-Plus. We exclude generalization benchmarks for language instructions or action compositionalities to study with limited scope on action-preserving visual generalization.
Also the experimental results are observational, our results do not isolate every causal effect of orthogonality or of pretraining objective, but study representational geometry and its relationship with various compounding effects and generalization performance.

abstract: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

body_start:
Abstract

There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand.
In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams).
Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families.
We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for information density rather than successful communication.
We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior.
Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

Figure 1: Overview of models studied, data collection procedure, and linguistic features under analysis.

## 1 Introduction

Your instinct is right; the convoluted sentence you are currently reading is quietly eating its own reader-patience budget — footnote it.
If you saw that sentence in the wild, you might suspect that it’s the product of a modern LLM.
It has several linguistic features that are overrepresented in frontier LLM text: an object relative clause, a denominal verb (“footnote”), an inanimate subject used with the verb “eat”, and stacked nouns leading to a low-frequency n-gram sequence (“reader-patience budget”).
All of these features are associated with linguistic processing difficulty.

But why would models trained on human text develop linguistic features that hurt intelligibility? And, if they are, is it happening systematically across model families?
Here, we study a set of features known to correlate with linguistic processing difficulty and find that they are overrepresented in text generated from recent LLMs, including both closed and open-weight models.
We collect a novel corpus of LLM-generated text across diverse domains (chat, coding, essay), and we show that the prevalence of these features, in many models, exceeds that of human-generated reference corpora.
Using a round-trip translation paradigm, we further show that these features do not occur in paraphrases that are controlled tightly for semantic content—further evidence they are a result of the specific features of modern post-trained models.

Having established this trend, we then propose and test a hypothesis as to why this pattern may have emerged in LLMs.
The psycholinguistics literature shows that human language is largely optimized for communication (Gibson et al., 2019), in the sense of striking an efficient balance between being easy to produce and easy to understand.
Empirically, human text is well-optimized relative to random baselines on a number of dimensions, such as minimizing dependency length (Futrell et al., 2015).
It follows that models trained to mimic human-generated text should also show a similar profile of linguistic features in their output, but that these patterns may not be preserved in models where communication is not the primary objective, and where humans are largely out of the loop.

Indeed, modern LLMs are not just trained on human-generated text, but undergo extensive post-training for math, coding, and other reasoning tasks.
In paradigms like those of Guo et al. (2025), models are rewarded for getting the right answer but not necessarily for clarity.
We hypothesize that optimization for these goals, alongside a limit on the context window available to models, leads to information compression in a way that competes with intelligibility.
To test that hypothesis, we fine-tune a pre-trained language model under a length penalty, and measure the linguistic profile of its outputs. The model learns to succeed at the task using fewer tokens by leveraging syntactic alternations (cases where there are two ways of expressing the same meaning), even when this makes their linguistic output less humanlike. Furthermore, their preference for information compression bleeds into linguistic alternations that were not seen in training.

In sum, this work tests two specific hypotheses about the intelligibility of AI-generated text.
H1: The language output of frontier and near-frontier LLMs overuses linguistic features associated with human comprehension difficulty.
H2: A pressure for information density during post-training shifts the language output of LLMs to be less humanlike.
Using a combination of linguistic analysis and direct post-training intervention, we find support for both hypotheses. Our findings highlight the dimensions along which human language processing and frontier LLMs are misaligned, and point to possible interventions for addressing this misalignment.

## 2 Background and Related Work

Recent scientific work has attempted to measure the idiosyncrasies of LLMs, such as their tendency to over-use particular words (Juzek and Ward, 2025), or their dense, noun-heavy style Reinhart et al. (2025).
These idiosyncrasies may emerge during the post-training process of modern LLMs, including rewards during reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF; Ouyang et al., 2022; Singhal et al., 2024), or reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR; Lambert et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025).
The distinctive tells of LLM-generated writing have led to AI-generated text detectors (Bao et al., 2024), and have raised questions regarding the impact of such AI-generated writing on linguistic content, with implications for diversity and representation (Padmakumar and He, 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025; Ryan et al., 2024).
As a growing share of the text people read is shaped by LLMs, the linguistic properties of AI-generated writing matter not only for detection but also for the human readers who must process it. Yet whether these properties make AI-generated text harder for humans to understand has received little academic attention, despite widespread anecdotal reports of issues with LLM intelligibility (University of Waterloo, 2026).

The field of psycholinguistics has extensively studied the linguistic features that drive comprehension difficulty. Words that are hard to predict are costly to process (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008), and so are long-distance dependencies, because of limits on memory (Gibson, 1998; Gibson, 2000). Memory-based accounts explain the difficulty of center-embedded sentences (Gibson and Thomas, 1999; Lewis, 1996) and of legalese (Martínez et al., 2022), and temporary ambiguity can derail comprehension in garden-path sentences (Christianson et al., 2001).

Crucially, the human mind operates under distinct pressures and limitations compared with those of LLMs.
LLMs are also trained on significantly more data than humans experience during language development Frank (2023). Modern LLMs are able to attend fully to very large context windows (Vaswani et al., 2017; Oh and Linzen, 2026), in contrast with the lossy and distance-sensitive memory of humans (Futrell et al., 2020). Larger LLMs often fit human behavior (e.g., reading times) less well than smaller LLMs (Oh and Schuler, 2023; Oh et al., 2024). Consistent with this pattern, LLMs with artificially constrained memory fit human behavior better (Kuribayashi et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2026; Clark et al., 2025). This suggests that LLMs’ ability to attend fully to long contexts may come at the cost of human-likeness.

Linguistic alternations, in which speakers and writers have multiple options for expressing a given meaning, provide a source of evidence for the preferences guiding human language generation.
One purported pressure on human language production is uniform information density (UID) — the idea that speakers spread information evenly across the signal to avoid overloading comprehenders, e.g. by inserting optional words (Levy and Jaeger, 2007; Meister et al., 2021).
UID is at odds with maximizing information density, by which shorter members of linguistic alternations would be categorically preferred, and has been proposed as a metric for preference optimization in LLM training to produce more human-aligned text (Li and Xu, 2026).
Meanwhile, psycholinguistic evidence also supports a pressure based on cognitive availability during incremental production (Bock, 1987; Clark et al., 2022; Futrell, 2024).
Pre-trained LLMs inherit these signatures from their human training text, but post-training for specific tasks (e.g. math, code) may favor information-dense constructions over those that ease human processing or resemble humans.

## 3 Experiment 1: Linguistic features in AI-generated conversations

## 3.1 Linguistic features of interest

The purpose of Experiment 1 is to test H1: do frontier and near-frontier LLMs disproportionately use linguistic features that are linked to human processing difficulty?
For each feature, we justify its association with processing difficulty, and explain why it might plausibly arise from a pressure toward information density. Example sentences for each feature are given in Table 2. All features are identified from spaCy dependency parses (Honnibal et al., 2020); for denominal verbs and inanimate subjects, parser-generated candidates are then judged by an automated classifier (Section B.1).

## N-gram statistics

Predictable words are associated with lower processing difficulty, as measured by reading times (Levy, 2008; Smith and Levy, 2013).
From an information-theoretic perspective, a word with a very high n-gram probability is more redundant than one with a low n-gram probability.
For a system designed to maximize information density, we might expect high-probability n-grams to be reduced (i.e. common, uninformative, and predictable words being skipped), and higher overall n-gram perplexity (when measured by an independent language model).
Against a reference corpus, we measure the rate of unattested pairs, bigrams that never occur in it, and perplexity under a trigram model (Section B.2).

## Dependency length

Words in a sentence relate to each other via syntactic dependency relations (e.g., between a noun and any determiners or adjectives that modify it, or between a verb and its subject, object, and adverbial modifiers).
Long-distance dependencies are known to be difficult to process for humans, due to the additional strain they place on working memory (Gibson, 1998; Gibson, 2000; Grodner and Gibson, 2005), and speakers tend to avoid them (Futrell et al., 2015; Temperley and Gildea, 2018).
We standardize dependency length across sentence lengths, as described in Appendix B.

## Object relative clauses

We measure the rate of object relative clauses (ORCs) in the language output of LLMs, differentiating between ORCs with an overt relativizer (most often that or which) and without one.
ORCs are known to present additional processing difficulty compared to subject relative clauses, potentially due to their non-canonical word order and longer dependencies (Staub, 2010), although animacy and frequency reduce the gap (Mak et al., 2006; Reali and Christiansen, 2007).
Under the hypothesis that LLMs tend to choose more compressed realizations of a given meaning, we predict object relative clauses will be over-represented, because they tend to replace a (longer) passive construction (The house that the contractors built vs. The house that was built by the contractors), and second, that reduced relative clauses (without the optional relativizer) would be over-represented, because they avoid an optional word.

Figure 2: Change in linguistic features under round-trip translation (NLLB-200 via Japanese), by model, in standard deviations of the original values across models (Section B.4). Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals; a dash marks a setting in which the model was not run.

## Stacked noun compounds

In English, nouns freely modify other nouns in an adjectival way: in the phrase coffee shop, coffee modifies shop, despite usually appearing as a noun.
This feature enables stacking multiple nouns into rich compound words which denote highly specific meanings.
However, such stacks can introduce bracketing ambiguity, as in the headline Squad Helps Dog Bite Victim (Cooper, 1980), and disrupt reading (Lauer, 1995; Nakov and Hearst, 2005; Staub et al., 2007; Cohen and Staub, 2014).
Here, we measure the rate of occurrence of stacked noun compounds, defined as three or more nouns in a modifier relationship.

## Denominal verbs

Verbs which are formed directly from nouns, such as in the phrase bottle the whiskey are known as denominal verbs.
While some denominal verbs are highly conventionalized and well-attested in human language, using a denominal verb in an ad-hoc way is marked (e.g., calendar it). Readers can interpret such innovations (Clark and Clark, 1979), but part-of-speech conversion triggers syntactic re-evaluation (Thierry et al., 2008), and noun/verb-ambiguous words are processed differently from unambiguous ones (Frazier and Rayner, 1987; Federmeier et al., 2000).
Often, the alternative to using a denominal verb is to use a longer, more syntactically complex phrase, e.g. put the whiskey in a bottle.
We therefore predict that a pressure for information compression will favor usage of denominal verbs beyond their base rate in humans, even at the expense of intelligibility.

(b) Round-trip translation vs. student essays.

Figure 3: Summary of changes to each linguistic feature across applicable models. (a) Changes across the chat, coding, and essay settings. (b) Comparison of round-trip translation vs. student essays as the reference.

## Inanimate subjects

We count the instances of inanimate subjects used with active verbs that typically take only animate subjects. Examples include “is_file() swallows that and returns False” and “Puzzle patterns where this asymmetry bites”.
Such sentences violate a selectional restriction (Chomsky, 1965) on which verbs typically take which subjects. They can be understood as personification or metonymy (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980), but readers use animacy as a cue during parsing (Trueswell et al., 1994), and without additional context, a mismatch may elicit a P600 response associated with reanalysis (Kim and Osterhout, 2005; Kuperberg, 2007).
However, rephrasing these sentences to avoid inanimate subjects would potentially require lengthening the sentence: for example, the word “bites” stands in for “causes an issue”.
We speculate that during training, models may have converged to using such constructions as efficient, albeit non-standard, ways of expressing meaning which would otherwise take up more tokens.

## 3.2 Data collection

We collect a corpus of AI-generated conversations (Figure 1) using a set of 14 frontier and non-frontier LLMs: Kimi K2.5, GLM 5, Claude (Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5), and GPT-5.6 (Luna, Terra, Sol), Olmo (Team Olmo et al., 2025) (Base, Instruct, Think), and Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024) (Base, Instruct).
We use a total of 15 conversational starting prompts, or seeds, consisting of 10 chat seeds and 5 coding seeds. Each coding seed involves a request to clone a real, public GitHub repo, identify bugs, and implement fixes within a sandbox environment. Chat sessions were capped at 12 turns (a simulated human query and a model response) and coding sessions at 11 turns plus a fixed closing message. In a third setting, each model writes single-turn essays to seven PERSUADE 2.0 assignments. Full data collection procedures and API costs are described in Appendix A.

## 3.3 Comparison to human baselines

Where available, we compute a human baseline for the linguistic feature of interest, on approximately genre-matched text: OpenSubtitles (Lison and Tiedemann, 2016) for chat, StackExchange for coding, and student essays from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus (Crossley et al., 2024) for essays. We additionally include a Wikipedia comparison.
The same corpora serve as the references for the n-gram measures (Section B.2).

## 3.4 Round-trip translation

We employ round-trip translation (bilingual pivoting), an established paraphrasing method that preserves meaning at scale Bannard and
Callison-Burch (2005); Mallinson et al. (2017); Wieting and Gimpel (2018); Federmann et al. (2019), as a method for separating a model output’s characteristic syntactic profile from its semantics. Translation normalizes the output to frequent forms, reducing lexical and syntactical richness Vanmassenhove et al. (2019); Vanmassenhove et al. (2021) and stripping stylistic and authorial traits Rabinovich et al. (2017); Prabhumoye et al. (2018).
The result is a parallel corpus in which each translation is paired with its source sentence. Because the round trip holds the semantic content of each response fixed while replacing its wording, a feature that becomes less frequent after the round trip is one that the model chose over an available alternative way of expressing the same content.
To create this parallel corpus, we translate each sentence independently from English to Japanese and back with NLLB-200 (3.3B; NLLB Team, 2024).
Japanese was chosen because pivot languages unrelated to English tend to yield more diverse paraphrases Federmann et al. (2019).

limitations:
We only examine a subset of commonly used models, only conduct analyses in English, and use a limited number of conversation seeds (chat topics and code repositories). Ideally, the study would be replicated on a larger number of seeds and model families.
Causally identifying sources of linguistic difficulty in frontier models would ideally involve studying them as they are post-trained, but this is not feasible to do at scale and so we rely on proxies. Similarly, limited compute makes studying post-training difficult.
conclusion:
We take these results as a proof of concept that a length penalty used during reinforcement learning with GRPO can directly affect grammatical features.
We note that the model was not directly instructed to use compressed or dense language, and was not directly given information about the availability of syntactic alternations. Rather, the penalty resulted in an emergent preference for shorter members of syntactic alternations. Without KL regularization this preference was near-categorical (over 98% short for both trained “that” alternations at every $\lambda>0$ ), unlike human speakers, who choose between the variants by context. Crucially, the models were still able to succeed at their task, since both members of an alternation were valid solutions to the training task. We speculate that the use of verifiable rewards creates an environment where correctness is decoupled from humanlike communication, leading models to converge toward a novel, potentially less comprehensible distribution of language use.

title: AI-Based End-to-End Automotive Design and Software Development for SDVs
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enable end-to-end automotive design and software development for Software-Defined Vehicles (SDVs). Based on our contributions within the Central Car Server (CeCaS) and follow-up EU-funded projects, we present an AI-driven toolchain integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) to automate the transformation of natural-language requirements into system architectures, executable software, and validation artifacts. The approach emphasizes traceability, consistency, and compliance with safety-critical automotive development requirements. Validation is performed on a centralized vehicle computing platform supporting adaptive cruise control and emergency braking, tested in Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) and Software-in-the-Loop (SiL) environments. We discuss current capabilities, practical limitations, and future directions toward increasingly automated, reliable, and quality-assured automotive software development with minimal human intervention.

body_start:
Abstract

A generated chest radiograph can be useful as declared augmentation, but the same image becomes unsupported evidence when submitted as the record of a real examination. We study this problem by separating three questions: whether an image passes an automated quality check, whether an origin classifier flags it as generated, and whether a trusted record supports the claimed acquisition. In our experiments, Qwen selects up to 20 images from pools of 1,000 existing Cheff-identified or SynthCheX candidates. A receiver evaluates quality with MedGemma and predicted origin with a classifier on frozen DINOv3 features. Quality-based selection raises quality passes from 12 to 19 of 20 for Cheff-identified images and from 8 to 17 for SynthCheX. We find no evidence that selection improves passage through both checks: no selected Cheff-identified image passes both, while uniform, quality, and quality-constrained surrogate selection produce 2, 1, and 2 SynthCheX passes. On unprocessed test images, the origin classifier flags 4,677 of 5,000 SynthCheX images, but it also misclassify 110 of 2,297 NIH (real) images and 568 of 957 genuine images from another collection as fake. Our results further show that JPEG compression reduces SynthCheX-versus-NIH AUROC from 0.987 to 0.841. Even without processing, 152 SynthCheX images pass both pixel checks. These checks can filter submissions, but they cannot verify an acquisition claim. We strongly advocate that source and intended use must be recorded and checked separately for admission of chest radiographs in medical datasets.

## 1 Introduction

Image generators can now produce high-resolution chest radiographs [27, 9]. Such images are useful when they are declared as synthetic, for example to augment training data. They cause a problem when they are submitted to a research dataset as records of real examinations. A receiving system may check whether an image has acceptable technical quality and whether a classifier considers it generated. Neither check shows that a real examination produced the image. A generated image may pass both checks, and its origin may be lost in later reuse. The dataset can then treat a generated image as a recorded examination without evidence that the examination took place.

We call such an image synthetic evidence: a generated image that is offered as evidence of a real examination without the support that this claim requires. The definition builds on earlier work on ground-truth drift and evidence grounding [1, 19]. Whether an image counts as synthetic evidence depends on the image, the claim made about it, and its intended use, because a generated image is not fraudulent in itself. Figure 1(a) shows an example from our study. This generated SynthCheX image passes our automated quality check, and our origin classifier does not flag it as generated. If it is submitted as a clinical acquisition, nothing supports that claim. If it is submitted as declared augmentation, the same pixels are acceptable.

The example shows that three questions must be kept apart. Quality: does the image meet the receiver’s technical requirements? Predicted origin: does an image classifier label it as genuine or generated? Claim support: does the accompanying record support the claim that the image came from the stated acquisition, and is the declared use allowed? A pass on one question does not answer the others. An image can pass the first two, and the third stays open.

Earlier work measures the fidelity of generated radiographs, detects generated or edited medical images, and shows that compression and resizing can change detector behavior (Section 2). Can a submitter who chooses which generated images to send pass both checks more often than one who sends random images? In a controlled laboratory test, a submitter uses Qwen to select up to 20 images from pools of existing generated images, and a receiver applies a MedGemma quality check and an origin classifier built on DINOv3 features. A separate registry records the source and intended use. We find the following.

• 

Selection. Selecting by Qwen’s quality score increases the number of images that pass the quality check, but we find no evidence that it increases the number that pass both the quality and origin checks.

• 

Processing. Image processing (JPEG compression and resizing) causes two separate problems for the origin classifier. Score shifts can invalidate a fixed threshold, which we call threshold drift. The classifier’s ranking can also deteriorate even after the threshold is reset, which we call ranking loss.

• 

Source shift. With the NIH-calibrated threshold unchanged, the primary classifier flags 568 of 957 genuine Open-I images.

Our contributions are (1) an intake test that keeps quality, predicted origin, and claim support separate, (2) measurements of how selection, processing, and a new genuine collection affect the quality and origin checks, and (3) a small registry experiment that records source and intended use apart from the pixels.

(a) Generated; passes both checks

(b) Genuine; passes quality, flagged as generated

(c) Genuine; fails quality, not flagged

(d) Generated; flagged as generated

Figure 1: One example for each outcome of the two checks, chosen after the analysis by a fixed hash rule. Images (a) and (d) are generated (SynthCheX), and (b) and (c) are genuine (NIH ChestX-ray14). Image (a) passes both checks, but its pixels do not support a claim that it records a clinical acquisition.

## 2 Related work

## Generated radiographs.

Cheff generates high-resolution chest radiographs with latent diffusion [27]. CheXGenBench measures their fidelity, privacy, and training utility [9], and its earlier version and release card describe the SynthCheX images we use [8, 18]. Prior reader studies ask whether radiologists can distinguish generated radiographs from real ones [25, 24]. We instead study an automated intake process with separate quality and origin checks.

## Detecting generated and edited images.

CT-GAN inserts and removes lesions in CT scans [15]. DSKI/MedForensics provides a medical deepfake benchmark and detector [13], and MedForge detects localized edits [4]. MedForge-RSI reports rejected authentic images, failed transfer, and transmission distortions, and it adds an adaptation method [3]. Detectors can learn shortcuts based on compression and image size [11], and WaRPAD scores images by how they respond to high-frequency perturbation and rescaling [5]. We do not propose a detector. We ask how such shortcuts interact with quality-based selection and threshold calibration.

## Calibration and provenance.

Conformal calibration uses genuine images to set a threshold whose false-alarm rate is controlled when the genuine images are exchangeable and the score is fixed in advance [2]. Such a threshold says how unusual a score is among genuine images, not whether an image was acquired. Signatures for medical images [22], C2PA content credentials (signed records of a file’s history) [6], and the PROV data model [16] record the integrity and history of a file, not whether its content supports a factual claim. Our laboratory registry (Section 6) stores signed records and an explicit unknown state, and it adds no new cryptography.

## 3 Task and threat model

We model how a research dataset receives images (Fig. 2). A submission contains an image, a claim about where it came from, and a declared purpose. The claim we test is that the image records a clinical acquisition. The submitted images carry no source record, so their claim support is missing by design (Section 6). Collection labels tell us which images are NIH and which are generated. They are our ground truth, but they do not certify any clinical history.

The experiment starts from fixed pools of existing generated images. Using only Qwen judgments, the submitter selects at most $K$ (Section 4.6) candidates that it expects to pass both receiver checks. The submitter has no access to MedGemma judgments, DINOv3-based origin scores, MedForge-Reasoner results, or receiver outcomes. The selected lists are fixed before the receiver applies the MedGemma quality check and the DINOv3-based origin check. A separate registry then checks the claimed source and declared purpose. This is a fixed, offline selection experiment over existing generated images, without receiver feedback.

An image passes the quality check if MedGemma judges it technically adequate (Section 4.5). The origin check flags an image when the origin classifier labels it as generated (Section 4.3). A flagged generated image is rejected, and a flagged genuine image is a false alarm. An image passes the origin check if it is not flagged, and it passes both checks if it also passes the quality check. If a model reply cannot be read or an image cannot be decoded, the outcome is unavailable, which is neither a pass nor a flag. A pass on both checks leaves the acquisition claim unresolved. Only the registry (Section 6) compares the claim with a source record.

Figure 2: Workflow of the intake test. The submitter selects at most $K$ of $B$ generated candidates using only Qwen judgments and has no access to receiver results. Two models with fixed thresholds answer the quality and predicted-origin questions, and a registry answers the claim-support question.

## 4 Data and methods

## 4.1 Data and splits

We split the images by purpose (Table 1). The fit split trains the classifier head, the development split chooses among the allowed settings of the head, the calibration split sets the decision threshold, and the test split gives the reported results.

Table 1: Images in each split. The calibration split holds genuine images only. The raw CLS head is fitted on NIH and Cheff-identified images, and the SynthCheX fit and development images serve secondary heads.
