Genuine images come from the ChestX-ray14 part of MaCheX [26, 23], which we call NIH. We keep its partitions and use one image per patient. Fit, development, and calibration patients are disjoint and come from the train/validation partition. The test split holds the 2,297 test-partition patients who remain after we remove the 500 pilot-study patients.

The Cheff-identified collection holds 3,000 legacy images identified as Cheff outputs [27]. Their checkpoint, seeds, and conditioning are unknown, so we treat the collection as observed images, not as the output of a known sampler. Fitting uses the 1,250 images from the pilot study plus 250 more, and development and testing use 500 and 1,000 unused images. SynthCheX is a fixed release of 75,649 images made with Sana 0.6B [8, 18]. We draw 6,500 of them at random for the splits and keep the 500 pilot-study images out of the test split.

To test a new genuine collection, we add 957 frontal Open-I images, grouped by radiology report [7]. We use them only for testing, with the NIH threshold unchanged. Report groups do not establish unique patients. We record each NIH image’s projection, anteroposterior (AP) or posteroanterior (PA), only for observational comparison.

## 4.2 Models and their roles

The models have distinct roles. Qwen ranks candidate images for the submitter. MedGemma applies the receiver’s quality check. DINOv3 and MedGemma’s vision encoder supply image features for the origin classifier. MedForge-Reasoner is used only in a separate transfer comparison.

Qwen is the unquantized Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint in BF16 (Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B) [17]. MedGemma is MedGemma 1.5 4B instruction-tuned (google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it) [20, 10]. DINOv3 ViT-7B/16 (facebook/dinov3-vit7b16-pretrain-lvd1689m) [21] was trained on web images. We use its CLS feature (the output of the token that summarizes the image) or the mean of its patch features. The medical representation is the mean of the 4,096 patch features of MedGemma’s SigLIP vision encoder, and the head on it is the medical head. MedForge-Reasoner (RichardChenZH/MedForge-Reasoner) [14, 3] answers directly whether an image is genuine or fake. It was trained to detect localized edits and belongs to the Qwen family.

## 4.3 Origin classifier and threshold

We train the main origin classifier on 1,500 genuine NIH images and 1,500 generated Cheff-identified images. DINOv3 extracts a feature vector for each image, and its weights stay frozen. We fit an $L_{2}$ -regularized logistic-regression head to these features. We choose the inverse regularization strength $C\in\{0.01,0.1,1,10\}$ that rejects the most generated development images at a 5% false-alarm rate on genuine development images, and ties go to the smaller $C$ . The head never sees SynthCheX, so SynthCheX tests transfer to a second generator. We call this head the raw CLS head. Here “raw” does not mean unprocessed pixels. It means that the head was fitted without the processing augmentation used by the augmented head (Section 4.4).

After choosing the head, we calibrate its decision threshold on a disjoint set of 3,000 genuine NIH images. The primary threshold has a nominal (target) false-alarm rate of 5%, the share of genuine images that the check flags. Let $s(x)$ be the classifier’s score for image $x$ , where a higher score means more generated, and let $s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}$ be the scores of the $n$ calibration images. The conformal p-value [2] is

 $p_{\rm real}(x)=\frac{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{s_{i}\geq s(x)\}}{n+1}.$ 

(1)

The indicator $\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}$ equals 1 when its condition holds and 0 otherwise, so the sum counts the calibration images that score at least as high as $x$ , and the extra 1 counts $x$ itself. Thus $p_{\rm real}(x)$ is about the share of genuine calibration images that look at least as suspicious as $x$ . It is not the probability that $x$ is real. The receiver flags $x$ as generated when $p_{\rm real}(x)\leq\alpha$ , the target false-alarm rate. We use $\alpha=0.05$ , and $\alpha=0.01$ and $0.10$ in the supplement. A score equal to the threshold is not flagged.

On genuine test images, the false-alarm rate is at most $\alpha$ on average if two assumptions hold. The genuine calibration and test images must be exchangeable, which means that any ordering of them is equally likely. The score must also be fixed without using the calibration images. This guarantee covers the origin check alone. It does not cover the combined quality-and-origin rule, a different collection, unavailable quality judgments, or the probability that an acquisition claim is true, and it need not hold after a processing shift.

We use two more reference sets only for secondary checks. One holds 2,914 images for the pilot head, after we remove the 86 images that the head saw during fitting or selection. The other holds 2,930 valid replies for a probe (a small classifier) that uses the eight numeric fields of the alternative quality rubric (Section 4.5), after we exclude 10 images used in rubric development and 60 images without a valid reply. We also compare the learned scores with a baseline on six pixel statistics, and with secondary heads fitted on one generator or on both (Supplement S6).

## 4.4 Processing experiment

We next test whether common image processing changes the origin classifier’s scores or its ability to separate genuine and generated images. The canonical condition converts each image to luminance, resizes it to 256 pixels with aspect-preserving Lanczos resampling, pads it with black to a square, and copies it into RGB, without histogram equalization. The receiver applies 12 further conditions: JPEG (quality 95, 85, 75, or 50), down- and up-sampling (through 192, 128, or 64 pixels), direct processing at 512 pixels from the original file (native 512), a 4-pixel border mask, 4-pixel padding, a 64-pixel central mask, and a severe 26-pixel border mask. Cheff-identified images are stored at 256 pixels, so native 512 only upscales them, and DINOv3 still receives 224-pixel input under every condition.

We process 1,000 test images per collection under all 13 conditions, so the 13 views of an image are related. We compare three settings. (1) The raw head with the canonical threshold, calibrated on canonical genuine images only. (2) The raw head with a matched threshold, recalibrated on genuine calibration images processed in the same way as the test images. (3) The augmented head with a matched threshold, fitted on five processed views of each training image (Supplement S6).

These settings separate two failures. In threshold drift, processing moves the scores, so the old threshold no longer gives the intended 5% false-alarm rate. In ranking loss, genuine and generated scores overlap more, so no new threshold can restore the original separation. Setting (2) resets the threshold and so isolates ranking loss from threshold drift. Setting (3) tests whether training on processed images reduces ranking loss. Before testing, we fixed a target for the augmented head: reject at least 5 points more Cheff-identified images than the raw head, with at most 1 point more genuine flags, averaged over the 13 conditions.

## 4.5 Quality check

A rubric is the set of scoring instructions that a model follows. The receiver’s quality check uses MedGemma with an alternative to the original rubric (below), chosen once on development data (Supplement S5). A response passes only if it identifies an assessable chest image, assigns visibility of at least 3 out of 4, assigns a non-null artifact severity of at most 1 out of 4, and passes the flat-image guard. The guard fails images whose grayscale range is at most 1 and whose standard deviation is at most 0.5 on the 0–255 scale.

The submitter does not use this rubric. Qwen rates each candidate with the original rubric, which scores technical quality $T$ , anatomical plausibility $A$ , and artifact severity $V$ , each
conclusion: We asked three questions about a generated chest radiograph submitted as the record of a real examination. Quality-based selection finds more images that pass the MedGemma quality check, but we find no evidence that it increases the number passing both receiver checks. On canonical images, the origin classifier rejects all Cheff-identified images and 93.5% of SynthCheX images while flagging 4.8% of NIH images. Processing can shift the threshold and reduce ranking quality. Matched recalibration lowers many genuine-image flags, but it also allows more generated images through and does not always recover the nominal rate. Genuine images from another dataset are also flagged frequently. Passing both pixel checks therefore does not by itself support the claimed acquisition. Thus, we strongly suggest that the source and intended use of each image must be recorded and checked separately.

When the generated voice does not match the target speaker, the problem often reflects imperfect separation of speaker-related timbre from content, making it important to identify where timbre information resides and which representations still carry it. headings: Where Does Timbre Hide? Localizing Speaker Information in Speech Signals
body_start:
Abstract

Timbre similarity is a key evaluation target for generative speech systems, including voice conversion, speaker-cloning text-to-speech, and zero-shot speech models.
When the generated voice does not match the target speaker, the problem often reflects imperfect separation of speaker-related timbre from content, making it important to identify where timbre information resides and which representations still carry it.
Using speaker identity as a measurable proxy, we probe frequency bands, phase/magnitude structure, WORLD source/filter decomposition, voiced/unvoiced regions, self-supervised learning (SSL) layers, EnCodec/HuBERT tokens, and a 45-listener test across Mandarin, English, and Japanese speech/singing data.
Speaker information is distributed: 1–8 kHz magnitude and vocal-tract spectral-envelope structure dominate perception, above-8 kHz bands remain machine-discriminative, shallow SSL layers expose compact speaker information, and token leakage depends on tokenizer/layer choice.
These findings indicate where generation systems should condition on or transform speaker information, and where content, codec, and token pipelines should audit residual speaker leakage.

Index Terms: 
speaker identity, timbre, speaker verification, voice conversion, self-supervised speech representations, listening test

## I Introduction

Timbre similarity is now a central evaluation target for generative speech systems.
Voice conversion (VC), speaker-cloning text-to-speech (TTS), and some zero-shot large speech models must preserve linguistic content while controlling the target speaker’s voice [1, 2, 3, 4].
This requirement makes speaker-independent content modeling a practical engineering concern rather than only a design choice in representation learning.
If speaker-related information remains in a content, codec, or self-supervised learning (SSL) representation, it can leak into generation; if the information needed for the target speaker is not injected or transformed at the right place, the generated speech may remain intelligible but sound like the wrong speaker.

It is therefore important to know where speaker-related timbre information resides and how it is coupled with content and other acoustic factors.
Timbre itself is perceptual and difficult to measure directly at scale, so we use speaker identity as a measurable proxy for speaker-related timbre while keeping machine discriminability separate from human similarity judgments.
Classical source-filter theory and perceptual studies point to vocal-tract and spectral-envelope structure [5, 6, 7, 8], while modern speaker verification and SSL models such as ECAPA-TDNN and WavLM provide strong but less interpretable speaker information [9, 10].
Earlier sub-band speaker-recognition studies also found that low- and mid-frequency bands carry substantial speaker information [11, 12, 13], but they predate high-sample-rate corpora, neural codecs, tokenized speech language models, and recent SSL probing work [14, 15, 16, 17].

This paper asks where speaker-related timbre information is preserved, transformed, or leaked in both speech signals and learned representations.
We systematically compare complementary probes: frequency filtering, phase/magnitude randomization, WORLD source/filter swaps, voiced/unvoiced extraction, WavLM and ECAPA speaker verification, mel classifiers, SSL-layer and PCA probes, EnCodec and HuBERT token histograms, cross-style robustness checks, and a 45-listener similarity test.
These probes allow the same speaker-related information to be viewed from signal, representation, and perceptual sides.

The experiments lead to three findings.
First, the combined probes give a structured view of where speaker-related timbre is concentrated.
Frequency-band manipulations and listener ratings place the perceptually important speaker information mainly in the 1–8 kHz region, rather than in very high bands.
Phase/magnitude edits show that this information is carried mainly by spectral magnitude, not phase.
WORLD source/filter swaps further identify the vocal-tract spectral envelope as a stronger carrier than fundamental frequency (F0) alone.
Second, representation probes show that speaker-related information remains accessible in shallow SSL layers and can survive in some token streams, so content and codec representations should be audited rather than assumed speaker-free.
Third, speaker information measured by a classifier is not the same as perceived timbre similarity.
High-frequency bands still contain speaker information that classifiers can use, but this information does not produce strong same-speaker similarity for listeners.
This suggests that high-band reconstruction may improve acoustic detail without restoring the perceived speaker similarity that listeners rely on.
Together, these findings can guide future VC, TTS, anonymization, codec, and speech language model work in deciding which components need speaker conditioning, transformation, suppression, or leakage checks.

## II Experimental Setup

This section defines the experimental setting used in the paper.
It contains two parts: the datasets and common evaluation setup, and the design of each experiment.

## II-A Datasets and Common Setup

The protocol uses multiple datasets because different probes require different data characteristics (e.g., sampling rate, language, style labels).
AISHELL-1 and AISHELL-3 provide Mandarin multi-speaker speech for frequency, SSL, token, and listening checks [18, 19].
VCTK provides 48 kHz English speech for high-band and voiced/unvoiced tests [20].
ESD and CREMA-D test whether speaker information survives emotion changes [21, 22].
NUS-48E and JVS/JVS-MuSiC test speech–singing transfer [23, 24, 25].
We also use a self-recorded 48 kHz Chinese–English corpus for controlled band-swap and voiced/unvoiced pilot experiments.
Table I summarizes the data used by each experiment group.

All experiments use speaker identity as the measurable target, but the metric depends on the probe.
WavLM-base-sv is the main speaker verification (SV) backend [10].
For signal edits that may depend on the backend, we repeat the phase/magnitude and source/filter tests with a SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN VoxCeleb model [9].
Embedding-based tests use cosine similarity between speaker embeddings, and report intra-speaker similarity, inter-speaker similarity, and discriminability, defined as the same-speaker score minus the different-speaker score.
Bandwidth curves also report equal error rate (EER).
Closed-set feature and token probes report speaker-classification accuracy.
The listening test reports mean voice-timbre similarity ratings (i.e., perceived same-speaker similarity) on a 1–5 scale.
Because WavLM-base-sv requires 16 kHz input, spectral content above 8 kHz is discarded before embedding extraction.
High-sample-rate spectra are therefore evaluated with mel multilayer perceptron (MLP) probes in the frequency-band experiment.
Fig. 1 summarizes the full protocol.

Fig. 1: Speaker-information localization protocol. The study combines signal edits, model-based and model-free measurements, representation probes, and human similarity ratings, so speaker information measured by models can be kept separate from perceived speaker-related timbre information.

## II-B Experiment Design

Frequency-band experiment:
This experiment tests which spectral regions preserve speaker information.
For lowpass and highpass analysis, we apply Butterworth filters to each utterance, extract WavLM-base-sv embeddings, and compute speaker discriminability and EER.
Lowpass curves show how speaker information changes as more bandwidth is retained from the bottom up.
Highpass curves show how speaker information changes when low and mid frequencies are removed.
For bands above 8 kHz, we cannot rely on WavLM-base-sv because its 16 kHz input removes this frequency range.
We therefore keep AISHELL-3 and VCTK at their original sampling rates, isolate fixed frequency bands, extract log-mel summaries from each band, and train a 2-layer closed-set MLP speaker classifier.
We also check shuffled labels and duration/energy baselines to make sure the classifier is not succeeding for trivial reasons.
Mel-cosine separability (the cosine-distance gap between same- and different-speaker mel features) provides an additional classifier-free check.
To compare machine-detectable information with perception, we also construct AISHELL-3 paired trials from full-band, lowpass, bandpass, highpass, and different-speaker conditions.
Listeners rate each pair on a 1–5 voice-timbre similarity scale.
The main metrics are discriminability and EER for the SV curves, speaker-classification accuracy for the mel MLP checks, and mean listener rating for the listening conditions.

Phase/magnitude experiment:
This experiment tests whether speaker information is carried mainly by spectral magnitude or phase.
For each utterance, we compute a short-time Fourier transform (STFT) and synthesize two variants.
The magnitude-kept variant keeps the original magnitude and randomizes phase.
The phase-kept variant keeps the original phase and randomizes magnitude.
We then compare the speaker discriminability of each variant against that of the unmodified signal.
This manipulation directly tests whether speaker information is carried by the spectral envelope or the phase structure.

Source/filter experiment:
This experiment tests whether speaker information is better explained by source pitch (F0) or vocal-tract filtering.
Using WORLD, we decompose each utterance into fundamental frequency (F0), spectral envelope, and aperiodicity [26].
We then create cross-speaker resynthesized signals by keeping one speaker’s F0 while replacing the spectral envelope, or by keeping the spectral envelope while replacing F0.
We judge the two conditions by same-speaker cosine similarity and retention (the fraction of the original same-speaker similarity preserved).
If the filter-kept signal preserves more speaker similarity than the F0-kept signal, the retained information is more closely linked to vocal-tract spectral-envelope structure than to pitch alone.
We repeat the phase/magnitude and source/filter tests with ECAPA-TDNN to check that the pattern is not specific to WavLM-base-sv.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) representation experiment:
This experiment tests where speaker information is exposed in continuous speech features.
We extract layer-wise features from WavLM, HuBERT, Wav2Vec 2.0, and Whisper-base, mean-pool each utterance, and train lightweight speaker classifiers.
We also apply principal component analysis (PCA) before classification to test whether speaker information remains accessible after dimensionality reduction.
This shows which layers are most speaker-discriminative and whether the information is compact enough to leak through content features when they are reused in downstream systems.
The main metric is closed-set speaker-classification accuracy.

Token experiment:
This experiment tests whether discrete speech units retain speaker information.
For EnCodec, we compute histograms from each residual vector quantization (RVQ) layer and from cumulative RVQ groups.
For HuBERT, we compute k-means token histograms from multiple SSL layers and codebook sizes, and add a bigram check to capture limited sequential dependencies.
These probes test whether speaker leakage depends on tokenizer, layer, codebook size, and RVQ depth.
The main metric is closed-set speaker-classification accuracy.

Robustness experiments:
These experiments test whether speaker information survives common style and phonation changes.
Emotion tests compare same-speaker cross-emotion similarity with different-speaker baselines, and include a CREMA-D leave-one-emotion-out validation.
Speech–singing tests compare same-speaker cross-modal similarity and train speech-based classifiers that are evaluated on singing.
Voiced/unvoiced tests separate active speech into voiced and unvoiced regions and evaluate whether speaker information survives outside pitch-bearing regions.
These checks prevent the main claims from relying only on neutral read speech.
The main metrics are cosine similarity gaps and speaker-classification accuracy.

## III Results

## III-A Frequency-Band Experiment Results

The frequency-band results show that the strongest speaker information lies in the low/mid spectrum, while higher bands retain weaker but measurable information.
In the WavLM-base-sv lowpass curves, discriminability increases as more bandwidth is retained and nearly reaches the full-band score by 7.5 kHz.
The highpass curves give the complementary pattern: performance remains stable when only sub-1 kHz content is removed, but drops sharply once the cutoff exceeds 1–2 kHz.
These two curves indicate that speaker information is not carried by sub-1 kHz content alone, but by a broader low/mid-frequency range.
Because WavLM-base-sv is limited by its 16 kHz input, the WavLM curves cannot determine whether bands above 8 kHz still contain speaker information.

limitations:
This study has several limitations.
Many probes are closed-set, so speaker-classification accuracy and SV-style scores should not be interpreted as open-set speaker verification performance.
WavLM-base-sv operates at 16 kHz, which limits SV-based frequency analysis above 8 kHz; the high-sample-rate mel probes, mel-cosine checks, and listening test reduce this issue but do not replace a high-sample-rate open-set SV backend.
The high-frequency listening stimuli are narrowband and less natural than full-band speech, so their low ratings describe perceived voice-timbre similarity under the present filtering conditions.
The emotion, singing, and token results would also benefit from more speaker backends, more detailed listener metadata, better-controlled playback conditions, and sequence-aware token probes.

Overall, this paper uses speaker identity as a measurable proxy to study where speaker-related timbre information resides in speech signals and learned representations.
First, the strongest perceived speaker-related information is concentrated in low/mid-frequency spectral-magnitude structure — specifically the vocal-tract spectral envelope in the 1–8 kHz region — while phase, F0, and high-frequency-only information is weaker under our probes.
Second, speaker information is not confined to explicit speaker embeddings: shallow SSL layers and some token streams still expose recoverable speaker information.
Third, machine speaker discriminability is not the same as perceived timbre similarity: high-frequency bands contain speaker information that classifiers can use, but they do not produce strong same-speaker ratings in the listening test.
Together, these findings indicate where VC, speaker-cloning TTS, anonymization, codec, and speech language model pipelines should inject, transform, suppress, or audit speaker-related information.
conclusion:
The results provide a consistent localization pattern.
The strongest perceived speaker-related timbre information is carried by low- and mid-frequency magnitude structure, especially in the 1–8 kHz region.
Phase/magnitude edits and WORLD source/filter swaps, validated with a second SV backend (ECAPA-TDNN), further point to the vocal-tract spectral envelope rather than phase or F0 alone.
This agrees with the source-filter view of speech: the vocal tract shapes formants and broad spectral balance, both of which remain relatively stable across utterances; vocal-tract filtering also applies to unvoiced segments, consistent with the unvoiced speaker-recognition results in Section III-F.

The high-frequency results need a separate interpretation.
Bands above 8 kHz remain useful for closed-set classifiers and mel-cosine checks, so they should not be treated as empty.
However, high-frequency-only same-speaker pairs receive low listener ratings.
This suggests that high-band reconstruction may contribute to acoustic detail (e.g., frication or airiness), but is unlikely to restore the speaker similarity that listeners primarily perceive.

Learned representations echo the signal-level findings.
Shallow SSL layers retain more speaker information and keep it in a compact subspace, while deeper layers expose less speaker information under our probes.
HuBERT and EnCodec results also show that discrete representations are not automatically speaker-free.
The amount of speaker information depends on the source layer, codebook size, and residual vector quantization layer.
Therefore, content, codec, and token pipelines should check speaker leakage at the actual representation used by the downstream system, not only in explicit speaker embeddings.

The robustness experiments show that this information is not limited to clean neutral voiced speech.
Speaker information remains measurable across emotion, speech–singing changes, and unvoiced segments.
The strength decreases under larger domain changes, especially speech-to-singing transfer, but remains above chance.
Combined with the signal-level findings, this supports the view that speaker-related spectral-envelope structure can survive changes in prosody, style, and phonation.

These findings provide a practical map for speaker-aware speech systems.

title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization
abstract: Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems, producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective, equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries. It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model-code match rate in all 72 benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact reconstruction restores a model-code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.

body_start:
Abstract

Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems,
producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem
across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective,
equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit
the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries.
It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and
objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts
when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes
the required relation checks.
Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model–code match rate in all 72
benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate
rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs,
certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for
ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact
reconstruction restores a model–code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.

## 1. Introduction

Optimization models support logistics, production planning, and energy scheduling by optimizing decisions under operational constraints. Decision quality depends on how natural-language requirements are translated into mathematical formulations, executable solver models, and reported decisions. Recent large language model (LLM) systems generate these artifacts together, while evaluation commonly focuses on solver execution and the final objective value. Establishing semantic agreement across these artifacts therefore motivates verification and repair at the level of the optimization problem itself.

Classical criteria such as feasibility and answer correctness evaluate the returned decision without assessing the agreement across the underlying artifacts (Ramamonjison et al., 2022; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024b; Huang et al., 2025a; Jiang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Different feasible regions can attain the same optimum, so a correct objective value does not identify the implemented problem. Conversely, equivalent models can differ in auxiliary variables, redundant constraints, and syntax. Agreement between written mathematics and executable code can also miss a source requirement from the natural language omitted by both. Output-based evaluation cannot distinguish these failures or establish whether a proposed repair restores the required relations.

Recent methods broaden feedback beyond the final value through behavioral tests, structural comparisons, model-based judgments, and counterexample searches (Zhang et al., 2026; Li and Hai, 2026; Zhai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Lian et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026).
Although these methods provide useful repair signals, passing behavioral tests or receiving a favorable model-based judgment does not establish semantic agreement between the math formulation and its code implementation.
A program can produce the expected outputs on tested cases while admitting decisions excluded by the formulation, whereas structural comparisons can reject equivalent models that use different auxiliary constructions.
Verification must therefore examine whether the different artifacts admit the same feasible decisions and preserve their objective preferences.
It should also localize discrepancies to guide repair and verify that the repaired artifacts satisfy the required relations before adoption.

This paper proposes ORSMT, a satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)-based verification and repair framework for source requirements, written mathematics, instantiated solver models, and returned reports.
ORSMT translates the written model and captures the solver model from code in a common exact representation, aligning observable decisions and projecting auxiliary variables. Within the affine rational core, SMT queries check admitted source requirements, feasible regions, objective relations, and reports for a fixed instance. A satisfiable violation query returns a localized counterexample; an unsatisfiable query certifies the corresponding relation. The evidence supports direct reconstruction between mathematics and code or guides revision, and every adopted candidate passes the required checks again. This keeps diagnosis, repair, and acceptance as distinct stages of one formally checked process. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

(i) We introduce ORSMT, a semantic verification framework for source requirements, mathematical formulations, solver codes, and returned reports. Its common representation supports exact SMT checks within the admitted affine rational core, providing certificates or localized counterexamples for decided relations.

(ii) We develop a verification and repair loop that combines bidirectional reconstruction with counterexample-guided revision. Each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks, connecting diagnosis, repair, and acceptance through the same verifier.

(iii) We evaluate ORSMT on 3,034 problems from 12 benchmarks and 6 generator sizes. Model–code match rates improve in all 72 benchmark–generator combinations before selection. Under protected selection, the aggregate match rate rises from 43.2% to 88.2%, and the share of outputs with both a correct answer and a model–code match rises from 25.2% to 40.2%. ORSMT further improves correct-and-matched outputs when integrated with existing OptiMUS-0.3 and OptiMind pipelines, supporting its use as a modular verification and repair layer.

## 2. Related Work

Autoformulation and evaluation. NL4Opt (Ramamonjison et al., 2022) studies formulation.
OptiMUS and OptiMUS-0.3 build modular formulation and execution
pipelines (AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024b; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024a), while OptiMind adds expert-guided training and inference (Zhang et al., 2025). ORLM, LLMOPT and ORThought generate and revise
mathematical models, code and solver outputs (Huang et al., 2025a; Jiang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). MAMO,
OptiBench and OPT Engine broaden evaluation tasks (Huang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026).
Feasibility and reference objectives assess final answers, but do not establish that the written
model, instantiated code and report describe the same optimization problem.

Verification and repair. ReLoop tests program behavior under parameter
changes (Lian et al., 2026). Opt-Verifier judges structure and solutions (Liu et al., 2026),
and SAC Opt uses semantic anchors for revision (Zhang et al., 2026). EquivaMap and ORGEval compare
variable mappings or graph structure (Zhai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Falsification uses solver-based testing under controlled instance transformations, whereas FLARE verifies MILP reformulations using theorem proving (Li and Hai, 2026; Robbins et al., 2026). ORSMT repairs instance-specific mathematical, executable and report artifacts. Therefore, repair comparisons use ReLoop and Opt-Verifier.

Formal semantic verification. Denotational tests evaluate program behavior beyond textual
similarity (Zhong et al., 2020). Z3 and cvc5 decide arithmetic formulas (de Moura and Bjørner, 2008; Barbosa et al., 2022), while neural symbolic methods translate proposed statements into formal
queries (Jha et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2023; Olausson et al., 2023). ORSMT verifies source
requirements, feasible regions, objective preferences and reports in this way. Its evidence identifies
missing, additional and redundant restrictions and supports repair from either usable model.

## 3. Problem Setting

An autoformulation pipeline maps a source statement $s$ and instance data to written
mathematics, a solver program $\widehat{P}$ , and a report
 $R=(\hat{x},\hat{z},\operatorname{status})$ , where $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{z}$ represent the returned solution and its objective value.
The written mathematics is lowered to the mathematical model $A$ .
The instantiated solver model is represented by
 $B=\mathcal{H}(\widehat{P})$ . A source adapter supplies formal requirements
 $C=\mathcal{F}_{\rm src}(s)$ , each linked to its supporting
source text and variable roles, when that
adapter admits the source. Verification checks the available relations among $C$ , $A$ , $B$ , and $R$ .

Define a model as $A=(X_{A},U_{A},\Phi_{A},f_{A},\delta_{A})$ , where $X_{A}$ contains observable decisions,
 $U_{A}$ contains auxiliary variables, $\Phi_{A}$ contains domains and constraints, $f_{A}$ is the
objective, and $\delta_{A}\in\{\min,\max\}$ . The executable model $B=(X_{B},U_{B},\Phi_{B},f_{B},\delta_{B})$ is defined in the same way. A fixed correspondence aligns
the observable decisions of the two models. Their comparison projects out the auxiliary variables.
The projected feasible region and objective graph are

 $F_{A}^{X}=\{x:\exists u_{A}\ \Phi_{A}(x,u_{A})\},\qquad G_{A}^{X}=\{(x,z):\exists u_{A}\ \Phi_{A}(x,u_{A})\land z=f_{A}(x,u_{A})\}.$ 

(1)

When $G_{A}^{X}$ is single-valued, $v_{A}(x)$ denotes the unique objective value associated with $x\in F_{A}^{X}$ .The relation $x\succ_{A}y$ 
denotes a strict improvement according to $\delta_{A}$ , and $x\succeq_{A}y$ also permits equal
values. Therefore we define semantic model agreement as

 $A\equiv_{\rm sem}B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(F_{A}^{X},\succ_{A})=(F_{B}^{X},\succ_{B}).$ 

(2)

This relation preserves feasible decisions and their preference order. Absolute objective values are
checked separately. Source satisfaction requires a feasible model that entails every applicable
requirement in a nonempty admitted $C$ . Untranslated source units retain an undecided source
verdict rather than a vacuous certificate. The report $R$ passes when its returned decision is feasible,
correctly valued and optimal. Instance parameters are substituted before comparison, and partial
reports use existential completion over unreported coordinates.

The task is to return matched artifacts and evidence for each required relation. A mathematical model
can supply a missing implementation, a captured solver model can supply missing mathematics, and a
source counterexample can expose an omission shared by both. Every decided relation is certified or
accompanied by a concrete refuting assignment.

## 4. ORSMT: Verification, Repair and Matching

ORSMT first translates the mathematical model $A$ and the executable model $B$ into a common exact representation, then uses SMT to check
their relations, and finally applies the same checks to every repaired candidate before adoption.

Figure 1: ORSMT translates source requirements, written mathematics, solver code and reports into a common exact representation. SMT checks either certify their relations or return a counterexample for direct reconstruction or revision. After repair, every relaton is checked again before adoption.

Figure 1 separates two models translation, SMT checking and the two repair routes.
The verifier supports affine models with rational coefficients over real, integer, and Boolean variables.
Appendix B.4 gives the complete verification and repair procedure.

## 4.1. Model representation and bidirectional construction

Mathematical translation. The translator $\mathcal{L}$ lowers admitted mathematical formulation into the model
representation $A$ defined in Section 3. Structured declarations, solver objects, LP/MPS files provide
variables, contraints and objectives,
while mathematical prose is transcribed together with links to the source text from which each element is
derived.
Finite decimal coefficients are represented as exact rationals. The resulting representation explicitly records variable bounds and domains, contraints, and contraint rows. Appendix A.2 presents the detailed input formats.

Executable model and correspondence. ORSMT aligns the observable
decisions $X_{A}$ and $X_{B}$ of A and B through a one-to-one correspondence based on normalized scalar
or index-tuple identifiers, variable roles, and types. Auxiliary variables $U_{A}$ and $U_{B}$ are not matched directly: they are projected out when comparing the model objects in
Eq. (1). A contradiction, type mismatch, or unmatched observable decision prevents
a syntactic correspondence from being accepted and leaves the corresponding relation Undecided.
This separation allows semantically equivalent models to use different auxiliary constructions or
redundant constraints without requiring a one-to-one match of all solver variables.

Target and normalization.
ORSMT supports reconstruction in both directions. When the mathematical model $A$ is available, ORSMT uses it as the primary construction target;
otherwise, it uses the captured executable model $B=\mathcal{H}(\widehat{P})$ as the target for reconstructing missing mathematical
artifacts.
Before construction, ORSMT applies a normalization operator ( $\mathcal{N}$ ) that preserves
the projected feasible region and objective graph relevant to the observable decisions. The
normalization may make implicit domains explicit and derive redundant constraints or auxiliary
definitions needed for compilation, while preserving the semantic model objects used for
verification. The resulting normalized representation is then used as the construction target.

Mathematics to program.
For the mathematical target $T=A$ , ORSMT computes

 $\widetilde{A}=T,\qquad\widetilde{P}=\operatorname{Compile}(\mathcal{N}(T)),\qquad\widetilde{B}=\mathcal{H}(\widetilde{P}),\qquad\widetilde{R}=\operatorname{Solve}(\widetilde{P}).$ 

(3)

The generated solver code declares the normalized model and reports its
decision, objective value, and status. ORSMT then captures the instantiated executable model
( $\widetilde{B}$ ) from the generated program and verifies its semantic agreement with
( $\widetilde{A}$ ), together with the correctness of the returned report ( $\widetilde{R}$ ).
Consequently, this direction can be used either to synthesize missing solver code from a mathematical
model or to repair existing code that fails to match the available formulation.

Program to mathematics. When the executable model is available but the mathematical formulation is missing or incomplete,
ORSMT sets (T=B). It exports the domains, bounds, constraints, objective, and optimization direction
of B into a mathematical representation ( $\widetilde{A}$ ), and uses this representation as the
construction target. The resulting artifacts are compiled, executed, and captured as in Eq. (3), after which the same verification queries are applied to certify their
correspondence. Thus, either representation can serve as the construction source, while both
directions return to the same semantic verification procedure.

Proposition 1: Artifact Construction. If the normalization operator $\mathcal{N}$ preserves the projected feasible region and
objective graph of its input, and that $\mathcal{H}$ faithfully captures the model compiled from the
normalized representation,
Eq. (3) constructs artifacts whose projected model semantics
agree with the construction target, up to the fixed correspondence of observable decisions.
Appendix B gives the full proof and the guarantees for
constraint reduction.

## 4.2. Verification queries and diagnosis

Feasible regions. ORSMT encodes domains and rows as exact arithmetic formulas and
computes the two directional violation queries

 $Q_{A\setminus B}=\operatorname{SAT}(F_{A}^{X}\land\neg F_{B}^{X}),\qquad Q_{B\setminus A}=\operatorname{SAT}(F_{B}^{X}\land\neg F_{A}^{X}).$ 

(4)

A witness in $A\setminus B$ identifies a mathematical decision excluded by the implementation.
A witness in $B\setminus A$ identifies an implemented decision excluded by the mathematics.
Unsatisfiability in both directions establishes equality of the projected
feasible regions which includes the case where both regions are empty.
Therefore, model feasibility is checked separately before certifying semantic agreement.

Verdict and diagnosis.
Each verification query returns either a certificate or a counterexample. A satisfiable violation query refutes the corresponding relation and returns a concrete witness, whereas an unsatisfiable query certifies that the relation holds. After substituting instance parameters, ORSMT extracts the implicated constraints, domains, and linked source texts from the witness and, when applicable, the unsatisfiable core. Objective diagnoses additionally record the evaluated preference relation, while source diagnoses identify the violated requirement and its applicable scope. The resulting diagnostic payload is used for deterministic reconstruction or counterexample-guided language-model revision.

Objective relatio
conclusion: ORSMT closes the verification–repair loop by combining exact certificates and concrete counterexamples with bidirectional reconstruction and rechecking every adopted artifact. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes (18,204 outputs), it raises the model–code match rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share of outputs that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. Among 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting yields 50.9% correct-and-matched outputs, while one source revision followed by reconstruction restores model–code agreement for 84.4% of refuted pairs. The analysis also reveals systematic asymmetries in generated artifacts: code is unavailable nearly twice as often as mathematics and is more likely to introduce additional constraints than to omit existing ones. ORSMT decides 2,869 of 3,034 problems, remains sub-second through 99 constraints, and achieves a 29.3 $\times$ speedup from component slicing. Its gains on both host systems further support its use as a modular verification and repair layer for LLM-based optimization pipelines.

body_start:
Abstract.

Engineering graduates in India enter a technology sector that is being reshaped by generative AI, yet the route into that sector runs through examinations and campus placement screens that largely exclude AI. Institutions in India have an approved intake of nearly 2.9 million seats in engineering and technology for 2026–2027 (All India Council for Technical Education, 2026), but HCI research on how students prepare for AI-mediated work has drawn mostly on Western and East Asian settings. We interviewed 23 students and recent graduates of Indian engineering and computing programmes about how they used generative AI across coursework, examinations and placements, and how they judged their own readiness for work. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we report five themes, covering AI-first workplaces and AI-free placement screens, how participants prepared for placement, how they used AI in coursework, the role of faculty authority and enforcement, and participants’ concerns about their readiness for work. Drawing on signaling theory, we discuss what grades and screen scores certify once AI can help produce them, and we offer recommendations for employers, institutions and AI tool designers.

Keywords: 
future of work, AI-first work, hiring, campus placements, engineering education, India, qualitative study, assessment, signaling theory, Global South

## 1. Introduction

Many students in Indian engineering programmes hope to join the technology sector, whether IT services firms, which give India a large share of the world’s outsourced technology services (NASSCOM, 2025), or product companies and large technology firms in India and abroad. The sector is itself being reshaped by generative AI (GenAI). In software engineering more broadly, work that once trained junior engineers is being redirected into workflows that pair senior engineers with AI (Yu and Moon, 2026). The route into this work, however, runs through a series of high-stakes gates, most of which still assess students without AI. Admission rests, depending on the institution, on national, state or institution-specific entrance examinations or on marks in the 12th-grade board examinations. Once enrolled, students are graded through semester-wise examinations and other forms of assessment, which together contribute to a cumulative grade point average (CGPA). In the later years, campus placements, in which companies recruit directly from institutions, screen students through CGPA cut-offs, online aptitude and coding tests and interviews (Table 1). Teaching is often lecture-centred, and assessment in this legacy system relies heavily on theory and rote learning.

Students in this system speak of clearing an examination, the word Indian students and universities commonly use for passing it. Our participants used the word in a sharper sense, for getting through an assessment with the marks it requires, and they set it against learning what the assessment was meant to teach. GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and GitHub Copilot entered this environment without institutional frameworks for their use. Students were left to decide for themselves how to use the tools to clear coursework, how to prepare with them for placement screens that mostly forbade them, and how to become ready for workplaces that would expect them.

Research in HCI and CSCW has begun to trace how GenAI is changing the transition from education into technical work, from the junior roles it absorbs (Yu and Moon, 2026) to the automated screens that filter applicants (Armstrong and Metaxa, 2025). Most of this work, like research on student AI use more broadly, draws on participants in North America, Europe, Australia and East Asia (Adnin et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2025; Henderson et al., 2026; Yu and Moon, 2026). The closest studies of Indian engineering students date from shortly after ChatGPT’s release and focus on how students used the tools and how the tools could be improved (Budhiraja et al., 2024; Joshi et al., 2023). Neither examined campus placements, although placements organise much of the later years of an Indian engineering degree and decide where many graduates begin their working lives. Less is known about how students move through these gates now that AI use has become routine, and about what they carry from them into AI-first work.

We draw on signaling theory (Spence, 1973) to interpret this transition. Grades and screen scores are signals that employers rely on because they cannot observe a candidate’s ability directly (Section 2.1), and we ask what these signals certify once AI can help students produce them.

To understand this transition, we ask three research questions:

• 

RQ1. How do engineering and computing students and recent graduates in India perceive their readiness for AI-first work, and how do they prepare for it?

• 

RQ2. How do they use generative AI to clear the coursework, examinations and placement screens that lead to that work?

• 

RQ3. How, in their accounts, do the institutions around them shape that use?

We address these questions through semi-structured interviews with 23 current students and recent graduates of engineering and computing programmes. Many participants began college around the time ChatGPT was released and have graduated, or will soon graduate, into workplaces that expect AI use, while others entered college with AI already part of their schooling.

We report five themes. 1) Placement screens largely excluded AI, while graduates described workplaces that expected it. 2) Participants prepared for placement through self-directed study, with AI as their main coach. 3) They used AI to clear coursework whose grades the screens later filtered on, a practice they distinguished from learning, although AI also helped them learn where teaching fell short. 4) Faculty authority and unstated rules shaped how openly they used AI, while peers taught one another how to use it. 5) Participants worried that dependence on AI, and work they could not fully claim as their own, would leave them unready for the jobs they sought.

This paper makes three contributions to research on work and its futures. First, it offers an empirical account, based on interviews conducted in 2026, of how students in an underrepresented setting move from education into AI-first technical work, centred on the gates between the two. Second, it uses signaling theory to show how AI-assisted clearing may weaken the grades and screen scores through which employers select graduates. Third, it identifies the responsibilities students take on when neither institutions nor employers define what readiness for AI-first work requires, and it derives implications for employers, institutions and AI tool designers.

Table 1. Indian engineering education: terms used in this paper.

Term

Meaning

Institution types

Engineering and computing degrees are offered by centrally funded technical institutes, state public universities, private universities, private colleges affiliated to a university, and arts-and-science colleges offering B.Sc. computing degrees. Admission routes vary. Some institutions admit through national or state entrance examinations, some through their own entrance tests and others through 12th-grade board examination marks, and institutions are informally ranked by how selective their admission is.

Board examinations

Examinations at the end of the 12th grade, the final year of school, set by state or national school boards. Some institutions admit students on their marks in these examinations.

Semester examinations

Examinations at the end of each semester, mostly closed-book and handwritten, set and marked within the institution. They usually carry a large part of a course’s grade.

Two-mark and five-mark answers

Question papers state the marks for each question, which tells students how long and how detailed an answer is expected to be.

Internals

Internal assessment marks from assignments, class tests and lab work, counted toward the course grade alongside the semester examination.

Lab record

A notebook of laboratory exercises submitted for marks.

Viva

A viva voce, or oral examination, in which students explain their work to an examiner.

Mug up

Colloquial for memorising material in order to reproduce it in an examination, usually without understanding it.

CGPA

Cumulative grade point average across all semesters, typically on a 10-point scale.

Campus placements

Recruitment drives that institutions organise in students’ pre-final and final years. Each company sets its own screens, usually a minimum CGPA, online aptitude and coding tests, sometimes group discussions, and technical and HR interviews.

DSA

Data structures and algorithms, the most demanding part of most coding tests and technical interviews. Screens also cover quantitative and logical aptitude, core subjects of the degree and other topics, but participants spoke mostly of DSA.

## 2. Related Work

Our study draws on three lines of research. We first review work on how GenAI is changing the transition from education into technical work, including hiring, and introduce the signaling lens we use. We then turn to studies of GenAI use by students in India and the Global South, and to research on how assessment, enforcement and reliance shape students’ use of AI. We close by identifying the gap this study addresses.

## 2.1. From Education to AI-First Work

Recent work traces how GenAI is reshaping the path into technical work. From interviews with eight Korean engineering and computer science students and recent graduates and six senior software engineers, Yu and Moon describe a process they call Absorption, in which GenAI redirects entry-level work into workflows shared by senior engineers and AI, and removes the productive struggle through which juniors once built expertise (Yu and Moon, 2026). Their juniors reported grades that stayed stable while learning diverged, and a curved grading system made opting out of AI costly. Research on knowledge work points to a related risk. Surveying 319 knowledge workers, Lee et al. found that those with more confidence in GenAI reported engaging in less critical thinking, particularly when tasks seemed trivial, when time was short or when they lacked the knowledge to evaluate the output, and they warn that skills left unpractised on routine tasks may deteriorate (Lee et al., 2025).

Hiring is changing too. Surveying 448 computer science students at three Philadelphia universities, Armstrong and Metaxa found that students saw automated screening as less fair than human review, and that only referrals and family household income predicted job offers, whereas more egalitarian strategies such as free coding-assessment practice did not (Armstrong and Metaxa, 2025). In India, the route into technical work runs largely through campus placements, which institutions organise but in which each recruiting company screens candidates in its own way (Table 1).

Signaling theory offers a way to read such gates. Spence modelled hiring as a decision under uncertainty, in which employers cannot observe a candidate’s productivity and instead infer it from observable signals such as education, which candidates choose to acquire at a cost (Spence, 1973). A signal separates candidates only if it is costlier to acquire for those who are less productive, and employers’ beliefs about what it indicates are sustained only as long as hiring outcomes confirm them. CGPA cut-offs and standardised placement tests operate as signals of this kind, applied at scale to cohorts that recruiters cannot assess individually. We ask what happens to these signals when AI can help students produce them.

## 2.2. Students and GenAI in India and the Global South

The closest prior work studied the same population shortly after ChatGPT’s release. Budhiraja et al. surveyed 480 computer science undergraduates at three Indian institutes and interviewed 17 students from eight universities (Budhiraja et al., 2024). Students used ChatGPT for information gathering, summarising and coding, but most worried about incorrect output and their inability to verify it. In a preprint from the same group, Joshi et al. extended this work to 1,306 survey responses and interviews with 112 students and 27 instructors at three Indian universities (Joshi et al., 2023). Some of their instructors had already withdrawn open-book assessments and expected closed-book examinations to remain important, and the instructors were divided on whether using ChatGPT to prepare teaching material was legitimate. Both studies date from 2023 and centre on usage, perceived benefits and challenges, and how the tools could be improved.

Beyond India, research on AI in Global South education has focused largely on school-age learners. Verma et al.’s review of 18 studies of child–computer interaction with AI-based educational tools in the Global South, in which India accounted for the largest share, identifies limited access to technology and models trained mainly in English among the main challenges (Verma et al., 2025). In an experiment with 118 participants from India and the United States, Agarwal et al. found that AI writing suggestions gave Indian participants smaller efficiency gains and moved their writing toward Western styles (Agarwal et al., 2025). Sebastian et al.’s design workshops with students in Finland and India attribute differences in how students oriented to AI to the pedagogical ecologies of their schools more than to national cultures (Sebastian et al., 2026). We adopt the same emphasis and attend to institutions instead of an essentialised “Indian culture.” Following Cao et al., who argue for building AI literacy education on what learners already bring instead of on what they lack (Cao et al., 2025), we also attend to the strategies participants developed without institutional guidance.

## 2.3. Assessment, Enforcement and Reliance

Assessment research offers a lens on how institutions respond to GenAI. Corbin et al. distinguish discursive changes to assessment, such as rules and declarations about permitted AI use, from structural changes to the task itself, such as supervised work and interactive oral assessment (Corbin et al., 2025). Because AI detection is unreliable, they argue, frameworks that rely on discursive rules create only an illusion of enforcement. In a small Swedish study of a course that paired an AI-permitted take-home examination with a viva, Lindkvist et al. found that, for the two students who chose not to use GenAI, the viva worked as a check that kept their own understanding in view (Lindkvist et al., 2026).

Where rules exist, students navigate them strategically. Adnin et al. document how U.S. students conceal GenAI use by paraphrasing output or adjusting tone, and calibrate this effort to each instructor’s perceived strictness (Adnin et al., 2025). Concealment also complicates measurement. Ling et al. found that about 60% of the undergraduates they surveyed reported using AI themselves while nearly 90% said their peers did, a gap students attributed to embarrassment (Ling et al., 2026), which informed our decision to ask participants about their peers as well as themselves. Where AI use is permitted, students decide where in a task to involve it, and Bodei et al. found that most students in a UK programme that permitted and taught AI use involved it in only one or two of five writing stages (Bodei et al., 2026).

GenAI is also changing whom students ask for help and how much they rely on it. Hou et al. found that help-seeking among North American computing students had become AI-mediated, with some reporting isolation and shame about using AI in front of peers (Hou et al., 2025), and Henderson et al. found that Australian students trusted teacher feedback far more than GenAI feedback but saw GenAI as less risky to approach (Henderson et al., 2026). Reliance research suggests that novices are poorly placed to notice when AI is wrong. Bo et al. found that most undergraduates in their experiment did not notice a chatbot’s sycophancy (Bo et al., 2026), and Ma et al. found that prior experience remained a significant predictor of success in a data-science course when students had ample time, even with LLM assistance (Ma et al., 2026). Ammari et al. propose repair literacy, the competencies students develop to diagnose and recover from AI failures, as a form of literacy learned through use (Ammari et al., 2026).

## 2.4. Research Gap

Research on how GenAI is changing the move into technical work comes mostly from the United States and Korea, and research on assessment, disclosure and help-seeking mostly from settings where AI use was permitted or taught (Bodei et al., 2026; Lindkvist et al., 2026). Existing studies of Indian engineering students date from 2023, focus on the tools and do not examine placements (Budhiraja et al., 2024; Joshi et al., 2023). No prior study follows students through an exam-oriented system with steep faculty hierarchies and little stated policy, past placement screens that largely exclude AI, and into workplaces that expect it. We address this gap through interviews with students and recent graduates whose education spanned the arrival of GenAI.

## 3. Methods

## 3.1. Participants and Recruitment

This study uses a qualitative design, with semi-structured interviews as the primary method of data collection, because our questions concern how participants experienced and reasoned about AI use, which requires interpretive depth more than numerical breadth. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling, supplemented by snowball sampling through participant referrals. Participants were required to be 1) current students, or 2026 graduates, of undergraduate or integrated engineering or computing programmes at Indian colleges or universities, 2) current or past users of AI tools in their academic work, and 3) a
limitations:
Our sample (Section 3.1) limits how far these findings travel. Students at less-resourced institutions, at rural colleges and in regional-language-medium programmes were not represented, and the inequalities we observed may be sharper there. With only two women in the sample, our findings largely reflect men’s experiences. Graduates’ accounts of college were retrospective and may have been shaped by their later work, and all accounts were self-reported, so participants may have under- or over-stated their own AI use. Some nuance may have been lost in translating the Tamil–English interviews. Finally, we did not interview faculty, administrators, recruiters or managers, so their positions appear here only through students’ perceptions, at a time when tools, offers and policies were changing rapidly.

Several directions follow. Interviews with recruiters and hiring managers would show how employers interpret CGPA and screen scores now that candidates prepare with AI, and whether the weakening of signals we infer from students’ accounts is visible from the other side of the gate. Longitudinal work following the cohort that entered college with AI already present would show how their concerns about readiness develop as they reach placements and work. Larger-scale surveys could test whether the patterns identified here hold across institution tiers, regions and disciplines, and intervention studies could evaluate the assessment and placement designs participants proposed, such as AI-permitted build tasks paired with oral explanation.
conclusion:
We first return to our research questions. For RQ1, participants saw themselves heading into workplaces that expected AI-first work, and they prepared for that transition mainly through their own, AI-coached placement preparation and learning they pursued outside the assessed curriculum, while worrying that dependence and weak ownership of AI-assisted work would leave them unready. For RQ2, they used AI to clear coursework and examinations that rewarded reproducible answers, to learn where teaching fell short and to prepare for placement screens that mostly excluded it. For RQ3, institutions shaped this use mostly through what they assessed, not through policy, which no participant could point to, and also through professors whose positions on AI often went unstated, through detection and through access left to company promotions.

Across the five themes, a single pattern recurs. The gates participants passed through, from semester examinations to placement screens, were built before generative AI and still largely assumed its absence, while the work beyond them assumed its presence. We discuss three consequences of this mismatch. We argue 1) that AI-assisted clearing weakens what grades and screen scores signal, 2) that AI-free gates leave both students and employers without a shared account of what readiness for AI-first work requires, and 3) that in the space between them, readiness becomes a burden students carry on their own. We then turn to implications for employers, institutions and tool designers.

title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. Models such as ELF now report autoregressive-level quality at a fraction of the sampling steps of discrete-token diffusion models, and this design principle -- no step-wise discretization -- is what their own ablations credit for the gain. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. Across three ELF scales and on LangFlow, an independent continuous dLLM, GRAFT restores the rare-word share of generated text from 0.42-0.77x the human rate to 0.82-1.10x, a relative gain of 34-109%, and moves the entire word-frequency profile closer to human on every model tested, by 2.7x on ELF-B and 12x on LangFlow.
